star-tv-cable-boom-india-1991.summary: During 1991 Gulf War, small operators in Bombay and Delhi string coaxial cable from rooftop dishes to deliver CNN, and when Hutchison's Star TV begins beaming five channels over Asia from AsiaSat-1 that year, these operators relay them too. Zee TV launches Hindi programming in October 1992. Cable homes grow from about 412,000 in January 1992 to 1.2 million by November 1992, and tens of thousands of neighbourhood cable businesses appear without any licence. Parliament regularises them through Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act 1995. Star and Zee reshaped Doordarshan's monopoly and news. Private satellite television becomes India's main medium within a decade.

star-tv-cable-boom-india-1991.detail: TRAI's 2021 consultation paper gives Gulf War demand, 1991 liberalisation, Star and Zee, and 1995 Act. Its count of 412,000 to 1.2 million homes in 1992 comes from a Frank Small study.

start-i-treaty-1991.summary: In July 1991 Bush and Gorbachev signed START I, limiting each side to 6,000 accountable warheads on 1,600 deployed ICBMs, submarine launched missiles and bombers; it entered into force on 5 December 1994 and expired on 5 December 2009. Ronald Reagan had proposed deep cuts in 1982, but pre-Gorbachev Soviet leaders treated US terms as nonnegotiable and his 1983 Strategic Defense Initiative stalled talks.

sources.title: START I (Wikipedia)

Treaty between the United States of America and the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics on the Reduction and Limitation of Strategic Offensive Arms (START), signed in Moscow 31 July 1991, U.S. Department of State
sources.author: United States and USSR
sources.confirms: The treaty text, signed in Moscow on 31 July 1991, with its limits of 1,600 deployed delivery vehicles and 6,000 accountable warheads.

sources.title: 'Strategic Arms Reduction Talks', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: START I was signed in July 1991 by Bush and Gorbachev and reduced each side to 6,000 warheads on at most 1,600 delivery vehicles.

start-i-treaty-1991.detail:
Reagan announced dramatic reductions in strategic forces in a commencement address at Eureka College on 9 May 1982 and presented them in Geneva on 29 June 1982. His plan had two phases: warhead counts cut to 5,000 with 2,500 on ICBMs and 850 ICBMs allowed, including 110 heavy missiles such as the SS-18, then similar limits on heavy bombers and other systems. In January 1985 George Shultz and Andrei Gromyko agreed a three-part negotiating formula covering intermediate-range forces, strategic defence and missile defence. The treaty was renamed START I once START II talks began, and after the Soviet collapse the 1992 Lisbon Protocol bound Russia, Belarus, Ukraine and Kazakhstan to its terms.

Implementation sent 375 B-52 bombers to Davis-Monthan Air Force Base in Arizona, where they were stripped of usable parts and chopped into five pieces by a 13,000-pound steel blade dropped from a crane. Verification cost estimates ranged widely; IDA put them near $760 million, and the Nunn-Lugar Cooperative Threat Reduction Program added $591 million for former Soviet republics. New START, signed in Prague on 8 April 2010, entered into force on 5 February 2011 and expired on 5 February 2026.

picture.alt: George H. W. Bush and Mikhail Gorbachev sign START treaty at Kremlin in Moscow on 31 July 1991.
picture.credit: Susan Biddle, White House, US National Archives (NAID 186435), Public domain, via US National Archives (mirrored on Wikimedia Commons)

terminator-2-film-1991.summary: In July 1991 Terminator 2 made Skynet the name for a machine that turns on humanity. James Cameron directed and co-wrote this sequel to 1984’s The Terminator, in which malevolent artificial intelligence Skynet sends its T-1000, a shape-shifting liquid-metal prototype, back to 1995 to kill young John Connor, future leader of humanity’s resistance, which sends a reprogrammed T-800 (Arnold Schwarzenegger) to protect him. Costing an estimated $94 to $102 million, it featured cinema’s first computer-generated main character in a blockbuster, grossed $519 to $520.9 million, and won four Academy Awards.

sources.title: Terminator 2: Judgment Day - Wikipedia
Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'History of film: United States, transition to the 21st century'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: After Tron (1982), computer-generated imagery advanced through films of the late 1980s and early 1990s including Terminator 2.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Terminator 2: Judgment Day'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Cameron's 1991 film, after which he co-founded the effects company Digital Domain in 1993.

sources.title: Prince, S., 'True Lies: Perceptual Realism, Digital Images, and Film Theory', Film Quarterly 49, no. 3 (1996) 27-37
sources.author: Prince, Stephen
sources.confirms: Names the shape-shifting Terminator 2 (1991) alongside Jurassic Park and Forrest Gump as the high-profile successes that demonstrated the possibilities of computer-generated imagery.

terminator-2-film-1991.detail:
Its budget made it the most expensive film made to that point, and its gross made it 1991’s highest-grossing film worldwide; it also won two BAFTAs. Linda Hamilton returned as Sarah Connor, confined at Pescadero State Hospital after violent efforts to prevent Judgment Day, 29 August 1997, when Skynet becomes self-aware and starts nuclear war. Robert Patrick played the T-1000 and Edward Furlong John Connor. Sequel work had stalled for years over animosity between Cameron, Schwarzenegger and Hemdale Film Corporation, which partly owned its rights.

Industrial Light & Magic’s effects caused a schedule overrun, and theatrical prints reached cinemas only one night before release. The Library of Congress added it to its National Film Registry in 2023, and sequels followed from Terminator 3 in 2003 despite Cameron’s intention to end his story.

thailand-100-percent-condom-1991.summary: Piloted in Ratchaburi province in 1989 by Wiwat Rojanapithayakorn, this programme enlisted provincial governors, police and brothel owners to enforce condom use in every commercial sex act, backed by free condom distribution, tracing of infections back to establishments and Mechai Viravaidya's mass media campaign. Cabinet made it national in 1991. Reported condom use in sex work rose from about 14 percent in 1989 to over 90 percent by 1992, male sexually transmitted infections at government clinics fell by more than three quarters, and new HIV infections among conscripts dropped sharply through 1990s. UNAIDS cited it as a model, and Cambodia and other countries adopted versions.

sources.title: Rojanapithayakorn, Wiwat and Robert Hanenberg, 'The 100% condom program in Thailand', AIDS 10 (1996)
sources.author: Rojanapithayakorn, Wiwat; Hanenberg, Robert
sources.confirms: Programme design, 1989 pilot and 1991 national adoption

sources.title: Hanenberg, Robert S. et al., 'Impact of Thailand's HIV-control programme as indicated by the decline of sexually transmitted diseases', Lancet 344 (1994)
sources.author: Hanenberg, Robert S.; Rojanapithayakorn, Wiwat; Kunasol, Prayura; Sokal, David C.
sources.confirms: Condom use rise and STI decline 1989-1993

thailand-100-percent-condom-1991.verification_note: Percentages follow PubMed-indexed articles as cited in later reviews.
thailand-100-percent-condom-1991.detail: Analysis in 1994 linked STI decline to programme, and Rojanapithayakorn co-wrote a 1996 review of its design. Critics noted limited reach to indirect and street-based sex work and to injecting drug users.

www-public-1991.summary: On 6 August 1991 Tim Berners-Lee posted the World Wide Web to a public newsgroup: the web was open to anyone. Web software had reached a limited CERN audience in March 1991 and general CERN release in May, so his post recruited volunteers for a working system. Unlike earlier hypertext systems, his Web required only one-way links, so anyone could link to a page without its owner’s action, which made servers and browsers easier to write. Fifty servers existed by January 1993 and more than 500 by October 1993.

sources.title: History of the World Wide Web
Berners-Lee, Tim, 'WorldWideWeb: Summary', message to alt.hypertext, 6 August 1991, archived by W3C
sources.author: Berners-Lee, Tim
sources.confirms: Berners-Lee's newsgroup post of 6 August 1991 describes the WorldWideWeb project, its NeXT editor, line-mode browser and server, and invites collaborators.

sources.title: CERN, 'A short history of the Web', home.cern
sources.author: CERN
sources.confirms: Berners-Lee released the WWW software to colleagues on specific CERN computers in March 1991 and announced it on Internet newsgroups in August 1991; the first US server came online at SLAC in December 1991 and over 500 servers existed by late 1993.
sources.qualifies: Dates the first servers outside Europe to December 1991.

sources.title: Berners-Lee, Tim, 'WWW Project History' (History to date), CERN, info.cern.ch
sources.author: Tim Berners-Lee
sources.confirms: The project log records the line mode browser released to a limited audience in March 1991, general release on central CERN machines on 17 May 1991, and files posted to alt.hypertext on 6, 16 and 19 August 1991.

www-public-1991.verification_note: W3C file art-6487.txt carries Berners-Lee's 6 August 1991 alt.hypertext summary (art-6484.txt is his reply promising it); CERN's history has software reaching a limited CERN audience in March 1991, general CERN release in May, first servers in European physics laboratories and a first server outside Europe at SLAC in December 1991.
www-public-1991.detail:
Paul Kunz of Stanford Linear Accelerator Center visited CERN in September 1991 and took Berners-Lee’s NeXT software home. There, librarian Louise Addis adapted it for SLAC’s IBM mainframe to host its SPIRES-HEP database, North America’s first web server, running by December 1991. One-way linking also brought link rot, pages pointing at documents that have moved or vanished.

CERN placed its Web software in the public domain on 30 April 1993, after the University of Minnesota announced licensing fees for its rival Gopher system. NCSA released Mosaic for Unix in February 1993 and for Macintosh and Windows in August 1993.

att-vrcp-speech-1992.summary: In 1992 AT&T began routing telephone calls by voice, matching callers' spoken requests to stored word patterns with no operator. Callers spoke their request aloud, and software matched those sounds against stored word patterns to choose what an operator would have chosen. Lawrence Rabiner's group at Bell Labs developed it.

sources.title: Automatic speech recognition
The way we were: Speech technology, platforms and applications in the 'Old' AT&T
sources.author: Perdue, Robert J.
sources.confirms: AT&T's Voice Recognition Call Processing used speaker-independent recognition of a few spoken words to route calls without an operator.
sources.qualifies: Does not fix the 1992 launch date.

sources.title: Los Angeles Times, 'AT&T Will Cut Up to a Third of Its Operators', 4 March 1992
sources.author: Los Angeles Times
sources.confirms: On 3 March 1992 AT&T said it would replace 3,000 to 6,000 operators by December 1994 with a voice recognition system, tested in Dallas-Fort Worth in 1991, that prompts callers to say collect and lets them say operator to reach a person.
sources.qualifies: A human operator remained available at any time.

sources.title: Perry, Tekla S., 'Sultan of Sound', IEEE Spectrum (2005)
sources.author: Tekla S. Perry
sources.confirms: Bell Labs' decades of speech recognition work under James Flanagan bore fruit in 1992 when Voice Recognition Call Processing was put into the AT&T telephone network.

att-vrcp-speech-1992.verification_note: Perdue's history in Speech Communication confirms AT&T's Voice Recognition Call Processing and its small routing vocabulary, with its 1992 national rollout resting on other accounts. Sources frame it narrowly: its system recognised a handful of words such as collect, calling card and operator by word spotting to replace 3,000 to 6,000 operators, a human operator remained available on request, so calls were classified by spoken request, and Los Angeles Times credits Jay Wilpon of Bell Labs with a key role alongside Rabiner's group.
att-vrcp-speech-1992.detail: That same year Xuedong Huang’s Sphinx-II system at Carnegie Mellon won DARPA’s 1992 evaluation. Sphinx-II was the first system to recognise continuous, large-vocabulary speech from any speaker; earlier systems needed pauses between words or training on each voice. Dragon Dictate, a consumer dictation product, had been released in 1990.

falcon-fraud-detection-1992.summary: In 1992 a neural network called Falcon began flagging fraudulent credit card transactions; most card payments are now screened this way. Counterfeit cards were then banks’ main problem, and transactions could only be reviewed after the fact. Falcon learned each cardholder’s normal spending from past transactions and scored every new one by how far it departed from that pattern, so banks could stop suspicious purchases while they were being made. FICO credits it with a dramatic reduction in payment-card fraud losses.

sources.title: Explainable AI in Fraud Detection - A Back to the Future Story
Evolution of Fraud Analytics – An Inside Story

falcon-fraud-detection-1992.detail:
HNC Software built Falcon; Scott Zoldi of FICO, which later owned it, writes that payment fraud prevention’s modern age began with its 1992 introduction. Transaction profiling, keeping a running summary of each card’s behaviour, arrived in 1992 and neural-network scoring models in 1993. Zoldi puts US card fraud at roughly 18 basis points of spending in 1992, falling to about 5 in later years.

In 1996 Falcon’s team filed a patent for Reason Reporter, which explained why a transaction scored high, an early form of what is now called explainable AI.

fifth-generation-end-1992.summary: In 1992 Japan's Fifth Generation project fizzled to a close after ¥54 billion, over $400 million by a June 1992 report; the logic machines it had promised never came, and AI funding froze. It aimed at an “epoch-making computer” built on massively parallel hardware and logic programming, in which a machine derives answers from stated facts and rules instead of following step-by-step instructions. It produced parallel inference machines and the KL1 language, but no commercial product; the hardware was overtaken in speed by less specialised machines such as Sun workstations and Intel x86 PCs.

sources.title: Start of the 5th Generation Computer Project for Knowledge ...
Fifth Generation Computer Systems
Pollack, Andrew, ''Fifth Generation' Became Japan's Lost Generation', New York Times (1992)
sources.author: Pollack, Andrew
sources.confirms: The page says the 10-year Fifth Generation effort was fizzling to a close after more than $400 million in spending and had failed to meet many ambitious goals.
sources.qualifies: The report dates to June 5, 1992, describes the project as fizzling to a close rather than explicitly saying it closed, and reports spending of more than $400 million rather than ¥54 billion.

fifth-generation-end-1992.verification_note: A 5 June 1992 report describes this project fizzling to a close with spending of more than $400 million; IPSJ's museum gives about ¥54 billion over 11 years.
fifth-generation-end-1992.detail:
Japan’s Institute for New Generation Computer Technology (ICOT) ran it. Its PIM/p machine had 512 processors and PIM/m 256; there were five PIM models (m, p, i, k, c), and applications included Kappa, a database system, HELIC-II, a legal reasoning system, and MGTP, a theorem prover. KL1 grew from Kazunori Ueda’s Guarded Horn Clauses.

Japan’s announcement alarmed Western governments and spurred America’s Strategic Computing Initiative and MCC, Britain’s Alvey programme and Europe’s ESPRIT. Afterwards MITI stopped funding large-scale computer research. Accounts differ: IPSJ’s museum puts spending at about ¥54 billion over 11 years ending 1992; others give 1982 to 1994 and a little under ¥57 billion (about US$320 million), probably counting a follow-on phase. Surviving PIM machines are preserved at Tokyo’s National Science Museum.

first-sms-1992.summary: In December 1992 an engineer sent the first text message, Merry Christmas, from a computer to a phone. Richard Jarvis of Vodafone received it on his Orbitel 901 handset over Vodafone’s GSM network in Britain. Friedhelm Hillebrand and Bernard Ghillebaert had specified SMS in 1984 so that short text could travel over signalling channels, spare capacity used to set up calls, which fixed its length at 160 seven-bit characters. Handsets of 1992 could not compose messages, hence the computer.

sources.title: SMS - Wikipedia
BBC World Service, "Texting turns 20" (Words in the News, 3 December 2012)
sources.author: BBC World Service
sources.confirms: Reports that on 3 December 1992 an engineer sent the message 'Merry Christmas' from a computer to a mobile phone over Vodafone's UK network.

sources.title: BBC Mundo, "Aniversario del SMS: como se logro enviar el primer mensaje de texto de la historia hace 25 anos" (3 December 2017)
sources.author: BBC News Mundo
sources.confirms: Anniversary report confirming the first text message was sent on 3 December 1992.

first-sms-1992.detail:
SMS grew from Franco-German GSM cooperation in 1984; its limit was first 128 bytes, later 160 seven-bit characters. Aldiscon built Sweden’s first commercial SMS centre with Logica for Telia in 1993, and Nokia was then alone among handset makers in supporting sending on its 1993 GSM line; its Nokia 2010 of January 1994 was the first phone on which composing messages was easy.

Traffic reached 366 billion messages in 2002 and 6.1 trillion in 2010, when SMS earned operators about US$114.6 billion.

nollywood-living-in-bondage-1992.summary: In 1992 Living in Bondage sold hundreds of thousands of videocassettes in Nigeria; Nollywood became one of the largest film industries. Chris Obi Rapu directed it and Kenneth Nnebue and Okechukwu Ogunjiofor wrote it. Ogunjiofor had his script but no money, so he partnered with Nnebue, a businessman who imported blank VHS tapes from Taiwan; they shot on a VHS camcorder and sold cassettes, bypassing cinemas. Its success encouraged other filmmakers to shoot straight to video, starting Nigeria’s low-budget video industry, later called Nollywood.

sources.title: Living in Bondage - Wikipedia
Living in Bondage (1992) | Nollywood
Nollywood: No longer living in bondage
J. Haynes, Nollywood: The Creation of Nigerian Film Genres (University of Chicago Press, 2016), ch. 1, 'Creating Nollywood: Conditions and Foundations', pp. 3-17
sources.author: Jonathan Haynes
sources.confirms: Identifies Living in Bondage (1992) as the inaugural Nollywood film, released amid a crisis in Nigeria's audiovisual sector.

nollywood-living-in-bondage-1992.detail:
Jafac Wine sponsored it, Ogunjiofor produced it, and Kenneth Okonkwo and Nnenna Nwabueze made their breakout appearances. Andy Okeke, worn down by unemployment and comparison with richer friends, joins a cult that promises wealth in return for sacrificing his wife Merit; he grows rich and is then haunted by her ghost. Part two followed in 1993, directed by Chika Christian Onu, and a sequel, Living in Bondage: Breaking Free, premiered in Lagos on 2 November 2019.

Nollywood.com lists its language as English and running time as 2 hours 43 minutes. Sales figures vary by account and are omitted here.

postman-technopoly-1992.summary: In 1992 Neil Postman's Technopoly argued that America had surrendered culture to technology; the book is reread with each new device. Postman argues that cultures pass through three stages: tool-using cultures, where tools serve existing beliefs; technocracies, from the nineteenth century, where tools begin to “attack the culture”; and technopoly, where culture “seeks its authorisation in technology, finds its satisfactions in technology, and takes its orders from technology.” He calls America the first technopoly, a society in which efficiency and measurement replace any shared sense of purpose.

sources.title: TECHNOPOLY
Technopoly - Wikipedia
Llorente, Renzo, 'Neil Postman', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.author: Llorente, Renzo
sources.confirms: Records that in Technopoly: The Surrender of Culture to Technology (1992) Postman criticised the deification of technology, under which social institutions surrender their sovereignty to it.

postman-technopoly-1992.detail:
Postman’s examples include bureaucracy, scientific management, opinion polls, IQ testing, schooling, television and computer culture. Kirkus Reviews called his 224-page book “amusing, learned, and prickling with intelligence” and summarised its thesis as America having become “the world’s first ‘totalitarian technocracy,’” quoting his line that in a technopoly “there can be no transcendent sense of purpose or meaning, no cultural coherence.”

Postman traces our impulse to invent to Francis Bacon, draws on Jacques Ellul, and describes information surplus, data no longer answering to any purpose.

saudi-desert-wheat-peak-1992.summary: Paying farmers up to 3,500 riyals a tonne, about five times the world price, with free land, subsidized credit and center-pivot irrigation on fossil groundwater, Saudi Arabia raises wheat output from about 3,000 tonnes in the 1970s to a peak of 4.1 million tonnes in 1992 and exports surplus. By one 2020 estimate agriculture drew around 85 percent of Saudi Arabia's roughly 23 billion cubic meters a year of water, mostly from non-renewable aquifers, depleting them. Riyadh announces in 2008 that it will cut wheat purchases 12.5 percent a year and end domestic production by 2016, shifting to imports and overseas farmland.

sources.title: Siderius, C., Conway, D., Yassine, M., Murken, L., Lostis, P.-L. and Dalin, C., 'Multi-scale analysis of the water-energy-food nexus in the Gulf region', Environmental Research Letters 15 (2020), 094024
sources.author: Siderius, Christian; Conway, Declan; Yassine, Mohamed; Murken, Lisa; Lostis, Pierre-Louis; Dalin, Carole
sources.confirms: Documents fossil groundwater overexploitation for Saudi wheat, about 23 billion cubic metres a year of water use with 85 percent in irrigation, and the policy shift away from self-sufficiency.
sources.qualifies: Dates the shift away from self-sufficiency to around 2006, before the 2008 phase-out announcement.

sources.title: Alrwis, K. N. et al., 'Measuring the impact of water scarcity on agricultural economic development in Saudi Arabia', Saudi Journal of Biological Sciences 28 (2021), 191-195
sources.author: Alrwis, Khalid N.; Ghanem, Abdulaziz M.; Alnashwan, Othman S.; Al Duwais, Abdulaziz A. M.; Alaagib, Sahar A. B.; Aldawdahi, Nageeb M.
sources.confirms: Documents groundwater depletion and agriculture's roughly 84 percent share of Saudi water use.

sources.title: USDA Foreign Agricultural Service, GAIN report 'Saudi Arabia: Grain and Feed Annual' (Riyadh, 2011)
sources.author: USDA Foreign Agricultural Service
sources.confirms: Gives 2008 decision to cut wheat procurement 12.5 percent a year and end production by 2016, and past peak output.

saudi-desert-wheat-peak-1992.detail: Policy dates from the 1973 oil embargo, which raised fears of a food boycott. Procurement price fell to 2,000 riyals in 1985 and 1,500 in the 1990s as costs mounted. One 2020 study dates its shift away from self-sufficiency to around 2006. Wheat growing resumed at small scale from 2018 for food security; Saudi firms meanwhile bought farmland in Sudan, Ethiopia, Argentina and Arizona. Another, from 2021, puts agriculture at about 84 percent of national water use.

snow-crash-metaverse-1992.summary: In 1992 Stephenson's Snow Crash coined metaverse for a shared virtual world with avatars; Facebook took the name when it became Meta in October 2021. In Stephenson’s future the global economy has collapsed and corporations hold most former government power, so people escape into a shared digital world, wearing goggles and earphones and appearing as avatars on one street tens of thousands of miles long. Its hero, Hiro Protagonist, is a broke hacker and pizza-delivery driver.

sources.title: How the 1992 sci-fi novel 'Snow Crash' predicted Facebook's ...
Neal Stephenson | American author
Dionisio, John David N., William G. Burns III and Richard Gilbert, "3D Virtual Worlds and the Metaverse: Current Status and Future Possibilities"
sources.author: John David N. Dionisio, William G. Burns III, Richard Gilbert
sources.confirms: Peer-reviewed survey that traces the term metaverse to Stephenson's 1992 novel and describes its avatars and shared virtual world.

snow-crash-metaverse-1992.detail: Stephenson’s metaverse includes an encrypted electronic currency and money spent on virtual property. Users entering through cheap public terminals are looked down on, and one virus damages users’ brains outside its simulation. Asked about the novel, Mark Zuckerberg told The Verge that “the book has this whole environment around [metaverses] that’s sort of negative. But I don’t think it has to be that way,” CNBC reported, adding that Stephenson told Axios he had “never had any communication with Zuckerberg.” Britannica describes its characters enjoying themselves as digital avatars as escape from grim 21st-century reality.

tapestry-collaborative-filtering-1992.summary: In December 1992 Xerox PARC's Tapestry filtered email using other readers' annotations and coined collaborative filtering. Growing use of electronic mail was leaving users “inundated by a huge stream of incoming documents,” and mailing lists rarely matched any one person’s interests. Tapestry let readers record reactions to documents they read, and other people’s filters could then act on those annotations, selecting messages that colleagues had found interesting or discarding what they had marked as not. Their paper named this approach “collaborative filtering,” the idea behind later recommendation systems.

sources.title: Using collaborative filtering to weave an information tapestry
Resnick, Paul, and Hal R. Varian. 'Recommender Systems.' Communications of the ACM 40, no. 3 (1997): 56-58.
sources.author: Paul Resnick; Hal R. Varian
sources.confirms: Field-defining introduction that traces the term collaborative filtering to the Tapestry paper of Goldberg, Nichols, Oki and Terry (1992).

tapestry-collaborative-filtering-1992.detail: David Goldberg, David Nichols and Douglas Terry of Xerox PARC wrote that paper with Brian Oki of Teknekron Systems. They stated “a basic tenet of the Tapestry work is that more effective filtering can be done by involving humans in the filtering process,” and counted implicit signals such as replying to a message as usable annotations. Tapestry also stored past mail so that one query language served both searches of its archive and filters on new arrivals, and it was designed for any incoming stream of documents, including newswire stories and NetNews articles.

td-gammon-1992.summary: In 1992 Tesauro's TD-Gammon learned backgammon from a million games against its own copy and matched the best humans. It played 38 exhibition games at a total of −7 points, about −0.18 points per game. Developed at IBM’s Thomas J. Watson Research Center, it was a neural network that nudged its estimate of each position’s winning chances toward whatever estimate it reached one move later, a method called temporal-difference learning. By 1993 version 2.1, trained on 1.5 million games, played just below top humans.

sources.title: TD-Gammon
Tesauro, Gerald, 'TD-Gammon, a Self-Teaching Backgammon Program, Achieves Master-Level Play', Neural Computation 6 (1994) 215-219
sources.author: Tesauro, Gerald
sources.confirms: TD-Gammon 2.0 and 2.1, trained by temporal-difference self-play, reached near world-class backgammon strength.

sources.title: Tesauro, Gerald, 'Temporal Difference Learning and TD-Gammon', Communications of the ACM 38 (1995) 58-68
sources.author: Tesauro, Gerald
sources.confirms: Overview of TD-Gammon's versions from 1.0 (1991 to 1992) to 2.1.

td-gammon-1992.detail:
Earlier, in late 1991, version 1.0 lost 51 games against Bill Robertie, Paul Magriel and Malcolm Davis at −0.25 points per game. Its final network took 198 inputs encoding expert-designed features, 80 hidden units and a single output, predicted probability of winning, and stopped improving after about 1.5 million self-play games. Versions 2.0 and 2.1 looked two moves ahead (2-ply search).

Because it learned only from self-play, TD-Gammon tried strategies humans had ruled out; expert Kit Woolsey praised its positional judgement, and its unorthodox opening assessments were adopted by top players. In 1998 it lost a 100-game series to the world champion by eight points. The papers introducing deep Q-learning and AlphaGo cite it.

apple-newton-1993.summary: In August 1993 Apple sold the Newton, a handheld that read handwriting badly; it failed, but the tablet idea waited inside it. Newton was Apple’s personal digital assistant, a handheld computer for notes, contacts and calendars controlled with a stylus; Apple’s chief executive John Sculley coined “personal digital assistant” for it. Its handwriting-recognition software, its most anticipated feature, was not ready by 1993 and often misread characters, drawing widespread media ridicule, and its high price hurt too. Apple sold Newtons until 1998, when Steve Jobs ended them.

sources.title: Apple Newton - Wikipedia
'Apple Reports Strong Early Newton Sales', United Press International, 2 September 1993
sources.author: United Press International
sources.confirms: The Newton MessagePad went on sale in early August 1993.

sources.title: Lewis, Peter H., 'The Executive Computer; So Far, the Newton Experience Is Less Than Fulfilling', New York Times, 26 September 1993
sources.author: Peter H. Lewis
sources.confirms: Apple's stylus-driven MessagePad launched in August 1993 from $699, sold over 10,000 units in its first weeks, and its handwriting recognition drew ridicule and remained slow even after training.

sources.title: Computer History Museum, 'Apple History in Prototypes' (CHM blog)
sources.author: Computer History Museum
sources.confirms: Sculley preannounced the Newton in January 1992, release slipped to August 1993, its handwriting recognition barely worked and was lampooned in Doonesbury, and Sculley coined the term personal digital assistant for it.

apple-newton-1993.detail:
Sculley said Apple invested approximately $100 million in Newton development. In The Simpsons episode “Lisa on Ice,” Newton turns “Beat up Martin” into “Eat up Martha,” and Garry Trudeau mocked it for a week in Doonesbury. Handheld organisers existed from Psion’s Organiser of 1984; Newton was first to feature handwriting recognition, and, unlike with Macintosh, Apple licensed Newton OS to other makers.

On his return in 1997 Jobs criticised its performance, management and stylus, and with Apple losing money unprofitable Newton was cut; Apple later put its Print Recognizer handwriting engine into Mac OS X 10.2.

bangladesh-arsenic-wells-1993.summary: In 1993 Department of Public Health Engineering confirmed arsenic in shallow tube well water in Chapai Nawabganj, after cases across border in West Bengal since 1983. Since 1970s UNICEF and government had promoted millions of hand pumped tube wells to cut diarrhoeal deaths from pond water. Natural arsenic in Ganges delta sediments contaminated an estimated one quarter to one third of wells above 50 micrograms per litre, exposing 35 to 77 million people. WHO called it largest mass poisoning of a population in history. Responses included well testing and painting, deep wells, filters and rainwater harvesting; a 2012 study still attributed about one in twenty deaths in exposed areas to arsenic.

blue-led-1993.summary: In 1993 Nakamura made a bright blue LED, the colour that had defeated researchers for decades; white LED light and a Nobel Prize followed. Bright blue LEDs, needed to mix white light, had defeated researchers since RCA’s attempts in the 1960s because gallium nitride could not be made strongly p-type, meaning positively conducting, as diodes require. Nakamura found that hydrogen was blocking his dopant and worked out how to remove it, producing devices about 1,000 times brighter than earlier blue LEDs. In 2014 he shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with Isamu Akasaki and Hiroshi Amano.

blue-led-1993.detail:
Nakamura joined Nichia in 1979 after degrees at Tokushima University. Nichia’s founder Nobuo Ogawa funded his gallium-nitride work when most considered it too hard; after Eiji Ogawa took over in 1989 Nichia ordered him to stop, and he continued alone. He built on Isamu Akasaki’s group, which had made p-type gallium nitride by electron-beam irradiation of magnesium-doped material, and found a method suited to mass production. Blue light partly converted to yellow by phosphor coating yields white LED lighting, which entered production in 1993.

Nakamura later said he received ¥20,000 (about US$180) for his patent; he sued Nichia in 2001, Tokyo’s district court awarded ¥20 billion, and both sides settled in 2005 for ¥840 million (about US$8.1 million), then Japan’s largest such payment by any company to an employee. He has been professor at University of California, Santa Barbara since 1999.

check-point-firewall-1993.summary: In 1993 three Israelis founded Check Point and sold FireWall-1, which tracked each connection's state. Founder Shwed had worked on securing classified networks in Unit 8200 of Israel’s Defense Forces, kept his idea in mind afterwards, and developed FireWall-1's core technology, stateful inspection, in April 1993; its patent was filed on 15 December 1993. Firewalls decide which network traffic may pass; stateful ones track each connection as it runs, so they can admit replies belonging to sessions already allowed and reject packets belonging to none.

check-point-firewall-1993.detail: Initial funding of US$250,000 came from venture fund BRM Group. Soon after FireWall-1 its founders developed VPN-1, an early VPN product. Check Point signed an OEM agreement with Sun Microsystems in 1994 and a distribution agreement with HP in 1995; by February 1996 IDC named it worldwide firewall market leader with 40 percent share, and in June 1996 it raised $67 million in its Nasdaq initial public offering.

clipper-chip-1993.summary: In April 1993 Clinton's White House proposed its Clipper chip, encryption with a government-held key; backlash began the crypto wars. Each chip carried its own key, split between two government escrow agents; with wiretap authorisation, agencies could obtain both halves and decode intercepted calls. Electronic Frontier Foundation and Electronic Privacy Information Center opposed it over surveillance and because its Skipjack algorithm was classified, so nobody outside government could check its strength. Consumers and manufacturers did not adopt it; by 1996 it was defunct.

sources.title: Clipper chip - Wikipedia
Key Escrow Encryption Testimony by Raymond G. Kammer ...
SJ_opp.txt

clipper-chip-1993.detail:
NIST deputy director Raymond Kammer told the Senate Intelligence Committee that Skipjack used an 80-bit key and that “there is no trapdoor in the algorithm,” as he put it. His June 1993 testimony called Skipjack “approximately 16 million times stronger than DES” and said outside cryptographers including Dorothy Denning had been invited to review it. Clinton's Administration called Clipper a voluntary programme that “preserves the ability of federal, state and local law enforcement agencies to intercept lawfully the phone conversations of criminals,” in EPIC’s court filing.

In 1994 Matt Blaze showed that Clipper’s 128-bit Law Enforcement Access Field, which carried key material, was protected by only a 16-bit checksum, so users could forge it and defeat escrow while still encrypting. Critics also noted that foreign makers could not be compelled to use Clipper. Only one significant purchaser bought Clipper phones, America's Department of Justice, and strong cryptography such as PGP made later escrow incentives moot.

doom-1993.summary: In December 1993 id Software released Doom as shareware; its swift 3D engine and network play set the shape of first-person shooters. Players saw through a space marine’s eyes while fighting undead humans and demons from Mars’s moons into hell, rendered by John Carmack’s new engine, which drew 3D spaces with enemies as flat images. Giving away episode one of three marketed the rest; id uploaded it to a University of Wisconsin server that 10,000 people tried to reach at once. Doom sold an estimated 3.5 million copies by 1999.

doom-1993.detail:
Doom was id’s third major release after Commander Keen and Wolfenstein 3D. Work began in May 1992; Tom Hall’s science-fiction plot was mostly discarded, and John Romero and Sandy Petersen shaped its action design. Within hours universities were banning its multiplayer games, in which two to four players cooperated or fought “deathmatch” over local networks; online play arrived one year later through DWANGO. GT Interactive published a retail version with a fourth episode as The Ultimate Doom in 1995.

Up to 20 million people are estimated to have played Doom within two years, and imitators were called “Doom clones” before “first-person shooter” became the genre name. Doom was selected for the Library of Congress game canon in 2007 and its soundtrack for the National Recording Registry in 2026.

era-statistical.summary: From the 1990s AI turned from hand-written rules to statistics and probability, quietly powering spam filters, search and speech. After expert systems' bubble burst, it fragmented into subfields that treated reasoning as calculation under uncertainty, using Bayesian networks, hidden Markov models, support vector machines and boosting, and judged methods by measured performance on data rather than resemblance to human thought. Results reached products such as data mining, speech recognition and Google’s search engine without being labelled AI. Its 1993 start and 2012 end are bounded by the second AI winter and AlexNet.

sources.confirms: Reviews the shift of AI toward data-driven statistical learning methods that power speech recognition, search and spam filtering.

sources.title: The Quest for Artificial Intelligence: A History of Ideas and Achievements

era-statistical.verification_note: One source supports 1990s to 2000s trends and AlexNet’s 2012 breakthrough and says more than 300 AI companies had shut down, gone bankrupt or been acquired by 1993's end, without identifying a “Statistical machine learning” event or a 1993 to 2012 period. Oxford's “Statistical Machine Learning” lecture lists 1990s methods and cites “ImageNet: Computer Eyesight Gets a Lot More Accurate, Krizhevsky et al, 2012,” without naming AlexNet, a second winter, 1993's company count, or an emphasis on mathematical rigor, probabilistic methods, intelligent agents, narrow applications or behind-the-scenes work.
era-statistical.detail:
Judea Pearl’s 1988 book Probabilistic Reasoning in Intelligent Systems brought probability and decision theory into AI. An “intelligent agent” model, a system that perceives its environment and acts to maximise its chances of success, was assembled from decision theory and economics by Pearl, Allen Newell, Leslie Kaelbling and others. Many researchers called their work informatics, knowledge-based systems or computational intelligence, partly to escape AI’s tarnished name and win funding.

Oxford’s statistical machine learning lecture lists a statistical lineage this field absorbed: Bayes in 1763, Fisher’s maximum likelihood, Baum’s hidden Markov models in 1970, Dempster’s expectation maximisation in 1978, Vapnik’s VC dimension, Lauritzen and Pearl’s graphical models in 1990, then 1990s Kalman filtering, belief nets, SVMs, learning theory, boosting and kernels, with computer science and statistics “forced back together” by cheap data capture. Deep Blue beat Garry Kasparov on 11 May 1997.

eternal-september-1993.summary: In September 1993 commercial providers began delivering Usenet newcomers without pause and its etiquette never recovered, a change remembered as Eternal September. Usenet was the Internet’s network of discussion groups. Before 1993 its only sudden intake of newcomers came each September, when North American students got university accounts and had to learn its etiquette, and each tide receded as they adjusted or left. Once commercial providers sold home access with Usenet included, newcomers swamped those forums’ ability to enforce their norms.

sources.confirms: Eternal September is a notion from Usenet culture describing the permanent influx of newcomers after 1993.

sources.confirms: Netizens (1997) was published after the so-called Eternal September when AOL users flooded Usenet.

eternal-september-1993.detail: Its name is traced to David Fischer. In a joke call to action on alt.folklore.urban he referred to growing numbers of Delphi users as “Never-Ending-September,” and on 25 January 1994 in alt.folklore.computers he wrote, “It’s moot now. September 1993 will go down in net.history as the September that never ended.”

gilder-metcalfe-1993.summary: In 1993 George Gilder named Metcalfe's Law: a network's value grows with the square of its users. Metcalfe, who invented Ethernet at Xerox PARC in 1973 and founded 3Com in 1981, had argued on a slide around 1980 that network value grows as user numbers squared while cost grows in step with them, so networks pay off only after reaching critical mass. His reasoning: each of n members can connect to n−1 others, giving about n² possible connections. Gilder’s “Metcalfe’s Law and Legacy” spread his idea during the Internet boom.

sources.title: MEtcALfE'S
Metcalfe's Law
Metcalf's Law and Legacy - Discovery Institute

gilder-metcalfe-1993.detail:
Gilder extends Metcalfe’s law to “n” machines of any kind, computers, phones or cars. He argues that rising processing power at network edges and growing bandwidth favour simple distributed networks such as Ethernet over centralised switching, notes that Ethernet then linked more than half of the world’s 40 million networked computers, and observes that Metcalfe had turned to ATM, calling Ethernet a “legacy LAN,” against his own law. Gale’s encyclopedia records 3Com’s formulation, that “the economic value of a network increases like the square of the number of its nodes,” as its definition.

In 2006 Bob Briscoe, Andrew Odlyzko and Benjamin Tilly argued in IEEE Spectrum that that law overvalues networks because it treats every connection as equally useful; they proposed n log n instead, under which doubling a network worth $1 million yields $2.1 million rather than $4 million.

ibm-loss-1993.summary: In January 1993 IBM reported a $4.97 billion loss for 1992, then the largest in American corporate history, and a year later an $8.1 billion loss for 1993; the mainframe firm nearly died of the PC. Its difficulties were linked to personal computers and client-server computing: a decade of growing local area networking, led by Novell and others, let companies run work on linked PCs and small servers, and mainframe sales, IBM’s core business, declined. Losses had topped $1 billion in each of two prior years; from 1991 to 1993 IBM lost nearly $16 billion, and hundreds of thousands of employees lost their jobs, including CEO John Akers.

ibm-loss-1993.detail: IBM had reorganised in September 1992, spinning its PC businesses into IBM Personal Computer Company after a price war cut margins. In April 1993 IBM hired Louis V. Gerstner Jr., formerly of RJR Nabisco and American Express, its first outside chief executive since 1914. He recommitted to mainframes, sold IBM’s Federal Systems Division to Loral, cut staff to a low of 220,000 in 1994 and reversed plans to split IBM into separate companies; IBM returned a $3 billion profit in 1994.

information-superhighway-1993.summary: In February 1993 Clinton and Gore announced an information superhighway; that phrase sold the internet to voters before the web did. Their plan, titled “Technology for America’s Economic Growth, A New Direction to Build Economic Strength,” treated government support of computing and networking as a way to create jobs and competitive businesses. It backed its High-Performance Computing and Communications Initiative, whose national network it called “information superhighways,” and its National Economic Council task force was to work with Congress and private industry on policies to accelerate deployment.

sources.title: 1993-02-22-press-release-on-technology- ...
Markoff, John. 'Clinton Proposes Changes in Policy to Aid Technology.' New York Times, 23 February 1993.
sources.author: John Markoff
sources.confirms: Contemporary report of the 22 February 1993 four-year, $17 billion technology initiative that included the national information infrastructure plan.

information-superhighway-1993.detail: Their release credits those “information superhighways” to legislation Gore introduced and steered through the Senate. It proposed applications of high-performance computing and networking in health care, lifelong learning and manufacturing, pilot projects in schools and other nonprofit bodies, work with industry on software and communications for learning, and “substantial increases in funding for the National Science Foundation,” without stating dollar figures. Clinton said it was “time for a dramatically new approach” drawing on America’s scientific and technological resources “to change and improve the quality of our lives.”

mesopotamian-marshes-drained-1993.summary: After 1991 uprisings, Iraq's government accelerates drainage schemes first sketched by British engineers in 1951, digging a 565-kilometre 'Third River' between Tigris and Euphrates, completed December 1992, and a 'Mother of Battles' channel and embankments that cut water to Central, Hammar and Hawizeh marshes. By 2000 satellite images show under 10 percent of original wetland surviving, mostly in Hawizeh fed from Iran. Marsh Arabs, Ma'dan, who had lived among reed houses, water buffalo and fishing canoes since Sumerian times, number perhaps 500,000 in 1950 and fewer than 20,000 remain; many flee to Iran. After April 2003 locals breach dikes, and Curtis Richardson's surveys find 40 percent reflooded by 2005 with birds and fish returning where salt and upstream Turkish dams allow.

mosaic-1993.summary: In 1993 Mosaic showed pictures and text on one web page with a point-and-click interface. Andreessen and Eric Bina had begun writing it in December 1992 at the National Center for Supercomputing Applications, University of Illinois, for Unix workstations. Earlier browsers showed text; Mosaic displayed pictures inside pages beside words, installed easily and ran on ordinary machines. Web growth followed: over 10,000 sites by August 1995 and millions by 1998.

mosaic-1993.detail:
Ports to Microsoft Windows and Macintosh appeared in September 1993 and to Amiga by October. Version 2.0 for Unix, released on November 10, 1993, added support for forms, which allowed web pages to take input for the first time. The National Science Foundation supported development from 1994 to 1997.

Mosaic lost most users to Netscape Navigator, started by Andreessen and Jim Clark, in late 1994, and NCSA discontinued it in January 1997. Microsoft licensed one commercial derivative, Spyglass Mosaic, to create Internet Explorer in 1995.

nepal-community-forestry-act-1993.summary: After decades in which nationalisation in 1957 left hill forests open to cutting, Nepal's Master Plan for the Forestry Sector in 1989 proposes handing accessible forests to villages. Forest Act 1993 and Forest Regulations 1995 make Community Forest User Groups legal bodies: once a district forest officer approves a constitution and operational plan, a group manages its forest and sells timber and fodder from it while land stays with state. Executive committees must include a third women. By 2009 over 14,000 groups manage about 1.2 million hectares, and satellite studies show forest cover returning across mid hills. A 2009 analysis examines governance gains and elite capture within groups.

r-language-auckland-1993.summary: Ihaka and Gentleman began R in 1992 as a Scheme-influenced implementation of S language syntax for teaching at Auckland. They announced it on S-news in August 1993, released source under GNU General Public License in 1995 at Martin Maechler's urging, and described design in Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics in 1996. A core team formed in 1997 with CRAN package archive. Ihaka's 1998 Interface paper recounts origins. R became dominant environment for academic statistics, bioinformatics via Bioconductor, and data science, with more than 20,000 CRAN packages by 2020s. Gentleman and Ihaka's 2000 paper explains lexical scoping that distinguished R from S.

vinge-coming-singularity-1993.summary: In 1993 Vernor Vinge predicted superhuman intelligence within 30 years, by 2023, while saying he would be surprised if it came before 2005 or after 2030, and named that moment the singularity. He forecast: “Within thirty years, we will have the technological means to create superhuman intelligence. Shortly after, the human era will be ended.” Vinge, mathematician and computer scientist at San Diego State University and science-fiction novelist, argued that once minds greater than ours drive progress, they will build still smarter minds on ever shorter timescales, a runaway he called a singularity.

vinge-coming-singularity-1993.detail:
Vinge defined his singularity as “a point where our models must be discarded and a new reality rules,” borrowing from Stan Ulam’s recollection of John von Neumann. Von Neumann had spoken of “some essential singularity in the history of the race beyond which human affairs, as we know them, could not continue,” in Ulam’s telling.

Vinge listed four routes: computers that are “awake” and superhumanly intelligent; large computer networks and their users waking up as one entity; computer and human interfaces so intimate that users count as superhuman; and biology improving natural intellect. On timing he wrote, “I’ll be surprised if this event occurs before 2005 or after 2030.”

His essay also ran in Whole Earth Review in 1993. Vinge had won Hugo Awards for A Fire Upon the Deep and other works, and his 1981 novella True Names is described as seminal.

wired-magazine-launch-1993.summary: In January 1993 Wired launched in fluorescent ink, treating a digital future as culture. Copies were first handed out at Macworld Expo in San Francisco and later that week at CES in Las Vegas, reaching newsstands two weeks later as Bill Clinton took office with Al Gore touting his Information Superhighway. Founders Rossetto and Metcalfe, American expatriates in Amsterdam, had conceived a magazine about digital technology’s people, companies and ideas rather than its hardware, since computer magazines carried no lifestyle coverage.

wired-magazine-launch-1993.detail:
Dutch entrepreneur Eckart Wintzen provided initial funding. His Origin software company bought advertising and its first 1,000 subscriptions, which carried its founders through twelve months of rejections from publishers and venture capitalists. Their breakthrough came at February 1992’s TED conference, where they showed a prototype to Nicholas Negroponte of MIT Media Lab; he became investor and columnist for six years. By September 1992 Wired had rented loft space in San Francisco’s SoMa district, with Kevin Kelly as executive editor, John Plunkett as creative director and John Battelle as managing editor.

Condé Nast consolidated Wired’s magazine and Wired.com under one owner in 2006. Wired coined “crowdsourcing” and has won multiple National Magazine Awards.

www-public-domain-1993.summary: In April 1993 CERN gave the World Wide Web away, royalty free; anyone could build a browser or a site without asking. Tim Berners-Lee had invented it at CERN in 1989 as a “universal linked information system,” whose documents hold both content and links to other documents. Its main rival, Gopher from the University of Minnesota, arranged information in menus, but Minnesota announced licensing fees in 1993. CERN’s free release let anyone run servers and browsers without paying.

www-public-domain-1993.detail: Gopher had reached nearly 7,000 servers by April 1994. After NCSA released Mosaic later in 1993, a graphical browser that displayed inline images and submitted forms to its HTTPd server, thousands of websites appeared in less than one year. Marc Andreessen and Jim Clark founded Netscape in 1994 and released Navigator. Gopher stagnated and declined while Web use accelerated.

yozma-venture-capital-israel-1993.summary: Israel's Office of Chief Scientist launches Yozma in 1993 with 100 million dollars: 80 million invested as up to 40 percent stakes in ten new private venture funds that must bring in a foreign financial institution as partner, plus 20 million for direct investments. Partners gain an option to buy out government share at cost plus low interest within five years, a design that rewards success rather than subsidising losses. Funds raise about 200 million dollars, back over 200 start-ups, and by 1998 all ten are privatised. Venture capital under management grows from near zero to several billion dollars by 2000, feeding a Nasdaq listing boom. Policy economists cite Yozma as a rare state programme that created a self-sustaining market, and governments from Korea to New Zealand copy its structure.

zanamivir-relenza-design-melbourne-1993.summary: Using crystal structure of influenza neuraminidase solved by Peter Colman's CSIRO group, researchers at Victorian College of Pharmacy led by Mark von Itzstein, with Biota Holdings, designed a sialic acid analogue that blocked the enzyme's active site. Their Nature paper of June 1993 reported potent inhibition in cells and animals, demonstrating structure-based drug design against a virus. Glaxo licensed compound as Relenza; US FDA approved it in July 1999, following Australian approval. Thomson and von Itzstein's 2011 chapter reviews development. Oseltamivir (Tamiflu) followed from same target. Relenza stockpiling during 2005 avian influenza fears and 2009 pandemic made Biota a case study in Australian biotech commercialisation.

channel-tunnel-1994.summary: In May 1994 the Channel Tunnel opened; Britain had its first land link to mainland Europe since the last Ice Age, about 8,000 years ago. Elizabeth II crossed by Eurostar train, which stopped nose to nose with Mitterrand’s train from Paris, and both leaders then rode Le Shuttle to Folkestone. This 50.46-kilometre rail tunnel has 37.9 kilometres underwater. Proposals dated from 1802; Eurotunnel began building in 1988 with private finance.

The Channel Tunnel is opened Queen Elizabeth II

sources.author: Anguera, Ricard
sources.venue: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

channel-tunnel-1994.verification_note: Anguera (Transportation Research Part A 2006) finds that ex post this project destroyed economic value overall, against its celebratory reception.
channel-tunnel-1994.detail:
National-security worries had delayed earlier schemes; 1986’s Treaty of Canterbury set terms for private companies to build and operate it. Tunnellers from each side met in its service tunnel on 1 December 1990, when Graham Fagg and Philippe Cozette broke through before cameras; both bores were misaligned by only 30 centimetres horizontally.

Full public service did not start for several months after opening; its first freight train ran on 1 June 1994 carrying Rover and Mini cars for Italy. At 1985 prices its final cost was £4.65 billion against £2.6 billion forecast, an 80 percent overrun, with financing costs 140 percent above forecast, and Anguera's 2006 economic evaluation found this project destroyed value overall. BBC footage records that building took eight years and billions of pounds, and that Elizabeth II called it one of the world’s great technological achievements.

chinook-1994.summary: In 1994 the program Chinook became checkers world champion when an ailing Marion Tinsley withdrew. Chinook, Jonathan Schaeffer’s checkers program from the University of Alberta, had earned its place in 1990 by finishing second to Tinsley at that year’s US Nationals. Its knowledge was programmed by hand rather than learned: opening book, deep search, handcrafted position evaluation and endgame databases covering every position with eight or fewer pieces.

Schaeffer, Jonathan; Lake, Robert; Lu, Paul; Bryant, Martin, 'Chinook: The World Man-Machine Checkers Champion', AI Magazine 17, no. 1 (1996)
sources.author: Schaeffer, Jonathan; Lake, Robert; Lu, Paul; Bryant, Martin
sources.confirms: The authors record that in the 1994 match, after six drawn games, Marion Tinsley withdrew on health grounds and the world championship title passed to Chinook, the first time a computer won a human world championship.

sources.author: New York Times
sources.confirms: The obituary records Tinsley's withdrawal from the 1994 match against Chinook and his death from cancer.

chinook-1994.detail:
The American Checkers Federation and English Draughts Association at first refused to let a computer enter their championship. When Tinsley resigned his title in protest, they created a Man versus Machine title; Tinsley won their 1992 match with four wins to Chinook’s two and 33 draws, and Chinook never beat him.

In 1995 Chinook defended its title against Don Lafferty, winning one game and drawing 31, after which Schaeffer withdrew it from competition to solve checkers outright. In July 2007 his team published “Checkers Is Solved” in Science, proving that perfect play by both sides ends in a draw.

cuba-organoponicos-urban-farming-1994.summary: After Soviet trade collapsed in 1991, Cuba lost most of its imported fertiliser, pesticides, fuel and animal feed, and food intake fell sharply during its Período Especial. In 1994 Cuba's Ministry of Agriculture created an urban agriculture department granting usufruct rights to vacant lots in Havana and other cities. Growers built organopónicos, long raised beds of soil mixed with compost in concrete or wooden frames, irrigated by drip and fed with worm humus, biofertilisers and biological pest controls developed at Cuban research institutes. A 1999 study counted over 8,000 gardens in Havana and found urban production supplying a large share of its fresh vegetables; agricultural markets reopened in 1994 to sell surpluses. Agroecology movements abroad took up Cuba's experience.

cuba-organoponicos-urban-farming-1994.detail: A CREE network of centres reproduced Trichoderma, Bacillus thuringiensis and parasitic wasps for distribution to growers. Yields rose after 2000 to several kilograms per square metre a year. Critics note that urban farming eased but did not solve Cuba's food deficit, which continued to depend on imports of rice, wheat and beans.

esrb-1994.summary: In 1994 game publishers created ESRB to rate games by age after Senate hearings on Mortal Kombat. Those hearings, led by Joe Lieberman and Herb Kohl, singled out Mortal Kombat, whose digitised actors performed bloody “fatality” moves, and Night Trap, with 90 minutes of filmed scenes considered sexually suggestive. No industry-wide rating standard existed, and Sega and Nintendo handled such content differently. Facing possible government-imposed ratings, publishers formed the Interactive Digital Software Association and within it a vendor-neutral board, launched on September 16, 1994.

sources.title: Entertainment Software Rating Board (Wikipedia)
Timeline of Computer History: 1994, ESRB founded
sources.author: Computer History Museum
sources.confirms: After congressional hearings on violent games such as Mortal Kombat and Night Trap, the largest game companies created the ESRB in 1994 to pre-empt a government rating board.
sources.qualifies: CHM dates the hearings to 1992; they were held in December 1993 and March 1994.

sources.title: Associated Press, 'Makers Say They'll Rate Video Games', New York Times, 5 March 1994

sources.qualifies: Reports the March 1994 pledge; the ESRB was formed later in 1994.

esrb-1994.detail: ESRB was announced to Congress on July 29, 1994. Its original system had five age ratings: Early Childhood, Kids to Adults (renamed Everyone in 1998), Teen, Mature and Adults Only. ESRB was the first rating system to add content “descriptors,” brief notes on what each game contains, because parents wanted that information before buying. Within one year of launch its ratings were in widespread use across console games, though adoption among PC games lagged; the Federal Trade Commission later praised ESRB as the “strongest” self-regulatory organisation in the entertainment sector.

flavr-savr-gmo-1994.summary: In May 1994 Flavr Savr tomatoes went on sale, the first genetically engineered food licensed for eating; production ceased in 1997. Calgene of Davis, California, developed them during the 1980s to solve shipping losses: tomatoes picked ripe soften and spoil before reaching distant shoppers, so growers pick green fruit. Calgene added a reversed copy of polygalacturonase's gene, an enzyme that softens fruit, which suppressed that enzyme and let tomatoes ripen on vines yet travel without going soft. FDA cleared Flavr Savr on May 18, 1994 and required no special label.

flavr-savr-gmo-1994.detail:
FDA concluded that Flavr Savr “is as safe as tomatoes bred by conventional means” and found no health risk and unchanged nutrition. Labelling was unnecessary, it held, because Flavr Savr kept essential characteristics of unmodified tomatoes. Calgene used Agrobacterium tumefaciens, stripped of its harmful genes, to carry new genetic material into tomato cells, together with a marker gene for antibiotic resistance, which FDA also cleared.

That variety was built on an old, low-yielding parent line, and Calgene had no experience growing and shipping tomatoes. Production ceased in 1997, and with research and production costs mounting, Monsanto bought Calgene that year for more than $200 million.

grouplens-1994.summary: In October 1994 GroupLens predicted how a Usenet reader would rate an article from readers who had agreed with them before. Usenet, the Internet’s discussion network, had grown past what anyone could read; by January 1994 more than 140,000 people had posted within two weeks, with traffic over 100 megabytes daily. GroupLens drew “not on an article’s content but on correlations between people’s ratings,” its authors wrote.

sources.title: AI Evolution Atlas

Paul Resnick, Neophytos Iacovou, Mitesh Suchak, Peter Bergstrom and John Riedl, 'GroupLens: an open architecture for collaborative filtering of netnews', Proceedings of the 1994 ACM Conference on Computer Supported Cooperative Work (CSCW '94), 175-186
sources.author: Paul Resnick, Neophytos Iacovou, Mitesh Suchak, Peter Bergstrom and John Riedl
sources.confirms: The original 1994 paper describing GroupLens, a collaborative filtering system that predicts which netnews articles a reader will like from the ratings of like-minded readers.

grouplens-1994.detail:
Readers rated articles, and rating servers called Better Bit Bureaus gathered those scores and computed predictions on one heuristic: people who agreed before will agree again. Ratings could be entered under pseudonyms, and GroupLens ran as an open service between sites, with no single organisation in control. Its paper describes GroupLens as “an open architecture for collaborative filtering of Usenet news,” with Xerox PARC’s single-site Tapestry as predecessor.

By 1994 it had been piloted with four people at Minnesota, after seven people at a Schlumberger research lab tried an endorsement mechanism, and a larger test between MIT and Minnesota was only planned. Amazon’s 2003 paper on its recommendation algorithm cites GroupLens as an example of finding customers with overlapping ratings, the source notes.

ibm-simon-1994.summary: In August 1994 BellSouth sold the IBM Simon, a phone with a touchscreen, email and a calendar; the first smartphone sold 50,000. IBM engineer Frank Canova had seen that chips and wireless parts were becoming small enough to combine mobile phone and personal digital assistant in one handheld. Simon had a 4.5-inch touchscreen used with finger or stylus, a modem for faxes and email, calendar, address book and notepad, and could load extra software, hence its retrospective title of first true smartphone.

sources.title: IBM Simon
Connelly, Charlotte, "Simon Says... 'be Smart'"
sources.author: Charlotte Connelly, Science Museum
sources.confirms: Museum account of the IBM Simon, sold by BellSouth from August 1994 with touchscreen, email and calendar, about 50,000 units.

sources.title: Tech Times, "IBM Simon, the grandfather of smartphones, turns 20"
sources.author: Tech Times
sources.confirms: Dates the retail launch to 16 August 1994.

ibm-simon-1994.detail:
Simon sold approximately 50,000 units during six months on the market. IBM had shown its prototype, code-named Sweetspot, at COMDEX in Las Vegas on November 16, 1992, demonstrating maps, stocks and news services before those were widely available, and USA Today featured it the next day. Mitsubishi Electric manufactured Simon. BellSouth planned to sell it from May 1994 but software problems delayed launch until August; it cost US$899 with a two-year contract or US$1,099 without, later cut to US$599.

Sales were held back by that price and by battery life of about one hour. IBM began a smaller successor, code-named Neon, but abandoned it.

nerica-rice-africa-1994.summary: At the West Africa Rice Development Association station in Bouake, Cote d'Ivoire, Sierra Leonean breeder Monty Jones's team uses embryo rescue and anther culture with backcrossing to overcome sterility between African rice Oryza glaberrima and Asian Oryza sativa; World Food Prize dates his breakthrough to 1994, after three years of crosses begun in 1992. Lines combine glaberrima's weed competitiveness, drought and pest tolerance with sativa's yield and mature in 75 to 100 days. First varieties, named New Rice for Africa, are released in Cote d'Ivoire in 2000; 18 upland NERICAs follow, covering about 1.4 million hectares by 2013, and a 2017 impact study credits them with lifting about 8 million people out of poverty in 16 countries.

sources.confirms: Reports fertile interspecific progenies from sativa x glaberrima crosses via embryo rescue and anther culture at WARDA, with glaberrima traits for weed competitiveness.

nerica-rice-africa-1994.detail: The World Food Prize credits NERICA with harvest gains of 25 to 250 percent and over 3,000 lines. Sixty lowland NERICA-L varieties with 6 to 7 tonne potential followed under Moussa Sie, who won Japan's International Rice Prize in 2006. WARDA became AfricaRice in 2009. Japan funded dissemination through JICA. Africa still imports a large share of its rice. CGIAR records 82 NERICA varieties in all: 18 upland, 60 lowland and 4 irrigated. Jones, Dingkuhn, Aluko and Semon described their progenies in 1997, and Jones shared the 2004 World Food Prize with Yuan Longping.

pakistan-lady-health-workers-1994.summary: Benazir Bhutto's government began National Programme for Family Planning and Primary Health Care in 1994, recruiting local women with at least eight years of schooling, training them for fifteen months and paying a stipend to serve about 1,000 people each from their homes. Lady Health Workers provide family planning, antenatal advice, immunisation referrals, treatment of common illnesses and health education, and have been backbone of polio campaigns. Numbers grew from a few thousand to over 100,000 by 2010s, covering more than half of rural population. Evaluations find higher contraceptive use and immunisation in served areas, though pay, supplies and security for workers remain persistent problems.

pentium-fdiv-1994.summary: In December 1994 Intel recalled Pentium chips for a division bug after insisting it did not matter; replacement and write-off costs came to a $475 million pretax charge. On December 20, amid growing dissatisfaction with its response, Intel offered to replace all flawed processors on request. Thomas Nicely, mathematics professor at Lynchburg College, had found while computing prime numbers that his Pentium divided certain pairs of numbers slightly wrong, because entries were missing from a lookup table in its division circuitry, and news spread over the Internet.

Coe, Tim, Mathisen, Terje, Moler, Cleve and Pratt, Vaughan, 'Computational Aspects of the Pentium Affair', IEEE Computational Science and Engineering 2 (1995) 18-30

sources.confirms: On 20 December 1994 Intel bowed to public pressure and offered free replacements of the Pentium, whose division errors its engineers had found in July and which a Virginia college mathematician had publicised in November.

sources.author: Los Angeles Times
sources.confirms: Intel took a $475 million charge to cover write-downs of flawed Pentium inventory and replacement of chips in customers' hands, after IBM's December decision to stop shipping Pentium PCs forced it to offer replacements to all.

pentium-fdiv-1994.detail:
Nicely emailed colleagues about that flaw on October 30, 1994. Pentium used a new division algorithm (SRT) producing two bits per clock cycle, against one on the 486, and relied on a lookup table; missing entries caused small errors in some high-precision divisions. Byte magazine estimated that 1 in 9 billion random divisions would be wrong, and Intel at first offered replacements only to users who could show they were affected.

That stance drew criticism from industry experts, shook consumer confidence and created demand for action even from people unlikely to meet the bug. Intel’s chief executive Andy Grove later told The Wall Street Journal, “I think the kernel of the issue we missed ... was that we presumed to tell somebody what they should or shouldn’t worry about, or should or shouldn’t do.”

playstation-1994.summary: In December 1994 Sony released the PlayStation on CD-ROM; it sold 100 million and made games an adult pastime. Sony had entered games through a failed 1988 partnership with Nintendo to build a CD-ROM add-on for the Super Nintendo; Nintendo cancelled it without telling Sony and signed with Philips instead. Ken Kutaragi, who had designed Nintendo’s sound chip, led Sony’s own console, built around compact discs and 3D polygon graphics. Within ten years it had shipped over 100 million units.

sources.title: PlayStation (console) (Wikipedia)
Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'PlayStation'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Sony Computer Entertainment released the 32-bit CD-based PlayStation in Japan in December 1994 and in America in September 1995.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Sony: Diversification and downturn'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Sony introduced the PlayStation to the Japanese market in 1994; by 2002 games gave more than 10 percent of revenue.

playstation-1994.detail:
Its Japanese launch, at ¥39,800 one week after Saturn, drew long queues. At the 1995 Electronic Entertainment Expo, after Sega announced its $399 Saturn, Sony’s Steve Race walked on stage, said “Two ninety-nine” and left to applause. Launch-era games included Ridge Racer, Tekken and Wipeout; later titles such as Gran Turismo, Final Fantasy VII and Metal Gear Solid defined PlayStation.

Its compact discs began gaming’s move from cartridges; 102.49 million units were sold, about 7,900 games released, and production ended on 23 March 2006.

predator-drone-1994.summary: In 1994 the Predator drone first flew; within a year it was watching Bosnia and by 2001 it carried missiles. Its first overseas deployment was to the Balkans from July to November 1995. Predator was a remotely piloted, propeller-driven reconnaissance aircraft. It could fly about 740 kilometres to its target, loiter overhead for 14 hours with cameras and sensors, and return, steered by satellite from its ground station.

National Museum of the United States Air Force, 'General Atomics Aeronautical Systems RQ-1 Predator', fact sheet
sources.author: National Museum of the United States Air Force
sources.confirms: The Defense Department ordered ten Predators in January 1994, the first flew in July 1994, and within a year Predators were operating over Bosnia from July 1995 to March 1996.

sources.title: U.S. Air Force, 'MQ-1B Predator', fact sheet
sources.author: U.S. Air Force
sources.confirms: The redesignation from RQ-1 to MQ-1 came in 2002 with the addition of AGM-114 Hellfire missiles.

predator-drone-1994.detail:
For the Balkans deployment, four disassembled aircraft were flown into Gjadër airbase in Albania and flown at first by civilian contractors. Predator’s design descended from Abraham Karem’s Amber drone. Karem, former chief designer for Israel’s air force, saw his company go bankrupt; CIA secretly bought five of its successors, Gnats, and Karem built a quieter engine for a craft that had sounded like “a lawnmower in the sky.” Its Advanced Concept Technology Demonstration ran from January 1994 to June 1996.

In 2000 its programme was told to explore armament, and on 16 February 2001 one Predator fired a Hellfire missile at a tank target near Indian Springs, Nevada. Armed MQ-1s later saw combat in Afghanistan and elsewhere; the Air Force took delivery of its last Predator in 2011 and retired them in 2018 in favour of Reapers.

qr-code-denso-wave-1994.summary: Engineers at Denso, a Toyota group parts maker in Aichi, release QR code in 1994 for tracking components on assembly lines. Three square finder patterns let a camera locate and orient a symbol in any direction, Reed-Solomon coding restores up to 30 percent damaged data, and one symbol holds up to 7,089 digits or 1,817 kanji. Denso files patents in Japan in 1994 and United States in 1995 but declares it will not enforce them against standard-compliant use. ISO/IEC 18004 standardises it in 2000, and camera phones in Japan from 2002, then Alipay and WeChat payments in China after 2011, made QR codes a universal interface between paper and screens.

rtlm-rwanda-radio-1994.summary: From July 1993 a private FM station in Kigali, RTLM, mixed popular music with attacks on Tutsi and moderate Hutu. After President Habyarimana's plane was shot down on 6 April 1994, its presenters read out names, directed militias to roadblocks and urged listeners to kill. Around 800,000 people died in about 100 days. David Yanagizawa-Drott, using transmitter coverage and hill-by-hill terrain, estimates broadcasts raised participation enough to account for roughly ten percent of violence, about 51,000 perpetrators. Scott Straus, using perpetrator interviews, argues radio was a marginal rather than primary driver compared with face-to-face mobilisation. RTLM founders were convicted of incitement by the UN tribunal in 2003.

rtlm-rwanda-radio-1994.detail: Yanagizawa-Drott (Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2014) exploits variation in radio reception caused by Rwanda's hills to identify effects on prosecutions for genocide violence, finding spillovers between villages. Straus (Politics and Society, 2007) finds limited and conditional effects, cautioning against a 'radio machete' narrative. Both accept RTLM broadcast incitement; they disagree on causal weight. Nahimana and Jean-Bosco Barayagwiza were convicted by ICTR in December 2003 in its 'media case'.

shor-algorithm-1994.summary: In 1994 Peter Shor showed a quantum computer could factor large numbers swiftly enough to break RSA; research into codes secure against such machines is now called post-quantum cryptography. On an ideal quantum computer it can factor integers in polynomial time, meaning its work grows modestly with a number’s length, whereas the best classical method, the general number field sieve, grows sub-exponentially and becomes hopeless for large numbers. RSA and Diffie-Hellman key exchange, which protect most encrypted traffic, rest on factoring and related problems being infeasible, so capable quantum computers could break them.

sources.title: Shor's algorithm
Shor, Peter W., "Algorithms for quantum computation: discrete logarithms and factoring"
sources.author: Peter W. Shor
sources.venue: Proceedings of the 35th Annual Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science, pp. 124-134
sources.confirms: The 1994 conference paper giving polynomial-time quantum algorithms for factoring and discrete logarithms; Crossref record confirmed, IEEE page not readable.

sources.author: Peter W. Shor
sources.confirms: The peer-reviewed journal version of the algorithm.

shor-algorithm-1994.detail:
Shor proposed related algorithms for factoring, discrete logarithms and period finding; his first two are instances of his third. Beating classical computers may require machines with millions of qubits because of quantum error correction overhead.

In 2001 an IBM group factored 15 into 3 times 5 with a seven-qubit nuclear magnetic resonance device, and later groups factored 15 and 21 with photonic, solid-state and trapped-ion qubits, though these demonstrations were compiled with knowledge of their answers. Research into cryptosystems secure against them is now called post-quantum cryptography.

sri-lanka-ckdu-1994.summary: From about 1994 physicians in Sri Lanka's North Central Province see rising chronic kidney failure in paddy farmers without diabetes or hypertension, its usual causes. Named chronic kidney disease of unknown aetiology, it clusters in dry zone districts where families drink from shallow wells and farm with agrochemicals. A national study with WHO from 2010 to 2012 finds age-standardised prevalence of 12.9 percent in men and 16.9 percent in women aged 15 to 70 in affected districts, with cadmium exposure through food and pesticide exposure as risk factors. Debate over arsenic, fluoride, glyphosate and heat stress continues; Sri Lanka restricts glyphosate in 2015 and builds reverse osmosis plants in affected villages.

sri-lanka-ckdu-1994.detail: Prevalence and cadmium findings from WHO's collaborative study appeared in 2013. Channa Jayasumana's group, in 2015, dated first reports to 1994 and linked disease to well water and herbicide exposure. Epidemiology Unit material covers policy responses.

thinking-machines-bankruptcy-1994.summary: In August 1994 Thinking Machines, a supercomputer firm that had drawn Feynman, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy. CM-1 and CM-2 used 65,536 one-bit processors working at once, and by 1993 the world's four fastest computers were Connection Machines. Thinking Machines turned profitable in 1989 largely on DARPA contracts, but in 1991 DARPA and the Department of Energy cut purchases amid criticism of favouritism, and by 1992 it was losing money.

sources.author: New York Times
sources.confirms: Reports the supercomputer maker's decision to seek Chapter 11 protection in August 1994 after failing to find an investor.
