sources.author: New York Times
sources.confirms: Confirms the firm entered bankruptcy fifteen months earlier and planned to re-emerge as a software company.

thinking-machines-bankruptcy-1994.detail:
Hillis’s MIT doctoral work proposed splitting problems across tens of thousands of simple processors. Thinking Machines moved to Kendall Square in Cambridge in 1984, near MIT’s AI Lab, and registered the third .com domain, think.com, in 1985. In 1990 it sold US$65 million of hardware and software, leading the parallel supercomputer market against Cray, nCUBE, MasPar and Meiko. Tightening export laws also blocked sales of its most powerful machines abroad, and Handler was forced out as chief executive in 1992.

Sun Microsystems eventually acquired its hardware and parallel software divisions. Brewster Kahle’s WAIS search system, built at Thinking Machines, influenced his later Internet Archive, and dummy Connection Machines appear in 1993’s film Jurassic Park.

yahoo-1994.summary: In 1994 two Stanford students made a list of their favourite websites; as Yahoo it became the web's front page. Their site was a directory edited by people and arranged in categories and subcategories, rather than a searchable index of pages. Its name is a backronym for “Yet Another Hierarchical Officious Oracle,” oracle meaning source of truth and wisdom. Yahoo was incorporated on March 2, 1995.

Editors, Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Yahoo Inc. | Internet Pioneer, History, & Ownership', Britannica Money (2026)
sources.author: Editors, Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: The page says Yahoo was founded in 1994 by Jerry Yang and David Filo, graduate students at Stanford University, and began as a simple list of their favorite Internet links.
sources.qualifies: Britannica gives a different expansion of Yahoo’s name: “Yet Another Hierarchical Officious Oracle.”

sources.title: Shontell, Alyson, 'After 20 Years, Yahoo Is Killing Its Founding Feature, The Yahoo Directory', Yahoo Finance (2014)

yahoo-1994.verification_note: Britannica gives Yahoo’s name as “Yet Another Hierarchical Officious Oracle” rather than “Hierarchically Organized Oracle.”
yahoo-1994.detail:
Yahoo’s domain, yahoo.com, was registered on January 18, 1995, and Yahoo Search was added that year to search its directory. Filo and Yang also say they liked the slang sense of “yahoo,” an unsophisticated, rural Southerner.

Yahoo went public in April 1996 and its stock rose 600 percent within two years. It added a portal to compete with Excite, Lycos and America Online; by 1998 it was web users’ most popular starting point, with 95 million page views daily, triple rival Excite, and it offered free email from October 1997 after buying RocketMail.

zapatista-internet-chiapas-1994.summary: When Ejército Zapatista de Liberación Nacional rose in Chiapas on 1 January 1994, as NAFTA took effect, its communiqués written by Subcomandante Marcos were typed into email by supporters in San Cristóbal de las Casas and Mexico City and relayed through Usenet groups, PeaceNet and La Neta, a Mexican NGO network, to lists and Gopher and Web sites abroad. Oliver Froehling's 1997 study traced how a movement of Maya communities with no connectivity of its own gained an international audience within days, mobilising observers and protests that constrained Mexico's army. A 1996 Intercontinental Encounter drew thousands to Lacandon jungle villages; RAND analysts coined 'social netwar' from this case. It became a template for later online activism.

sources.title: Froehling, Oliver, 'The Cyberspace "War of Ink and Internet" in Chiapas, Mexico', Geographical Review 87 (1997)
sources.author: Froehling, Oliver
sources.confirms: Mechanics of communiqué circulation via La Neta, PeaceNet and lists, and its political effects.

sources.title: Cleaver, Harry, 'The Zapatista Effect: The Internet and the Rise of an Alternative Political Fabric', Journal of International Affairs 51 (1998)
sources.author: Cleaver, Harry
sources.confirms: Analysis of network circulation and solidarity mobilisation.

zapatista-internet-chiapas-1994.detail: Harry Cleaver's writings on a 'Zapatista effect' argued that electronic networks let a local insurgency reshape global politics. Mexican newspapers La Jornada and Proceso printed communiqués that were then scanned and posted. Later Zapatista autonomous municipalities built their own radio and, after 2005, web presence through Enlace Zapatista.

picture.credit: Mr. Theklan, via Wikimedia Commons

adaboost-1995.summary: In 1995 Freund and Schapire's AdaBoost combined many weak guesses into a strong classifier; it ran the first face detectors in cameras. AdaBoost, short for adaptive boosting, combines multiple weak learners, simple classifiers each only slightly better than guessing, into one weighted sum. It trains them in sequence, giving extra weight to examples earlier learners got wrong, so each new learner concentrates on hard cases. As long as each learner beats random guessing, their combination provably converges to a strong classifier.

sources.title: AdaBoost
Freund, Yoav, and Schapire, Robert E., 'A Decision-Theoretic Generalization of On-Line Learning and an Application to Boosting', Journal of Computer and System Sciences 55, no. 1 (1997), 119-139
sources.author: Freund, Yoav; Schapire, Robert E.
sources.venue: Journal of Computer and System Sciences
sources.confirms: The archival AdaBoost paper, first presented in 1995, derives the adaptive boosting algorithm that combines weak learners into a strong classifier.

sources.title: Freund, Yoav; Schapire, Robert E., 'A desicion-theoretic generalization of on-line learning and an application to boosting', in Computational Learning Theory: EuroCOLT '95, Lecture Notes in Computer Science 904 (Berlin: Springer, 1995), pp. 23-37
sources.author: Freund, Yoav; Schapire, Robert E.
sources.confirms: The 1995 conference version of the paper introducing AdaBoost, preceding the 1997 journal version already cited.

adaboost-1995.detail: AdaBoost can be less prone to overfitting than other learning methods. It is usually presented for two-class problems but extends to several classes or numeric outputs, and works with many kinds of learning algorithm; AdaBoost with decision trees as weak learner is often called the best out-of-the-box classifier. Viola and Jones’s object-detection framework used it in a cascade of boosted classifiers that discards obvious negatives early, speeding up face detection.

amazon-1995.summary: In July 1995 Amazon began selling books online; it grew into a store for almost anything and cloud computing's largest business. Jeff Bezos had founded it as Cadabra on July 5, 1994 after moving from New York City to Bellevue, Washington; he chose Seattle for technical talent from Microsoft and the University of Washington and for its nearness to a major book distribution warehouse in Roseburg, Oregon. In November 1994 he renamed it Amazon, after the world’s largest river, to reflect his ambitions. Amazon went public in May 1997.

sources.title: Amazon (company) - Wikipedia
Amazon.com, Inc., Registration Statement on Form S-1 (US Securities and Exchange Commission, filed 24 March 1997)
sources.author: Amazon.com, Inc.
sources.venue: US Securities and Exchange Commission, EDGAR
sources.confirms: Amazon's IPO prospectus describing the company's founding, the opening of its website in July 1995 and its early sales.

sources.title: 'Jeff Bezos', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Bezos quit D. E. Shaw in 1994, moved to Seattle to open a virtual bookstore, incorporated the company that year, and Amazon sold its first book in July 1995.

sources.title: 'Jeffrey Bezos', Gale Encyclopedia of E-Commerce, via Encyclopedia.com
sources.author: Gale Encyclopedia of E-Commerce
sources.confirms: Bezos chose Seattle for proximity to the Ingram book warehouse and a pool of technology professionals, dropped the name Cadabra for Amazon, and launched the site in July 1995, shipping books to all 50 states and 45 countries in its first months.

amazon-1995.detail: Seattle beat Portland, Oregon and Boulder, Colorado as company home. Known as “The Everything Store,” Amazon expanded from books to virtually all consumer products and by 2026 was the world’s biggest online retailer, with businesses in cloud computing, advertising, streaming and artificial intelligence.

californian-ideology-1995.summary: In September 1995 two British critics named a Californian Ideology, hippie freedom married to free markets, and their label stuck. Their essay described an ideology combining cybernetics, free market economics and counter-culture libertarianism, promulgated by Wired, Mondo 2000 and books by Stewart Brand and Kevin Kelly, and criticized its technological determinism. Barbrook and Cameron, of Westminster University’s Hypermedia Research Centre, argued that West Coast technology workers, their “virtual class,” fused hippie freedom with New Right market individualism while ignoring public money behind computing and the Net.

sources.title: The Californian Ideology - Mute Magazine
[PDF] Afterlives of the Californian Ideology

californian-ideology-1995.detail:
Their essay calls this hybrid “only made possible through a nearly universal belief in technological determinism.” They add that computing and networking “were invented with the aid of massive state subsidies,” contrast Howard Rheingold’s “electronic agora” with Newt Gingrich’s and the Tofflers’ electronic marketplace, call Wired “the monthly bible of the ‘virtual class’,” and warn of apartheid between “information-rich” and “information-poor” Americans. Thomas Jefferson, slave-owner and democrat, serves as their emblem of liberal individualism’s double nature, and France’s Minitel as proof that state intervention and markets can spread new technology together.

An extended version appeared in Science as Culture in 1996. Hepp, Schmitz and Schneider’s 2023 introduction in International Journal of Communication treats their essay as naming Silicon Valley’s political economy and outlook, which still shape imaginaries of digital futures.

digital-divide-1995.summary: In 1995 America's Commerce Department reported that poor and rural Americans lacked computers and modems, first of three such reports; 1999's third, “Falling Through the Net: Defining the Digital Divide,” defined that divide as being “between those with access to new technologies and those without.” Much early literature adopted this definition, and its term, coined among consumer groups, spread into a global movement.

sources.title: Digital divide
Falling Through the Net: A Survey of the 'Have Nots' in Rural and Urban America
sources.author: National Telecommunications and Information Administration
sources.venue: US Department of Commerce, NTIA, July 1995
sources.confirms: Rural households with incomes under $10,000 had the lowest computer ownership (4.5 percent) and modem penetration (23.6 percent) in 1994 data.

sources.title: National Telecommunications and Information Administration. Falling Through the Net: Defining the Digital Divide. Washington, DC: US Department of Commerce, 8 July 1999.
sources.author: NTIA
sources.confirms: The third report in the series, which gave the digital divide its name in its title.

sources.title: van Dijk, Jan A. G. M. 'Digital Divide Research, Achievements and Shortcomings.' Poetics 34, no. 4-5 (2006): 221-235.
sources.author: Jan A. G. M. van Dijk
sources.confirms: Peer-reviewed review tracing digital divide research to the mid-1990s NTIA surveys; Crossref metadata confirmed, Elsevier page did not open.

digital-divide-1995.detail:
NTIA’s second report appeared in 1998. Consumer groups seeking to tax and regulate communications companies coined it around 1996’s Telecommunications Act, when Federal Communications Commission officials weighed regulatory and tax strategies to close that gap, before debate moved to World Trade Organization talks. President Bill Clinton used that term in his 2000 State of the Union address.

Researchers now describe digital divide across four dimensions, motivation, material access, skills and usage; it is commonly framed as “haves” and “have-nots.”

digital-divide-ntia-1995.summary: In July 1995 NTIA's Falling Through the Net measured who lacked modems by income and race. Vice President Al Gore had requested it. Its data came from questions NTIA added to Census Bureau interviews in November 1994, which NTIA calls Census's first survey about owning personal computers and modems. It extended universal service, until then about telephones, to information services, and Springer’s civil society encyclopedia credits it with introducing information technology's haves and have nots.

sources.title: Falling Through the Net: A Survey of the “Have Nots” in Rural and …
Digital Divide

digital-divide-ntia-1995.detail:
NTIA calls this report first of two profiles of telephone and computer penetration; a sequel, Falling Through the Net II, followed in July 1998 with new data on that divide.

Dalia Yusuf’s entry in Springer’s International Encyclopedia of Civil Society calls it history's first digital divide study and distinguishes technocratic readings of such divides, about access to equipment, from information-sociological ones about how people use it.

ebay-1995.summary: In September 1995 Pierre Omidyar wrote an auction site over a weekend; its first sale was a broken laser pointer for $14.83, bought by someone who told Omidyar, “I’m a collector of broken laser pointers.” In February 1996 his internet provider raised his monthly fee from $30 to $250 because of traffic, so Omidyar began charging sellers; AuctionWeb earned $1,000 that first month and $2,500 the next. Renamed eBay in September 1997, it went public a year later.

sources.title: eBay - Wikipedia
eBay Inc., "Meet the Buyer of the Broken Laser Pointer"
sources.author: eBay Inc.
sources.confirms: Company account identifying Mark Fraser as buyer of Omidyar's broken laser pointer for $14.83 in 1995.

sources.title: Sunday Times (South Africa), "20 things you didn't know about 20-year-old eBay"
sources.author: Sunday Times
sources.confirms: Independent report of the September 1995 AuctionWeb launch and first sale.

ebay-1995.detail:
Chris Agarpao became its first employee, and Jeffrey Skoll joined as first president in early 1996. By November 1996 AuctionWeb had hosted more than 200,000 auctions. Omidyar wanted to name it after his consulting firm, Echo Bay Technology Group, but Echo Bay Mines held echobay.com, so he shortened it to eBay. Benchmark invested $6.7 million in 1997, when Beanie Babies, scarce in shops, made up 10 percent of all listings.

Meg Whitman became CEO in March 1998, when eBay had 30 employees, 500,000 users and $4.7 million in revenue. Its September 1998 IPO priced at $18 and closed the first day at $53, valuing eBay near $1.9 billion.

gartner-hype-cycle-1995.summary: In 1995 Gartner's Jackie Fenn drew her hype cycle: a peak of expectations, a trough and a slow climb that technologies tend to follow. Her research note, “When to Leap on the Hype Cycle,” drew five phases along one curve: Technology Trigger, Peak of Inflated Expectations, Trough of Disillusionment, Slope of Enlightenment and Plateau of Productivity. Fenn says she and her colleagues “rapidly realized it was about people’s reaction to anything new”: enthusiasm floods in, disillusionment follows when technology misses early expectations, then practical use grows. That one-off report became Gartner’s annual Hype Cycle of Emerging Technologies.

sources.title: The First Hype Cycle: An Origin Story - Jackie Fenn
Gartner hype cycle
Why the Hype?

Lezama-Nicolas, R., Rodriguez-Salvador, M., Rio-Belver, R., and Bildosola, I., 'A Bibliometric Method for Assessing Technological Maturity: The Case of Additive Manufacturing', Scientometrics 117 (2018): 1425-1452
sources.author: Lezama-Nicolas, Rene; Rodriguez-Salvador, Marisela; Rio-Belver, Rosa; Bildosola, Inaki
sources.confirms: The peer-reviewed article states that Gartner has depicted hype cycles since 1995 and describes the five phases from innovation trigger through peak of inflated expectations, trough of disillusionment and slope of enlightenment to plateau of productivity.

sources.title: Badenhorst, D. P., et al., 'Does Gartner's Hype Cycle Theory Match Practice?', in Human-Centred Technology Management for a Sustainable Future, IAMOT 2024 (Cham: Springer, 2025), 333-341
sources.author: Badenhorst, D. P.; Mashabane, S. T.; Morele, J. X.; Mutizwa, T.; Vundla, P. Q. M.; Grobbelaar, S.
sources.confirms: A systematic review treats the Gartner Hype Cycle as a widely used industry tool for assessing emerging technology maturity.

gartner-hype-cycle-1995.detail:
Fenn joined Gartner in 1994 and drew her first curve in MacDraw in February 1995. She took its phase labels from John Bunyan’s Pilgrim’s Progress, which headmistress Miss Mackie had read to her at school. Gartner’s 1996 edition placed Java, Internet Terminals and Worldwide Web near its peak, and by 2003 Alexander Linden had turned Fenn’s chart into an annual special report. Critics say it is neither cyclical nor scientific.

In an Ideaconnection interview Fenn described bandwagon behaviour: “people are reactive to the hype cycle, so they’re rushing in when the hype’s up and abandoning it when the hype’s down again.”

gps-full-operational-1995.summary: In 1995 GPS was declared fully operational, 24 satellites telling anyone on Earth where they are. The Defense Department had started GPS in 1973, launched a prototype in 1978 and completed its 24-satellite constellation in 1993, when the civilian Standard Positioning Service reached initial capability in December. After Soviet forces shot down Korean Air Lines Flight 007 in 1983, President Reagan ordered GPS opened to civilians from 1988, though Selective Availability limited civilian accuracy to about 100 metres until President Clinton switched it off on May 1, 2000.

Parkinson, Bradford W., "Origins, Evolution, and Future of Satellite Navigation", Journal of Guidance, Control, and Dynamics 20, no. 1 (1997), pp. 11-25
sources.author: Parkinson, Bradford W.
sources.venue: Journal of Guidance, Control, and Dynamics

gps-full-operational-1995.detail: Selective Availability was a deliberate error in GPS data that military receivers could correct. As civilian use grew, pressure to remove it grew too; it was disabled temporarily during the Gulf War, when a shortage of military receivers left many troops using civilian units. Defense Secretary William Perry proposed ending it because private differential GPS services were already improving civilian accuracy and because the military was developing ways to deny GPS regionally. After May 2000, GPS was accurate to about five metres, and in 2007 Washington announced that its next generation of satellites would omit Selective Availability.

iptn-n250-first-flight-1995.summary: On 10 August 1995, fiftieth anniversary of independence, IPTN's N-250 Gatotkaca makes its maiden flight at Bandung, a 50 to 70 seat turboprop with fly-by-wire controls designed in Indonesia under B. J. Habibie's technology-led industrial strategy. IPTN claims 192 orders at about 14 million dollars each and plans US certification with a plant in Alabama. Sulfikar Amir's account traces how state funds, including a disputed reforestation fund loan, kept development going until the 1997 financial crisis. A January 1998 IMF letter of intent cuts all budget support for IPTN aircraft, and N-250 never enters service. Its successor firm, PT Dirgantara Indonesia, builds CN-235 variants and parts for Airbus.

java-1995.summary: In 1995 Sun announced Java at SunWorld, a language whose programs ran unchanged across many platforms; it still runs most Android apps and banks. James Gosling, Mike Sheridan and Patrick Naughton had begun the language in June 1991, naming it Oak after a tree outside Gosling’s office, then Green, and finally Java after the coffee. Its syntax resembled C and C++, but programs compiled to bytecode that ran on any Java virtual machine, which Java 1.0 in 1996 promoted as “write once, run anywhere.” Major browsers soon ran Java applets inside web pages.

java-1995.detail: Java 1.0 promised no-cost runtimes on popular platforms and configurable security. J2SE 1.2 followed in December 1998. Sun released most of its Java virtual machine as free software between November 2006 and May 2007, Oracle acquired Sun in 2010, and Java 9 deprecated applets in 2017.

javascript-1995.summary: In 1995 Brendan Eich wrote JavaScript in ten days for Netscape's browser; it is now the language of every web page. Netscape had pursued two routes, adopting Sun’s Java and asking Eich to embed Scheme; management then chose a new language with Java-like syntax, meant “to help nonprogrammers create dynamic, interactive Web sites.” Shipped as LiveScript in Navigator’s September 1995 beta, it became JavaScript at its December release, a name Eich considered a marketing ploy. Netscape submitted it to Ecma International in November 1996, yielding ECMAScript in 1997.

sources.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages (HOPL IV)
sources.confirms: The peer-reviewed history by Eich and Wirfs-Brock describes JavaScript as a sidekick scripting language for Java created at Netscape in a ten-day hack in 1995 that became the world's most widely used language.

javascript-1995.detail: Microsoft reverse-engineered it as JScript in 1996, and incompatible implementations led sites to display “best viewed in” logos for each browser. Node.js is its most-used runtime outside browsers. JavaScript was prototype-based and supported functional programming from its start; Netscape’s aim was a “language for the masses.”

kdd-conference-1995.summary: In August 1995 the first KDD conference met in Montreal; data mining had grown from a workshop into a field. It continued the KDD workshops of 1989, 1991, 1993 and 1994, reorganised as an open conference because demand for participation and for formal proceedings had grown. Its call said rapid growth of data and information had created both need and opportunity to extract knowledge from databases, drawing on machine learning, statistics and database research, with applications in astronomy, biology, finance, insurance, marketing and medicine.

sources.title: KDD-95: First International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining - AAAI

kimchi-refrigerator-dimchae-1995.summary: In 1995 Korean car-parts maker Mando Machinery launches Dimchae, a chest-style refrigerator that uses direct cooling to hold kimchi at a steady temperature just below freezing, mimicking clay jars Koreans once buried in the ground to ferment it through winter. GoldStar, later LG, had sold a kimchi refrigerator in 1984 that found few buyers; Dimchae sold 5,000 in its first year, 80,000 in 1997, 228,000 in 1998 and 530,000 in 1999 as apartment living left no garden for jars. The Korea Times reported industry sales of 1.1 million units worth 1.1 trillion won in 2010, and Samsung and LG followed with their own lines.

metcalfe-internet-collapse-1995.summary: In December 1995 Robert Metcalfe predicted the internet would collapse within a year; he later ate his column, blended, on stage. He promised to eat his words if it did not; his column expected overload as ever more people tried to connect. When no collapse came, he kept his promise at his 1997 keynote to the sixth International World Wide Web Conference. Attendees rejected his offer to eat his words printed on a very large cake, so he put his printed column in a blender with liquid and swallowed that pulp.

metcalfe-internet-collapse-1995.detail: Metcalfe had co-invented Ethernet in 1973 and co-founded 3Com, and after leaving 3Com spent ten years as publisher and pundit writing an internet column for InfoWorld. He co-founded Pop!Tech in 1996, became a venture capitalist in 2001 and later a general partner at Polaris Venture Partners, and taught at UT Austin from 2011 to 2021. His column’s headline was “From the Ether: Predicting the Internet’s Catastrophic Collapse and Ghost Sites Galore in 1996,” and its forecast read: “I predict the Internet, which only just recently got this section here in InfoWorld, will soon go spectacularly supernova and in 1996 catastrophically collapse.”

negroponte-being-digital-1995.summary: In January 1995 Nicholas Negroponte's Being Digital said bits would replace atoms. Its first part rests on the difference between atoms and bits: atoms have physical mass, like printed books, while bits, which “move at the speed of light,” allow “instantaneous and inexpensive transfer of electronic data,” in his words. Negroponte named decentralizing, globalizing, harmonizing and empowering as four qualities of a digital age, predicted that high-definition television would become obsolete as television went digital, and introduced his “Daily Me,” a virtual daily newspaper customised to one reader’s tastes.

negroponte-being-digital-1995.detail:
Being Digital has an introduction, three parts and an epilogue, and gives a general history of digital media technologies, many of which Negroponte helped develop. Part two concerns computer interfaces and how poor design makes being digital needlessly complicated; part three, “Digital Life,” declares that humanity has entered its post-information age, where “true personalization” is imminent, with machines understanding individuals as humans understand humans.

Negroponte views good interface design as computers’ ability to “know you, learn about your needs, and understand verbal and nonverbal languages,” and he noted this drawback of bits, their “constraints of the medium on which it is stored or through which it is delivered.”

neo-luddite-sale-1995.summary: In 1995 Kirkpatrick Sale smashed a computer with a sledgehammer on a New York stage. Before 1,500 people he spoke for about ninety seconds on how technology, as he saw it, was destroying the biosphere, then broke screen and keyboard with two blows; some listeners applauded. He later said, “It was a statement,” better than anything he could say in four minutes. His book of that year, subtitled “Lessons for the Computer Age,” made him one of 1990s Neo-Luddism’s most visible figures; its Second Luddite Congress met in 1996.

sources.title: [PDF] Generative AI and the (Re)turn to Luddism - T. Philip Nichols

neo-luddite-sale-1995.detail:
The original Luddites were English clothworkers who in 1811 and 1812 broke into factories and destroyed gig mills, stocking frames and other machines that threatened their wages. They took their name from Ned Ludd, an apocryphal apprentice said to have smashed a stocking frame after his employer punished him. Sale told Wired’s Kevin Kelly, in “Interview with the Luddite” of June 1, 1995, that they raised the “machinery question”: whether machines served only industrialists or whether people affected by technology should have a say in its use. He predicted that industrial civilization could collapse “within decades” through economic collapse, social unrest and environmental degradation, and accepted Kelly’s bet against it.

Sale distinguished his spectacle from Neo-Luddism’s non-violent ethos, telling the Second Luddite Congress that violent resistance was “misguided and counterproductive.”

netscape-ipo-1995.summary: On 9 August 1995 Netscape's shares went public and nearly tripled on their first day, and money poured into internet companies for five years. Shares were to be offered at $14, but a last-minute decision doubled that to $28; they soared to $75 during first-day trading, nearly a record gain, and closed at $58.25, valuing Netscape at $2.9 billion. Going public while unprofitable was unusual, though Netscape’s revenues had doubled every quarter in 1995. “Netscape moment” became a term for high-visibility IPOs signalling new industries.

netscape-ipo-1995.detail:
Jim Clark founded Mosaic Communications Corporation on April 4, 1994, sixteen months before its IPO. He recruited Marc Andreessen, who had worked on NCSA Mosaic at the University of Illinois, as co-founder and Kleiner Perkins as investors; Jim Barksdale became CEO in January 1995. Its first browser, Mosaic Netscape 0.9, shipped on October 13, 1994 and took three-quarters of the browser market within four months. Netscape stock listed on NASDAQ as NSCP.

Public relations head Rosanne Siino packaged Andreessen as Netscape’s “rock star,” and he appeared barefoot on Time’s cover. Netscape’s browser share fell from more than 90 percent in the mid-1990s to under one percent by 2006 after losing the first browser war to Microsoft’s Internet Explorer, and AOL acquired Netscape in 1999 in a deal worth $10 billion.

no-hands-across-america-1995.summary: In July 1995 a Carnegie Mellon minivan steered 98 percent of the way from Pittsburgh to San Diego on its own; humans worked the pedals. They dubbed this proof-of-concept trip “No Hands Across America,” because its computer steered for all but 50 of 2,850 miles while averaging over 60 mph. Navlab is Carnegie Mellon Robotics Institute’s series of autonomous and semi-autonomous vehicles; its research on computer-controlled vehicles began in 1984 under DARPA’s Strategic Computing Initiative, and Navlab 1 followed in 1986. Navlab 5 joined the Robot Hall of Fame’s class of 2008.

no-hands-across-america-1995.detail:
Navlab 1 was built in 1986 from a Chevrolet panel van carrying five racks of computer hardware, including three Sun workstations. It burned in 1989 when its conditioning system leaked liquid onto the computers. Navlabs 1 and 2 were semi-autonomous, estimating position with steering wheel and drive shaft encoders and an expensive inertial navigation system. Later vehicles ran to Navlab 11, built from cars, vans, SUVs and buses for off-road scouting, automated highways, run-off-road collision prevention and driver assistance in crowded cities.

Carnegie Mellon also developed ALVINN in 1988, a three-layer neural network trained by backpropagation to steer from camera images.

rabbit-calicivirus-escape-wardang-1995.summary: CSIRO and state agencies were testing rabbit calicivirus (RHDV) in pens on Wardang Island, South Australia, when in October 1995 virus reached mainland near Yunta, probably carried by flies. Within months it killed millions of rabbits across arid zones, with mortality above 90 percent in some districts, before formal release was approved in October 1996. Cooke and Fenner's 2002 review records vegetation recovery and knock-on effects on predators; Cooke's 2014 book and 2018 monitoring paper assess long-term impact and growing resistance. New Zealand farmers smuggled virus in 1997 after regulators refused import. Escape echoed myxomatosis release of 1950 and renewed debate on biological control.

random-forest-1995.summary: In 1995 Tin Kam Ho built the first random decision forest, many trees voting on random subsets of features. Random forests build many decision trees during training and combine them, by majority vote for classification and by averaging for regression, which corrects a single tree’s habit of overfitting its training set. Ho showed that such forests gain accuracy as they grow, without overtraining, provided each tree is randomly restricted to selected feature dimensions. Leo Breiman and Adele Cutler’s extension combined Breiman’s bagging with random feature selection, and they trademarked “Random Forests” in 2006.

random-forest-1995.detail: Salzberg and Heath first proposed random decision forests in 1993, growing multiple trees with a randomized algorithm and combining them by majority vote. Ho’s formulation implements the “stochastic discrimination” approach proposed by Eugene Kleinberg, whose theory explains why forests resist overtraining. Her finding that larger forests grow more accurate nearly monotonically contradicts common belief that classifier complexity can only grow so far before overfitting hurts. Amit and Geman later introduced random feature selection independently. Bagging repeatedly draws random samples with replacement from its training set and fits trees to them. Minitab, Inc. owned that trademark as of 2019.

rifkin-end-of-work-1995.summary: In 1995 Jeremy Rifkin's The End of Work predicted machines would make most labour unnecessary; unemployment then fell for five years. Rifkin argued that computers, robotics, telecommunications and other technologies were replacing workers in virtually every sector, from manufacturing, retail and financial services to transportation, agriculture and government, bringing steady decline in jobs. He urged preparing institutions for a world without mass employment, with alternatives to formal work and new sources of income and purchasing power, in chapters titled “Re-engineering the work week,” “A new social contract” and “Empowering the third sector.”

rifkin-end-of-work-1995.detail:
ERIC’s record (ED391963) describes five sections. Section one surveys effects of a technology revolution on employment and two competing visions of technological progress. Section two examines early automation’s effects on African-American workers and trade unionists as harbingers for service, white-collar and professional employees worldwide. Section three describes changes in agriculture, manufacturing and services; section four traces a “third industrial revolution” across global labor forces; section five proposes practical steps to mitigate mass technological displacement while reaping high technology’s rewards. Its bibliography holds 140 references.

Other chapters cover trickle-down technology and market realities, a great automation debate, farmers’ disappearance, blue-collar jobs’ end, service workers’ last stand, a requiem for working-class labour and globalizing social economies.

sampoong-department-store-collapse-1995.summary: At 5:57 pm on 29 June 1995, south wing of Sampoong Department Store in Seocho district, Seoul, fell into its basements in about twenty seconds, killing 502 people and injuring 937. Investigators found a flat-slab reinforced concrete structure converted from offices to retail during construction, columns thinned and spaced to add escalators, a fifth floor added for restaurants with heated floors, and 87-tonne air-conditioning units dragged across roof two years earlier, which cracked slabs. Managers saw widening cracks that morning and kept store open. Owners were convicted of negligence. Korea's government responded with building inspection reform and a disaster management act.

stoll-internet-bah-1995.summary: In February 1995 Clifford Stoll wrote in Newsweek that no online database would replace a newspaper. His essay “The Internet? Bah!” appeared on February 27, summarising his book Silicon Snake Oil. Stoll, who had caught hackers online, called it “this most trendy and oversold community,” unfit for commerce since his local mall did more business in one afternoon than the entire Internet handled in a month, and predicted networks would not change how government works. Poynter notes his essay became an online cult classic, rediscovered as its forecasts fell flat; Newsweek revisited it in 2017 as laughably inaccurate.

sources.title: We Red-Penned This Laughably Inaccurate Internet Essay

stoll-internet-bah-1995.detail:
Silicon Snake Oil’s subtitle was Second Thoughts on the Information Highway. Stoll complained that online life lacked editors, reviewers or critics and isolated people rather than connecting them, and dismissed catalog shopping because networks lacked trustworthy payment and “a most essential ingredient of capitalism: salespeople.”

His forecast read: “no online database will replace your daily newspaper, no CD-ROM can take the place of a competent teacher and no computer network will change the way government works.”

On community he wrote: “Computers and networks isolate us from one another. A network chat line is a limp substitute for meeting friends over coffee.” Gizmodo and Poynter reproduce these passages; Newsweek’s 2017 revisit says it resurfaced in 2010 as an insta-meme, long enough for Stoll to see his predictions fall flat.

svm-1995.summary: In 1995 Cortes and Vapnik published the support vector machine; it was the best classifier for a decade before deep learning passed it. Support vector machines classify data by choosing, among many possible boundaries (hyperplanes), one with maximum margin between two classes, which makes them resilient to noisy or misclassified examples. Vapnik and Alexey Chervonenkis invented its original algorithm in 1964; in 1992 Bernhard Boser, Isabelle Guyon and Vapnik added the kernel trick for nonlinear classification. Their soft-margin version, now common in software packages, extends SVMs to data that no hyperplane separates cleanly.

svm-1995.detail: SVMs are among the most studied models, grounded in VC theory of statistical learning, which Vapnik and Chervonenkis proposed. That kernel trick maps inputs implicitly into higher-dimensional space where linear separation becomes possible; kernel functions represent data through pairwise similarity comparisons so that dot products in that space can be computed from original variables, keeping computation manageable. Their soft-margin version uses what is called hinge loss. SVMs also serve regression tasks.

times-mirror-online-survey-1995.summary: In 1995 a Times Mirror survey found 14 percent of Americans had ever gone online and 4 percent had the day before. Princeton Survey Research Associates interviewed 3,603 adults in May and June 1995 for this second annual study, plus 402 extra online users. Online meant connecting by home computer and modem, or from work or school, to information services, bulletin boards or other computers, including the Internet. Online service subscribers had grown from 5 million in winter 1994 to nearly 12 million by June 1995; users were younger, better educated and more affluent than Americans overall.

sources.title: Americans Going Online…Explosive Growth, Uncertain ...

About this Survey

times-mirror-online-survey-1995.detail:
Its overview refers to 4,005 respondents; margins of error were plus or minus 2 points for all adults and 3 points for 997 online users. Andrew Kohut directed the Times Mirror Center for The People & The Press, which published it as “Technology in the American Household: Americans Going Online… Explosive Growth, Uncertain Destinations.”

It estimated nearly 6 million Americans went online daily, nearly 18 million at least weekly and as many as 25 million ever; just 20 percent of online users went online every day, and 2 million connected to the Internet without a commercial service. Households with a home PC modem rose from 12 percent in 1994 to 20 percent in 1995, 18 million homes, yet more than 8 million of those modems went unused. Twelve million Americans were regular e-mail users, 7 million regularly read news online and 5 million navigated the World Wide Web. Weekly use ran from 22 percent of college graduates to 1 percent of people without a high school diploma, and from 15 percent of those aged 18 to 29 to 2 percent of those 65 and older.

unabomber-manifesto-1995.summary: In September 1995 the Washington Post and New York Times together printed the Unabomber’s manifesto against industrial society. Its author, who had sent at least sixteen bombs since 1978, mailed both papers copies in June, threatening to kill again unless they printed it in full within 90 days. Their publishers agreed at Justice Department and FBI urging, saying publication “could help save lives”; it ran as an eight-page Post insert, half paid by the Times. Its text gave critical clues: David Kaczynski recognised his brother Ted’s writing, and Ted was arrested in Montana on April 3, 1996.

sources.title: Newspapers Printed Unabomber’s Manifesto in 1995. It’s Still ...

unabomber-manifesto-1995.detail:
EBSCO describes its themes as antigovernment, anti-big business and antitechnology, dwelling on technology’s control over individuals. Its author’s bombs, mailed or hand-delivered, killed three people and wounded twenty-three in just under seventeen years. David Kaczynski had seen letters from his brother that resembled it and contacted authorities; FBI forensic linguists matched these writings. Ted Kaczynski, living in a small cabin in Montana’s mountains, pleaded guilty to federal charges in 1998 and received four life terms without parole, escaping execution, which prosecutors had sought.

In 2023 the New York Times wrote that both papers took nearly all 90 days to decide, that publishers rather than newsroom leaders made that call, that the Post printed it apart from its news sections because of weekday printing capacity, and that printing still divides journalists.

vsnl-internet-india-1995.summary: In August 1995 India's state carrier opened internet access to the public in five cities; India's software industry had its market. Its chairman B. K. Syngal was later called India's father of the internet. Accounts cost 15,000 rupees for individuals and 5,000 for text only, and dial-up users endured busy signals, dropped calls and disconnection every three minutes. Syngal admitted, “I goofed up big time,” asked for ten weeks, and within about eight had added servers, moved to fibre, cut tariffs by half or more and recruited private franchisees.

vsnl-internet-india-1995.detail:
VSNL was founded in March 1986 to manage India’s international telecommunications; Syngal chaired it from 1991 to 1998. Business accounts cost 25,000 rupees and callers outside those five cities paid 35 rupees a minute. Syngal borrowed ideas from British Telecom, AT&T and early Indian enthusiasts including actor Shammi Kapoor, who had used an Apple beta online account since 1994, and let customers carry over unused time. He called those tariffs obscene: “Quite simply, the charges were too much, the quality of service was poor.”

After government disinvestment, Tata Group acquired VSNL in 2002, and it became Tata Communications on 13 February 2008. BBC says India was among Asia’s first countries with commercial internet service, and newspapers called its launch India’s “Second Independence Day.”

windows-95-1995.summary: In August 1995 Windows 95 launched with a $1 billion campaign and the Start button. Its commercial used The Rolling Stones’ 1981 single “Start Me Up,” alluding to its Start button, and a 30-minute promotional video, billed as a “cyber sitcom,” starred Jennifer Aniston and Matthew Perry. Windows 95 replaced Windows 3.1, merging MS-DOS and Windows into one product with 32-bit preemptive multitasking, Windows Explorer, a taskbar with Start menu, desktop shortcuts, Plug and Play drivers and filenames up to 255 characters. One million copies shipped worldwide in four days.

windows-95-1995.detail:
Microsoft released Windows 95 to manufacturing on July 14, 1995, and release-day sales were projected as high as $720 million. Its predecessor used mainly cooperative 16-bit multitasking. Reports said Microsoft paid $8 to $14 million for Mick Jagger’s song; Microsoft said it paid $3 million and called the higher figure a rumour spread by band members to raise their market value. Its $200 million advertising campaign featured people queuing outside stores; in Britain PC World branches opened at midnight, and Microsoft paid for 1.5 million free copies of The Times, twice its daily circulation. New York’s Empire State Building was lit in Windows colours and a 100-metre banner hung from Toronto’s CN Tower.

Windows 95 shipped with Microsoft’s dial-up service, The Microsoft Network, and its desktop, taskbar, Start menu and Windows Explorer stayed fundamentally unchanged in later Windows versions. Brian Eno composed its startup sound. International Data Corporation found it running 57.4 percent of desktops at 1998’s end, with Windows 98 second at 17.2 percent.

wirths-law-1995.summary: In 1995 Niklaus Wirth wrote that software was getting slower faster than hardware was getting faster; Wirth's law, which one source states as software's girth outpacing its functionality. Wirth credited Martin Reiser’s preface to his Oberon System book, which warned that software “manages to outgrow hardware in size and sluggishness,” and Reiser is independently associated with it too. He blamed two factors, “rapidly growing hardware performance” and “customers’ ignorance of features that are essential versus nice-to-have,” since customers mistake complexity for sophistication, and argued for leaner software.

wirths-law-1995.detail:
Wirth pointed to his own Oberon system of 1986 to 1989, which ran on a fraction of typical memory and processor power. Others had noticed this trend by 1987. Of inessential features Wirth wrote: “these details are cute but not essential, and they have a hidden cost.”

Variants include Gates’s law, which holds that “the speed of software halves every 18 months,” the saying “What Andy giveth, Bill taketh away,” and Page’s law, which Sergey Brin cited at Google I/O in 2009.

al-jazeera-launch-1996.summary: In November 1996 Al Jazeera went on air from Doha, the first Arab channel to broadcast open debate. It filled a gap left by BBC Arabic Television, closed after Saudi backers tried to block a documentary on executions, and hired many of its journalists. After a six-hour test broadcast screened in London, the emir chose an all-news format. It aired six hours daily at launch, twelve by late 1997 and 24 hours from 1 January 1999, free by satellite to Arab viewers.

al-jazeera-launch-1996.detail: Qatar’s government lent about $137 million at launch, later converted to a grant, with a mandate of independence. In March 1998 Qatar’s emir disbanded its Ministry of Information, which had overseen press censorship. Staff more than tripled within twelve months to about 500, with bureaus in twelve places including the European Union, Russia and Taliban-controlled Afghanistan, and yearly spending estimated at $30 million.

bermuda-principles-1996.summary: In February 1996 genome scientists in Bermuda agreed to post DNA sequence within 24 hours of reading it; the human genome stayed public. Scientists had normally held data until publication, so this agreement, also called the Bermuda Accord, broke with standard practice. Its three principles called for automatic release of sequence assemblies larger than 1 kilobase, preferably within 24 hours, immediate publication of finished annotated sequences, and placing whole sequences in the public domain for research and development. They made rapid pre-publication release standard in genomics.

sources.title: Bermuda Principles (Wikipedia)

Maxson Jones, Kathryn, Ankeny, Rachel A. and Cook-Deegan, Robert, 'The Bermuda Triangle: The Pragmatics, Policies, and Principles for Data Sharing in the History of the Human Genome Project', Journal of the History of Biology 51 (2018) 693-805
sources.author: Maxson Jones, Kathryn; Ankeny, Rachel A.; Cook-Deegan, Robert
sources.venue: Journal of the History of Biology
sources.confirms: The February 1996 Bermuda meeting agreed to release sequence data within 24 hours.

sources.title: Wellcome Trust, Report of the International Strategy Meeting on Human Genome Sequencing held at the Princess Hotel, Southampton, Bermuda, 25-28 February 1996 (archived by NHGRI)
sources.author: Wellcome Trust
sources.venue: National Human Genome Research Institute archive
sources.confirms: Participants from the Wellcome Trust, MRC, NIH NCHGR, DOE, Germany, the European Commission, HUGO and Japan agreed that human genomic sequence from large-scale centres should be in the public domain, with assemblies over 1 kb released automatically, preferably daily, and finished annotated sequence submitted immediately.
sources.qualifies: The principles said preferably daily; the explicit 24-hour rule entered NHGRI policy in April 1997.

sources.title: National Institutes of Health, 'Human Genome Project Timeline: 1996, Bermuda Principles encourage open data access'
sources.author: National Institutes of Health
sources.confirms: In February 1996 Human Genome Project leaders meeting in Bermuda decided that human sequence from federally funded centres should be freely available within 24 hours of generation, a break with the practice of releasing data only after publication.

bermuda-principles-1996.detail: Their practice spread to other fields beyond genomics, and public-domain release was meant to maximise benefits to society.

brazil-electronic-voting-1996.summary: In 1996 Brazil began voting on electronic machines; by 2000 all of Brazil counted its votes in hours. Omnitech, Microbase and Unisys do Brasil built its first machine, UE96, modified from IBM PC 80386 clone hardware, for the Superior Electoral Court. Each urna eletrônica records ballots locally, encrypts and stores them, and produces digital tallies at day’s end. In 2000 Brazil completed its first fully automated election, and as of 2023 it is the only country voting entirely electronically.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Electronic voting in Brazil
'How to Implement Anywhere Voting: A Case Study of Brazil', Springer Lecture Notes (Springer, 2025), ch. 8
sources.author: Springer
sources.confirms: Before 1996 Brazilian elections used paper ballots counted by hand, which enabled fraud; electronic voting began in 1996.

sources.title: Article on the phased introduction of electronic voting in Brazil and enfranchisement, Journal of Applied Economics 23 (2020)
sources.author: Journal of Applied Economics
sources.confirms: Brazil's phased introduction of electronic voting enfranchised low-income voters.

brazil-electronic-voting-1996.detail:
Brazil’s Electoral Justice, headed by the Superior Electoral Court and Regional Electoral Courts, runs voter registration, vote collection, tabulation, transmission and certification; the machine is one component. Later models were UE98, from Diebold-Procomp, Microbase and Samurai, and UE2000. Microbase’s VirtuOS operating system served in 1996, 1998 and 2000; Microsoft supplied Windows CE licences free in 2002, and in 2008 the court moved to Linux, dubbed UEnux, to cut costs.

Critics note that voters get no receipt, although printed tallies allow audits; no case of election fraud has been uncovered.

brazil-universal-antiretroviral-access-1.summary: On 13 November 1996 President Fernando Henrique Cardoso signed Law 9.313, obliging Sistema Único de Saúde to supply every medicine needed for HIV treatment free of charge, months after combination therapy was shown effective. Brazil's health ministry negotiated prices with multinationals, had public laboratories such as Far-Manguinhos produce generic versions of older drugs, and threatened compulsory licences, cutting per-patient costs by more than two thirds in five years. By 2002 about 125,000 people were on therapy and AIDS mortality had fallen by around half from its 1995 peak, with hospitalisations down sharply. The programme, built with activist networks, became the reference case cited at World Trade Organization debates over patents and public health and inspired treatment programmes in other middle-income countries.

sources.title: Nunn, Amy S.; Fonseca, Elize M.; Bastos, Francisco I.; Gruskin, Sofia; Salomon, Joshua A., 'Evolution of Antiretroviral Drug Costs in Brazil in the Context of Free and Universal Access to AIDS Treatment', PLoS Medicine 4, no. 11 (2007)
sources.author: Nunn, Amy S.; Fonseca, Elize M.; Bastos, Francisco I.; Gruskin, Sofia; Salomon, Joshua A.

sources.title: Galvão, Jane, 'Access to antiretroviral drugs in Brazil', The Lancet 360 (2002)
sources.author: Galvão, Jane
sources.confirms: Mortality and hospitalisation declines, patient numbers around 2002.

sources.title: Brasil, Lei nº 9.313, de 13 de novembro de 1996
sources.confirms: Text and date of law guaranteeing free distribution of HIV medicines by SUS.

brazil-universal-antiretroviral-access-1.detail: Brazil issued its first compulsory licence, on efavirenz, in 2007. Brazil's 1988 constitution had defined health as a right and duty of state, which courts enforced in AIDS cases from 1991. Public labs produced zidovudine from 1993. In 2001 United States filed and then withdrew a WTO complaint over Brazil's patent law. A 2001 Doha Declaration on TRIPS and public health drew on Brazilian and South African arguments.

cloud-computing-term-1996.summary: In 1996 a Compaq business plan used “cloud computing”, by Regalado's 2011 report; NetCentric filed a trademark in May 1997, its earliest archived use; a name for renting computers over the internet preceded its business. Compaq hoped to supercharge sales with “cloud computing-enabled applications,” and since its plan foresaw commercial success for online consumer file storage, it decided to sell server hardware to internet service providers. This cloud metaphor dates to 1994, when General Magic used it for places mobile agents could go in its Telescript environment, drawing on long-standing use in networking and telecom. Cloud services arrived in the 2000s.

sources.title: Cloud computing (Wikipedia)
Regalado, Antonio, 'Who Coined "Cloud Computing"?', MIT Technology Review, 31 October 2011
sources.author: Regalado, Antonio
sources.confirms: Regalado documents a 50-page Compaq plan, 'Internet Solutions Division Strategy for Cloud Computing', dated 14 November 1996, as the earliest known printed use of the phrase, with George Favaloro and Sean O'Sullivan each claiming the coinage.

sources.title: United States Patent and Trademark Office, Trademark Status and Document Retrieval, Serial No. 75291765, 'CLOUD COMPUTING', NetCentric Corporation, filed 14 May 1997, abandoned 21 April 1999
sources.venue: United States Patent and Trademark Office
sources.confirms: Official record that NetCentric Corporation of Cambridge, Massachusetts, the Compaq-backed startup named in the record, applied to register 'cloud computing' as a service mark on 14 May 1997 and abandoned the application in 1999.

cloud-computing-term-1996.verification_note: Only Regalado's 2011 report documents Compaq's November 1996 plan, whose scan is no longer online; NetCentric's May 1997 trademark application is its earliest independently archived use.
cloud-computing-term-1996.detail: Amazon Web Services was established in 2002, and Amazon S3 and EC2 followed in 2006. Microsoft launched Azure in 2010, as Rackspace and NASA began OpenStack that same year; IBM SmartCloud came in 2011 and Oracle Cloud in 2012. This idea traces further back, to time-sharing and remote job entry in the 1960s.

copaxone-fda-approval-1996.summary: US Food and Drug Administration approves glatiramer acetate, sold by Teva as Copaxone, on 20 December 1996 for relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis. Compound began in late 1960s at Weizmann Institute in Rehovot, where Michael Sela, Ruth Arnon and Dvora Teitelbaum synthesised random copolymers of four amino acids to mimic myelin basic protein and induce disease in animals; copolymer 1 instead suppressed it. Bornstein's pilot trial in 1987 and a multicentre trial in 1990s carried it to approval. It becomes Israel's first original drug to reach world market and, for two decades, Teva's largest product with sales above 4 billion dollars a year. Its mechanism, immune modulation by a synthetic peptide mixture, remains partly unexplained.

sources.title: Bornstein, M. B., Miller, A., Slagle, S., et al. (1987). A pilot trial of Cop 1 in exacerbating-remitting multiple sclerosis. New England Journal of Medicine 317(7), 408-414.

csiro-wlan-patent-1996.summary: In January 1996 CSIRO patented a wireless technique born of radio astronomy; it became part of Wi-Fi and earned Australia $430 million. John O’Sullivan, Graham Daniels, Terence Percival, Diethelm Ostry and John Deane had sought wireless networks matching wired speeds inside buildings such as offices, and combined forward error correction, frequency-domain interleaving and multi-carrier modulation to get there. In 1998 the patent proved pertinent to the IEEE 802.11a Wi-Fi standard, and CSIRO promised licences on reasonable and non-discriminatory terms. Settlements with equipment makers and carriers eventually earned it nearly $430 million.

sources.title: Wikipedia: CSIRO
O'Sullivan, John; Daniels, Graham; Percival, Terence; Ostry, Diethelm; Deane, John, US Patent 5,487,069, "Wireless LAN", granted 23 January 1996 (assignee CSIRO)
sources.author: O'Sullivan, John; Daniels, Graham; Percival, Terence; Ostry, Diethelm; Deane, John

sources.author: Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation
sources.confirms: The agency's account of the radio-astronomy origins of the technique, its inclusion in the 802.11 standards and the licensing income from settlements.
sources.qualifies: Institutional self-history; the $430 million total is CSIRO's own figure.

csiro-wlan-patent-1996.detail:
Radiata, founded in 1997 by David Skellern and Neil Weste of Macquarie University, took a nonexclusive licence and was bought by Cisco in November 2000 for US$295 million in stock. Controversy began in 2006 when CSIRO won an injunction against Buffalo Technology in the Eastern District of Texas, later suspended on appeal. Hewlett-Packard settled first in April 2009, followed by Microsoft, Fujitsu, Asus, Dell, Intel, Nintendo, Toshiba, Netgear, Buffalo, D-Link, Belkin, SMC, Accton and 3Com.

After CSIRO sued AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile in 2010, critics called it “Australia’s biggest patent troll” and accused it of a “WiFi tax”; the carriers settled for about $229 million in March 2012. O’Sullivan’s team received the European Inventor Award on 14 June 2012.

cyberspace-declaration-1996.summary: In 1996 John Perry Barlow told governments they had no sovereignty online, an early-web creed later policy reversed. Commissioned for 24 Hours in Cyberspace, it answered America’s Telecommunications Act of 1996, which he said “repudiates your own Constitution.” In sixteen paragraphs echoing America’s Declaration of Independence, it told governments “You have no sovereignty where we gather,” arguing that they lacked consent of the governed online and that cyberspace was forming its own social contracts. Within nine months about 40,000 sites had copied it.

sources.title: Critical response
A Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace
A Cyberspace Independence Declaration

cyberspace-declaration-1996.detail:
Its opening line addresses governments directly. “Governments of the Industrial World, you weary giants of flesh and steel, I come from Cyberspace, the new home of Mind.” Besides America, it accuses China, Germany, France, Russia, Singapore and Italy of stifling the internet. Barlow emailed it from Davos on 9 February 1996, and Carnegie Mellon’s copy preserves that message.

Critics faulted its inconsistencies and its neglect of cyberspace’s physical geography. Larry Irving of the Commerce Department said a lack of safeguards would “slow down the growth of what is likely to be a major boon for consumers and business.” Copies fell to about 20,000 sites by 2002. In 2004 Barlow said “we all get older and smarter,” but told Wired in 2016 that he stood by his words.

picture.alt: John Perry Barlow, author of A Declaration of Independence of Cyberspace, photographed in 2012
picture.credit: Mohamed Nanabhay, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

deep-blue-kasparov-1996.summary: In February 1996 Kasparov beat Deep Blue 4 to 2 after losing Game 1, a champion’s first loss to a machine; a rematch followed. Game 1 was the first game any computer had won against a reigning world champion under normal tournament conditions and classical time controls. Kasparov won Game 2 after a configuration error left Deep Blue without its opening book, drew Games 3 and 4, then took Games 5 and 6 with long-term planning and anti-computer tactics. IBM Research offered prizes of $400,000 and $100,000.

sources.title: 1997 rematch
'February 10: Deep Blue Defeats Kasparov | This Day in History', Computer History Museum (1996)
sources.confirms: The page says that in the first game of a six-game match on February 10, 1996, Deep Blue defeated world champion Garry Kasparov, who eventually won the series 4-2 and lost to Deep Blue in a rematch a year later.

sources.title: Long, Tony, 'Feb. 10, 1996: Checkmate', Wired (2007)
sources.author: Long, Tony
sources.confirms: The page says Kasparov lost the initial game against Deep Blue in their 1996 match, then won the next game, drew the following two, and won games five and six to secure a 4-2 victory; it also says he lost a rematch to Deep Blue the following year.

deep-blue-kasparov-1996.detail: Game 2 ran 73 moves; Deep Blue’s “extended book” reproduced opening theory to move 13 by scoring moves against 700,000 grandmaster games. Game 5 on February 16 was decisive: Deep Blue’s team declined Kasparov’s draw offer after move 23, and it became the only game Black won. The rematch in New York in May 1997 went to Deep Blue, 3½ to 2½.

dolly-the-sheep-1996.summary: In July 1996 Dolly the sheep was cloned from an adult cell at Roslin; a grown animal's cell could start a new life. Keith Campbell and Ian Wilmut's team, with PPL Therapeutics, used somatic cell nuclear transfer: donor nuclei from mammary gland cells went into unfertilised eggs stripped of their own nuclei, electric shocks started division, and surrogate ewes carried those embryos. Of 277 attempts she alone survived to adulthood, proof that mature cells’ genes can revert to embryonic form.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Dolly (sheep)
I. Wilmut, A. E. Schnieke, J. McWhir, A. J. Kind and K. H. S. Campbell, 'Viable offspring derived from fetal and adult mammalian cells', Nature 385 (1997), 810-813
sources.author: Ian Wilmut; Angelika E. Schnieke; Jim McWhir; Alex J. Kind; Keith H. S. Campbell
sources.confirms: Reports the lamb cloned from an adult mammary cell by nuclear transfer, born in 1996 and published February 1997.

sources.title: 'Dolly', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Records that Dolly, born 5 July 1996 at the Roslin Institute and announced in February 1997, was the first mammal cloned from an adult somatic cell.

dolly-the-sheep-1996.detail:
Three ewes count as her mothers: egg donor, DNA donor and surrogate. Her birth was announced on 22 February 1997, and Science named it breakthrough of the year; her name honours Dolly Parton because her donor cell came from mammary tissue. She was not the first cloned animal, since John Gurdon had cloned frogs in 1958.

She bore six lambs between 1998 and 2000, developed arthritis in late 2001 and was euthanised on 14 February 2003 for progressive lung disease, aged six and a half against breed expectancy of 11 to 12 years; no link to cloning was found. Her preserved body has been exhibited at the National Museum of Scotland since 2003.

picture.alt: Preserved Dolly the sheep on display at National Museum of Scotland in Edinburgh, photographed 2017.
picture.credit: london road, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

dvd-1996.summary: In November 1996 the DVD went on sale in Japan, holding 4.7 gigabytes on a single layer, seven times a CD; film distributors adopted it to replace VHS tape. Two rival discs had competed in 1995, Philips and Sony’s Multimedia Compact Disc and the Super Density disc backed by Toshiba, Time Warner and others, until five computer companies led by IBM threatened to boycott both; both camps agreed to unify on September 15, 1995 and finalised details on December 8.

sources.title: Wikipedia: DVD
Toshiba Corporation, "Toshiba Introduces its First DVD-Video Player in Japan"
sources.author: Toshiba Corporation
sources.confirms: Announcement of the SD-3000 player for Japanese release in November 1996, single-layer discs holding 4.7 GB.

sources.author: Kees A. Schouhamer Immink
sources.confirms: Contemporary peer-reviewed description of the DVD format's 4.7 gigabyte single-layer capacity and coding; Crossref metadata confirmed.

sources.author: National Museum of Nature and Science
sources.venue: Center of the History of Japanese Industrial Technology
sources.confirms: Registers Toshiba's 1996 SD-3000 as the DVD player that marked the start of the DVD era.

dvd-1996.detail:
The computer group, IBM, Apple, Compaq, Hewlett-Packard and Microsoft, issued its ultimatum on May 3, 1995 and recruited IBM’s Lou Gerstner to pressure both camps. One compromise adopted proposal SD 9, reading both layers of a dual-layer disc from one side rather than making users flip discs. The name shifted from digital video disc to digital versatile disc after computer companies complained that video left out their uses.

Warner Home Video’s first four titles arrived on December 20, 1996; the U.S. launch, delayed several times, came on March 24, 1997 in seven test markets with about 32 titles. DVD players outsold VCRs in the United States in 2001, and DVD rentals overtook VHS rentals in June 2003.

gm-ev1-1996.summary: In 1996 General Motors leased the EV1, the first mass-produced electric car from Detroit; in 2003 it took every one back and crushed them. It answered California’s 1990 Air Resources Board mandate requiring seven leading automakers to sell zero-emission vehicles to keep access to that market, and grew from GM’s 1990 Impact concept. GM leased them through its Saturn division under terms forbidding purchase; 288 went out in year one and 1,117 were built in all. Judging electric cars an unprofitable niche, GM recalled its leased cars from 2002 and crushed most of them.

sources.confirms: General Motors leased 1,117 EV1s from 1996 before recalling and destroying nearly all of them.

sources.author: Donald W. Nauss
sources.confirms: Reports first EV1 deliveries on 5 December 1996 through 24 Saturn dealerships in Southern California and Arizona, lease only, at $34,000.

sources.title: 'Electric Appliances Come Alive to Sell Their G.M. Sibling, the EV1.' New York Times, 4 December 1996.
sources.author: New York Times
sources.confirms: Confirms GM offered the two-seat EV1 for lease through Saturn dealers in four western markets from December 1996.

gm-ev1-1996.detail:
Early leases went mostly to drivers in California, Arizona and Georgia. First-generation cars used Delco lead-acid packs rated at 16.5 kWh, giving 60 to 100 miles of range; second-generation cars from 1999 moved to Panasonic lead-acid packs and later Ovonics nickel-metal hydride batteries. Estimates put GM’s cost per car between $80,000 and $100,000, and GM spent just under $500 million on the EV1 and related technology.

Fifty-eight drivers sent letters and deposit checks proposing lease extensions at no cost to GM, which refused and ended its program in late 2003 under CEO Rick Wagoner. Former lessees and environmental groups accused GM of sabotaging its own program. Its cancellation inspired a 2006 documentary, Who Killed the Electric Car?

hiv-haart-1996.summary: Protease inhibitor saquinavir reached the US market in December 1995, and at the eleventh International AIDS Conference in Vancouver in July 1996 researchers reported that three drugs together pushed virus in blood below detection and kept it there. ACTG 320, a trial of indinavir with zidovudine and lamivudine in 1,156 patients with advanced disease, halved progression to AIDS or death (6 percent against 11 percent). Deaths from AIDS in rich countries fell by more than half within two years. Brazil's Law 9,313 of November 1996 made it the first middle-income country to guarantee free antiretrovirals to every patient through its public health system, producing generics and bargaining prices down; its programme became a template for global treatment scale-up in the 2000s.

icq-1996.summary: In 1996 ICQ let internet users see who was online and message them. Live chat already existed on Internet Relay Chat, but ICQ offered centralised individual accounts built for one-to-one conversation, a design later messengers such as AIM followed. It spread by word of mouth without conventional marketing and became the first widely adopted instant messaging platform. AOL bought Mirabilis on June 8, 1998 for $287 million plus up to $120 million in performance payments.

'America Online to Buy Internet Chat Service for $287 Million', New York Times, 9 June 1998
sources.confirms: Mirabilis, an Israeli start-up, launched ICQ in 1996 and had some 12 million users when AOL bought it in 1998.

sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica

icq-1996.detail: Yair Goldfinger, Sefi Vigiser, Amnon Amir, Arik Vardi and Arik’s father Yossi Vardi had founded Mirabilis in June 1996. AOL patented the technology in 2002. At its peak around 2001 ICQ had more than 100 million registered accounts; Mail.Ru Group, now VK, acquired it in 2010, when it had about 42 million daily users. By 2022 use had fallen to about 11 million monthly users, and the service shut down on June 26, 2024.

ingard-bt-cotton-australia-1996.summary: In 1996-97 season Australian cotton farmers sowed Ingard varieties carrying Monsanto's Cry1Ac gene licensed to Cotton Seed Distributors and CSIRO. Regulators limited Ingard to 30 percent of each farm's cotton area to slow resistance in Helicoverpa armigera, with mandatory refuges, a stewardship scheme Fitt's 2000 paper describes as part of integrated pest management. Nature Biotechnology reported US infestations that same year, sharpening Australian caution. Two-gene Bollgard II replaced Ingard in 2004-05 and cap was lifted; insecticide sprays per hectare fell by about 80 percent. Wilson, Mensah and Fitt document adoption. Australia's approach became a reference case for resistance management worldwide.

internet-archive-1996.summary: In May 1996 Brewster Kahle founded the Internet Archive to save the web; its Wayback Machine now holds nearly a trillion pages. With Bruce Gilliat he began taking snapshots of a growing web while also starting Alexa Internet, a for-profit company. By October 1996 it was archiving in bulk; its oldest surviving page is USA Today from December 1996. Automated collection of public web pages supplies most of its data, and its Wayback Machine, which opened those captures to public view in 2001, now holds more than one trillion.

sources.title: Internet Archive - Wikipedia
C. Freeland, 'Looking back on Preserving the Internet from 1996', Internet Archive Blogs, 2 September 2025
sources.author: Chris Freeland
sources.confirms: Brewster Kahle founded the Internet Archive in April 1996, and the Wayback Machine passed one trillion archived web pages in 2025.

sources.confirms: Earlier in 1996 Brewster Kahle, 35, started a shoestring nonprofit Internet Archive in a renovated Army hospital in San Francisco's Presidio, storing web snapshots on a 2 terabyte tape robot, with a first public project archiving the 1996 presidential election web with the Smithsonian.

sources.author: Jill Lepore
sources.confirms: Kahle started the Internet Archive in 1996 in his attic with the aim of building a second Library of Alexandria; its Wayback Machine is the web archive against which all others are measured.

internet-archive-1996.detail: From late 1999 it grew beyond web pages, starting with Prelinger Archives, and now holds texts, audio, moving images and software, plus projects such as Archive-It and Open Library. Its headquarters sat in San Francisco’s Presidio until 2009, then moved to a former Christian Science church on Funston Avenue. Four publishers sued it in June 2020 over controlled digital lending and won in March 2023; in July 2025 the U.S. Senate designated it a Federal Depository Library.

korea-cdma-commercial-service-1996.summary: Korea chose Qualcomm's code-division multiple access as its national digital cellular standard in 1993, and ETRI with Samsung, LG and Hyundai Electronics built base stations and handsets around it. On 1 January 1996 Korea Mobile Telecom switched on 28 base stations across Incheon and Bucheon and signed its first subscriber on 3 January. Subscribers passed one million within fifteen months and 'one phone per person' followed within a few years. This launch proved that spread-spectrum cellular worked at scale, gave Korean manufacturers a lead in digital handsets and shaped CDMA2000 and later 3G standards. IEEE marked it with a Milestone in 2024.

sources.author: Shin, Sungmoon; Lee, Hun; Han, Ki Chul
sources.confirms: Architecture of Korean CDMA system developed by ETRI and manufacturers

sources.confirms: 28 base stations on 1 January 1996; first subscriber 3 January; 0.9 million by end 1996

korea-cdma-commercial-service-1996.verification_note: Launch chronology follows IEEE's Milestone citation; an ETRI Journal article is cited as supporting literature.
korea-cdma-commercial-service-1996.detail: ETRI Journal's 1997 special issue documents system development; ETHW Milestone page records launch dates and subscriber counts. Qualcomm royalties and Korea's bet on an untested standard drew criticism at the time, and GSM dominated elsewhere.

malaysia-multimedia-super-corridor-1996.summary: At Multimedia Asia conference in Kuala Lumpur on 1 August 1996, Mahathir Mohamad launches Multimedia Super Corridor, a greenfield strip from Petronas Towers to new Kuala Lumpur International Airport containing Putrajaya, a government city, and Cyberjaya, a planned technology town. A Bill of Guarantees promises MSC-status firms unrestricted foreign knowledge workers, full foreign ownership, ten-year tax exemption and no Internet censorship. Multimedia Development Corporation, formed in June 1996, administers status and an international advisory panel including Bill Gates. Tim Bunnell's geography of MSC argues it reproduced spatial inequality while recasting Malaysia as an information economy. MSC status later covered thousands of firms and became Malaysia Digital in 2022.

sources.title: Bunnell, Tim, 'Multimedia utopia? A geographical critique of high-tech development in Malaysia's Multimedia Super Corridor', Antipode 34:2 (2002) 265-295
sources.author: Bunnell, Tim
sources.confirms: August 1996 announcement; zone geography; Bill of Guarantees; spatial inequality critique

sources.title: Mahathir Mohamad, speech at the Tokyo Investor Conference on the Multimedia Super Corridor, Okura Hotel, Tokyo, 20 January 1997 (Prime Minister's Office speech archive)

sources.confirms: 15 km by 50 km corridor from KLCC to the new airport; Putrajaya and Cyberjaya; cyberlaws; Multimedia Development Corporation as one-stop agency

sources.confirms: MDC set up 5 June 1996; Cyberjaya launched 17 May 1997

malaysia-multimedia-super-corridor-1996.verification_note: Some corporate histories date MSC inauguration to 12 February 1996; Mahathir's speech and Bunnell give public launch as 1 August 1996, used here.

picture.alt: Cyberjaya, planned technology town inside Multimedia Super Corridor
picture.credit: Daibo Taku

opioid-oxycontin-1996.summary: In 1996 Purdue Pharma launched OxyContin, marketed as hard to abuse; the opioid epidemic that followed has killed over 700,000 Americans. Its label said delayed absorption “is believed to reduce the abuse liability of a drug,” and Purdue trained sales representatives to tell doctors addiction risk was “less than one percent,” courting them with paid speeches and seminar trips. Promotion for non-cancer pain raised prescriptions nearly tenfold, from about 670,000 in 1997 to about 6.2 million in 2002, as overdose deaths and heroin use rose.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Purdue Pharma
The Promotion and Marketing of OxyContin: Commercial Triumph, Public Health Tragedy
sources.author: Van Zee, Art
sources.confirms: OxyContin was approved and launched in 1996; Purdue's marketing to primary care doctors drove prescriptions for non-cancer pain from about 670,000 in 1997 to about 6.2 million in 2002.

sources.title: Prescription Drugs: OxyContin Abuse and Diversion and Efforts to Address the Problem, GAO-04-110
sources.author: US Government Accountability Office
sources.confirms: Government review of OxyContin's marketing after FDA approval in December 1995 and sales from 1996, noting it became the most prescribed brand-name narcotic by 2001.

opioid-oxycontin-1996.detail:
Non-cancer pain made up 86% of the opioid market in 1999. In 2007 Purdue paid fines ranking among history’s largest for drug firms, for misleading the public about OxyContin’s addictiveness; former FDA commissioner David Kessler later called its approval “one of the worst medical mistakes.”

Purdue filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on September 15, 2019. In October 2020 it reached a settlement potentially worth $8.3 billion, and on November 24, 2020 pleaded guilty to three federal felonies over OxyContin marketing; Sackler family members were to pay $225 million more and Purdue was to close.

picture.alt: OxyContin branded 10 mg oxycodone tablet showing OC marking, photographed 2018.
picture.credit: Psiĥedelisto, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

qatar-first-lng-cargo-1996.summary: Tanker Al Zubarah leaves Ras Laffan on 23 December 1996 with Qatar's first cargo of liquefied natural gas and docks at Chubu Electric's Kawagoe terminal on 10 January 1997. Qatargas, a venture of Qatar General Petroleum Corporation with Mobil, Total, Marubeni and Mitsui, built two trains of 2 million tonnes a year on North Field gas, largest non-associated gas field known, after a decade of financing and start-up problems. Ras Laffan grows into a complex of 14 trains and 77 million tonnes a year by 2011, making Qatar largest LNG exporter and one of richest states per head. Revenue funds Al Jazeera, Education City and a sovereign fund, and gas diplomacy with Japan, Korea, India and Europe reshapes Gulf politics.

qatar-first-lng-cargo-1996.detail: Oil & Gas Journal reports first cargo and start-up difficulties; an IAEA INIS-indexed Middle East gas study gives project structure; Ibrahim and Harrigan (QScience Connect 2012) place LNG in Qatar's economic history. Some accounts date event to January 1997 arrival in Japan.

picture.credit: Matthew Smith @ Flickr, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

roundup-ready-soy-bollgard-cotton-1996.summary: In 1996 Monsanto commercializes Roundup Ready soybeans carrying a bacterial EPSPS gene that tolerates glyphosate, and Bollgard cotton expressing Bacillus thuringiensis Cry1Ac toxin against bollworms, the first widely grown genetically engineered row crops; Bt maize from Ciba-Geigy and Mycogen appears the same season. Adoption outpaces any earlier farm technology: glyphosate-tolerant soybeans go from 7 percent of US acreage in 1996 to 54 percent in 2000 and over 90 percent by 2007, and Bt cotton reaches 60 percent by 2005. Herbicide-resistant weeds followed near-universal glyphosate use; a 2016 study found glyphosate-tolerant soy growers used 28 percent more herbicide than non-adopters while Bt maize growers used 11 percent less insecticide.

sources.title: Bonny, S., 'Herbicide-tolerant Transgenic Soybean over 15 Years of Cultivation: Pesticide Use, Weed Resistance, and Some Economic Issues. The Case of the USA', Sustainability 3 (2011), 1302-1322

sources.confirms: Documents 1996 introduction of Roundup Ready soybeans, adoption trajectory and rise of glyphosate-resistant weeds.
