sources.author: USDA Economic Research Service
sources.confirms: Gives annual adoption percentages for HT soybeans and Bt cotton from 1996 onward.

roundup-ready-soy-bollgard-cotton-1996.detail: The Roundup Ready trait derives from Agrobacterium strain CP4 EPSPS found at Monsanto's Luling, Louisiana, waste pond. Seed patents, technology agreements barring saved seed and Monsanto's 1996 to 2008 acquisition spree concentrated the seed industry. Europe largely refused to grow GM crops; Argentina and Brazil adopted soy wholesale. Glyphosate-resistant Palmer amaranth emerged by 2005, pushing stacked traits with dicamba and 2,4-D tolerance.

picture.credit: Lynn Betts, USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

section-230-1996.summary: In February 1996 Section 230 said an online service is not the publisher of what its users post; platforms could moderate without liability. Congress had passed it by near-unanimous votes; its language came from Representatives Christopher Cox and Ron Wyden and took effect on 8 February 1996. Two rulings had prompted it: CompuServe, which left posts unmoderated, escaped libel liability as a distributor, while Prodigy, which moderated, was held liable as a publisher.

sources.title: Section 230 - Wikipedia
Telecommunications Act of 1996, Public Law 104-104, 110 Stat. 56, section 509 (Communications Decency Act section 230)
sources.author: United States Congress
sources.venue: United States Statutes at Large, vol. 110
sources.confirms: The Act, approved 8 February 1996, provides in section 230(c)(1) that no provider or user of an interactive computer service shall be treated as the publisher or speaker of information provided by another information content provider.

sources.title: Reuters, 'Explainer: What's in the U.S. law protecting internet companies', 28 October 2020
sources.author: Reuters
sources.confirms: Section 230 was enacted in 1996 as part of the Communications Decency Act, protects interactive computer services from liability for third-party posts, and lets them remove objectionable content in good faith.

section-230-1996.detail:
Cox later recalled reading about those two cases. “It struck me that if that rule was going to take hold then the internet would become the Wild West and nobody would have any incentive to keep the internet civil,” he said. Section 230(c)(2) also shields good-faith removal of material a service “considers to be obscene, lewd, lascivious, filthy, excessively violent, harassing, or otherwise objectionable.” Jeff Kosseff calls Section 230 “the 26 words that made the Internet.”

In 1997 Reno v. ACLU struck down most of 1996’s Communications Decency Act, but Section 230 was severable and survived. It does not cover federal crimes, intellectual property or human trafficking, and FOSTA-SESTA amended it in 2018 to require removal of sex-trafficking material. Scrutiny from left and right alike has grown since about 2010.

tamagotchi-1996.summary: In November 1996 Bandai sold the Tamagotchi, a pixel pet on a keychain that died if nobody fed it. Caring for a piece of software became an ordinary childhood chore, and more than 100 million have shipped since.

sources.confirms: Since its launch the previous November on a keychain, Bandai had sold about five million Tamagotchis in Japan, a game in which players must feed and care for a virtual chick, and the toy went on sale in the United States and Canada in May 1997 at $15 to $18.

sources.title: Japan Times, 'Tamagotchi hatches 100 million shipments worldwide thanks to 90s nostalgia', 2 September 2025
sources.author: Japan Times
sources.confirms: Cumulative Tamagotchi shipments from the 1996 debut through August 2025 topped 100 million worldwide.

picture.credit: David, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

aim-1997.summary: In 1997 AOL released Instant Messenger, open to outsiders from May; a generation typed to friends after school, and its away message prefigured status updates. AIM held 52 percent of North America’s market in 2006 and was shut down on 15 December 2017.

sources.title: AIM (software), Wikipedia
Greenman, Catherine, 'Yakety-Yak, Clackety-Clack: On Net, Teen-Agers Talk', The New York Times (1998)
sources.author: Greenman, Catherine
sources.confirms: The article says AOL had let people outside its service sign up for Instant Messenger since May 1997 and that teens tended to sign on and chat with friends after school.
sources.qualifies: The article says AOL opened sign-ups to people outside its service in May 1997, rather than identifying May as the release date.

sources.title: Larson, Gary W.; Editors, Britannica, 'Instant messaging | Definition, History, & Facts', Encyclopaedia Britannica (2026)

aim-1997.verification_note: A news article says AOL had let people outside its service sign up since May 1997, and Britannica dates its rollout to 1997 as its first at large scale.

attention-economy-goldhaber-1997.summary: In December 1997 Michael Goldhaber wrote in Wired that attention, not money, was what was scarce online; Charlie Warzel’s 2021 New York Times column says his essay helped popularise “attention economy.”

sources.title: Attention Shoppers! | WIRED - Public Services Alliance
Opinion | I Talked to the Cassandra of the Internet Age (Published 2021)

attention-economy-goldhaber-1997.detail: Goldhaber added that attention “can’t be bought” and needs no encryption, unlike electronic money, and that it takes many forms, from love and recognition to obedience and critical appraisal. Charlie Warzel’s 2021 New York Times column says Goldhaber’s essay helped popularise “attention economy,” psychologist Herbert A. Simon’s term, and predicted a “star system” in which “whoever you are, however you express yourself, you can now have a crack at the global audience.” Goldhaber had pursued this idea since the mid-1980s and told Warzel: “When you have attention, you have power, and some people will try and succeed in getting huge amounts of attention, and they would not use it in equal or positive ways.”

babel-fish-1997.summary: In December 1997 DEC and SYSTRAN launched Babel Fish on AltaVista, the web’s oldest free translation service, across 13 languages. It rendered text or whole web pages across 36 pairs among 13 languages. Yahoo acquired it through its 2003 purchase of Overture, and in May 2012 Microsoft’s Bing Translator replaced it.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Babel Fish (website)
Gaspari, Federico and John Hutchins, "Online and Free! Ten Years of Online Machine Translation: Origins, Developments, Current Use and Future Prospects"
sources.author: Federico Gaspari, John Hutchins

sources.author: Kurt Ament
sources.confirms: Contemporary report that DEC and SYSTRAN launched the service on 9 December 1997.

babel-fish-1997.detail: Its languages were English, Simplified and Traditional Chinese, Dutch, French, German, Greek, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, Russian and Spanish. Overture Services bought AltaVista in February 2003 and Yahoo took over Overture that July; its address moved to babelfish.yahoo.com on May 9, 2008. Yahoo redirected queries to Bing Translator rather than selling its application to Microsoft, and by June 2013 the old address pointed back to Yahoo’s home page.

cassava-mosaic-pandemic-1997.summary: From late 1980s Uganda, an unusually severe form of cassava mosaic disease moved south and east at about 20 km a year, carried by whitefly, reaching Kenya and Tanzania by mid-1990s and Rwanda by 2000. Plants lost most leaf area and roots; whole districts abandoned cassava, a staple that normally survives drought. James Legg's team identified a recombinant virus, EACMV-Uganda, and found it in a synergistic mixed infection with African cassava mosaic virus. Uganda's response multiplied resistant varieties from IITA breeding lines and distributed cuttings through farmer groups, and production recovered by around 2000.

sources.title: Legg, J. P. et al., 'Cassava mosaic virus disease in East Africa: a dynamic disease in a changing environment', Plant Pathology 50 (2001)
sources.author: Legg, James P.; et al.
sources.confirms: 1990s pandemic spread from Uganda into Kenya, Tanzania and Rwanda; EACMV-Ug recombinant; whitefly vector; resistant varieties

sources.title: Otim-Nape, G. W. and Thresh, J. M., 'The current pandemic of cassava mosaic virus disease in Uganda', in Jones, D. G. (ed.), The Epidemiology of Plant Diseases (Springer, 1998)
sources.author: Otim-Nape, G. W.; Thresh, J. M.
sources.confirms: Uganda pandemic account and control programme
sources.qualifies: Chapter text not opened; cited from Legg et al.

cassava-mosaic-pandemic-1997.verification_note: Pandemic has no single date; 1997 marks its arrival across Kenya and Tanzania. Spread rate of about 20 km a year and recovery date are from Legg et al.'s review of earlier work.
cassava-mosaic-pandemic-1997.detail: Otim-Nape and Thresh documented Uganda's resistant variety programme. Superabundant whitefly populations remain a research problem. Losses in Uganda were estimated at 60,000 hectares of cassava abandoned in early 1990s and food shortages in Luwero and surrounding districts. Later work showed EACMV-Uganda spread into Burundi, Rwanda and Democratic Republic of Congo by mid-2000s, prompting regional breeding networks.

picture.alt: A woman harvesting cassava tubers in a field in Uganda
picture.credit: Oliversamson1, via Wikimedia Commons

christensen-disruptive-innovation-1997.summary: In 1997 Christensen's The Innovator's Dilemma explained why good companies lose to cheaper, worse products that improve. Christensen advised large firms to keep small, nimble divisions that replicate this pattern internally.

sources.title: The Innovator's Dilemma: When New Technologies Cause ...
The innovator's dilemma :: when new technologies cause great firms to fail /: Clayton M. Christensen.
The Innovator's Dilemma
Bower, Joseph L., and Clayton M. Christensen, 'Customer Power, Strategic Investment, and the Failure of Leading Firms', Strategic Management Journal 17 (1996), pp. 197-218
sources.author: Bower, Joseph L.; Christensen, Clayton M.
sources.confirms: The peer-reviewed article in which Christensen set out the disruptive-technology argument of The Innovator's Dilemma (1997): leading firms fail because they follow their best customers away from cheaper, initially inferior technologies.

christensen-disruptive-innovation-1997.detail: Its jacket also promises rules for managers. They help “determine when it is right not to listen to customers, when to invest in developing lower-performance products that promise lower margins, and when to pursue small markets at the expense of seemingly larger and more lucrative ones.” Christensen describes value to innovation as an S-curve, with little gain from early iterations and most in the middle, and notes that incumbents, needing large yearly sales, leave niches to entrants. Harvard Business School’s page says his work is cited by figures from Steve Jobs to Malcolm Gladwell.

picture.alt: Clayton Christensen speaking at World Economic Forum in Davos in January 2013.
picture.credit: World Economic Forum from Cologny, Switzerland, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

clippy-office-assistant-1997.summary: In 1997 Office 97 shipped with an animated assistant that guessed what users were trying to do and offered help unasked; its paperclip became known as Clippy. Lumiere aimed at “harnessing probability and utility to provide assistance to computer software users”: Bayesian models inferred what users were trying to do from their background, actions and queries, so software could offer help unasked. Horvitz’s project page describes models of users’ changing goals, methods for turning application events into observations, persistent profiles of user expertise and an intelligent-interface architecture, plus video of a Lumiere Excel prototype from January 1995.

sources.title: The Lumiere Project: Bayesian User Modeling for Inferring the Goals ...

Horvitz, Eric, Breese, Jack, Heckerman, David, Hovel, David and Rommelse, Koos, 'The Lumiere Project: Bayesian User Modeling for Inferring the Goals and Needs of Software Users', Proceedings of the Fourteenth Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (1998) 256-265
sources.author: Eric Horvitz, Jack Breese, David Heckerman, David Hovel and Koos Rommelse
sources.confirms: Lumiere used Bayesian user models to infer users' goals and needs from their actions and queries, and its prototypes served as the basis for the Office Assistant in Microsoft Office 97.

sources.title: Meyer, Robinson, 'Even Early Focus Groups Hated Clippy', The Atlantic, 23 June 2015
sources.author: Robinson Meyer
sources.confirms: Clippit, the Office assistant introduced with Office 97 in November 1996, interrupted users to offer help with basic tasks, tested badly in focus groups, was turned off by default in Office XP and removed in Office 2007.
sources.qualifies: Dates the introduction to November 1996, when Office 97 was announced, ahead of its 1997 retail release.

clippy-office-assistant-1997.detail: Eric Horvitz, Jack Breese, David Heckerman, David Hovel and Koos Rommelse published their method in July 1998. Their paper, “The Lumiere Project: Bayesian User Modeling for Inferring the Goals and Needs of Software Users,” appeared at the Fourteenth Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence in Madison, Wisconsin. Horvitz’s project page names neither Clippy nor which Assistant components came from Lumiere, and does not say how shipped software differed from research prototypes.

deep-blue-kasparov-1997.summary: In May 1997 IBM's Deep Blue beat world champion Garry Kasparov, the first time a machine won a match against chess's best. No computer had beaten a reigning champion under tournament conditions before. Kasparov won Game 1, then resigned Game 2 though perpetual check would have drawn it, and accused IBM of cheating, alleging human grandmaster help behind its 37th move. After three draws, Deep Blue took decisive Game 6, a Caro-Kann, with a knight sacrifice forcing resignation in under twenty moves. Prizes were $700,000 and $400,000.

sources.title: 1997 rematch
Deep Blue
sources.author: Campbell, Murray; Hoane, A. Joseph; Hsu, Feng-hsiung
sources.confirms: The IBM team's account of the system that defeated Kasparov 3.5 to 2.5 in the May 1997 rematch, the first match win by a computer over a reigning world champion.

sources.title: 'Chess: Computer chess', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: In the six-game rematch of 3 to 11 May 1997 in New York an upgraded Deep Blue examined 200 million positions per second; Kasparov resigned Game 2 in a position later found drawable, and with the match tied Deep Blue won the final game in 19 moves.

sources.title: Weber, Bruce, 'Deep Blue and Kasparov Face Final Game', New York Times, 11 May 1997
sources.author: Bruce Weber
sources.confirms: After five games, one win each and three draws, the match stood 2.5 to 2.5 before the sixth game at the Equitable Center in Manhattan, where Kasparov, visibly angry, renewed his request for Deep Blue's computer logs.

deep-blue-kasparov-1997.detail:
Deep Blue’s 44th move in Game 1 was later put down to a bug’s fail-safe, and Kasparov missed a Game 5 win with 44.Rg7+. Deep Blue also collected Carnegie Mellon’s $100,000 Fredkin Prize, created in 1980 for whichever computer first beat a world champion. Reports that IBM dismantled Deep Blue were wrong; it ran for several more years.

Observers saw AI catching up with humans; later analysts put it down to Kasparov’s poor play and brute-force search. Kasparov said in 2016 that he had come to respect Deep Blue’s team more. Go then became computing’s canonical hard game until AlphaGo beat Fan Hui in 2015 and Lee Sedol in 2016. Game Over: Kasparov and the Machine, a documentary, covers it.

picture.alt: Cabinet of IBM Deep Blue, which beat Garry Kasparov in 1997, displayed at Computer History Museum in 2011
picture.credit: Anton Chiang, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docsis-1997.summary: In 1997 cable operators agreed on DOCSIS, one standard for cable modems. The Data Over Cable Service Interface Specification is an international standard that adds high-bandwidth data transfer to existing cable television systems, so operators could sell internet access over hybrid fiber-coaxial networks they already owned. Version 1.0 gathered functional elements from the proprietary cable modems that preceded it, replacing incompatible designs with equipment any operator could buy. Later versions added quality-of-service controls, higher upstream rates and far higher speeds both ways.

sources.title: DOCSIS (Wikipedia)
Data-Over-Cable Service Interface Specifications, DOCSIS 1.0: Operations Support System Interface Specification (SP-OSSI-C01-011119)
sources.author: Cable Television Laboratories, Inc.
sources.venue: CableLabs specification; first release I01 issued 3 April 1997
sources.confirms: The DOCSIS 1.0 specification was first released in 1997 as the cable industry's common cable modem standard.

sources.title: Fellows, D.; Jones, D., 'DOCSIS cable modem technology', IEEE Communications Magazine 39, no. 3 (2001): 202-209
sources.author: Fellows, D.; Jones, D.
sources.confirms: Peer-reviewed overview recording that cable operators agreed at the end of 1995 to create the DOCSIS specifications under CableLabs and that more than 100 interoperable modem models from 36 companies had been certified by 2001.
sources.qualifies: Does not give the 1997 issue date of DOCSIS 1.0.

docsis-1997.detail: DOCSIS 1.1, released in April 1999, standardised the quality-of-service mechanisms outlined in 1.0. DOCSIS 2.0, from December 2001, raised upstream rates for symmetric services such as IP telephony, and DOCSIS 3.0, from August 2006, increased rates both ways and added IPv6 support. DOCSIS 3.1 first appeared in October 2013. Because European cable uses 8 MHz channels under PAL and DVB-C rather than North America’s 6 MHz, versions before 3.1 were adapted as EuroDOCSIS.

dragon-naturallyspeaking-1997.summary: In 1997 Dragon NaturallySpeaking let a PC take dictation in normal speech for $695. James Baker had described a speech understanding system called DRAGON in 1975 and founded Dragon Systems with his wife Janet Baker in 1982. Their earlier DragonDictate used hidden Markov models, a probabilistic method for recognising patterns over time, but hardware could not find word boundaries in flowing speech, so users had to pause after every word; NaturallySpeaking removed that constraint.

sources.title: Dragon NaturallySpeaking
Lewis, Peter H., "Just Speaking Plainly Controls the Machine", New York Times, 8 July 1997
sources.author: Lewis, Peter H.
sources.confirms: Contemporary review describing Dragon NaturallySpeaking as the first consumer product to take continuous dictation on a PC.

sources.title: Wired, "Finally, a Computer That Understands You" (June 1997)
sources.author: Wired staff
sources.confirms: Contemporary report on Dragon Systems' launch of continuous speech dictation software.

dragon-naturallyspeaking-1997.detail: Dictated words appear in floating tooltips as they are spoken and, once speech pauses, land in whichever window is active, at the cursor. Lernout & Hauspie of Belgium bought Dragon Systems in June 2000 in an all-share deal advised by Goldman Sachs; Lernout & Hauspie was then found to have committed financial fraud and declared bankruptcy in November 2000. ScanSoft of Burlington, Massachusetts acquired Dragon’s product line, took over Nuance Communications in 2005 and adopted Nuance’s name; Microsoft later acquired Nuance.

gattaca-1997.summary: In 1997 Gattaca imagined a society where children are conceived by genetic selection and the naturally born are shut out of good jobs. Those conceived naturally, called in-valids, are shut out of professional work; genetic discrimination is illegal there, but genotype profiling steers valids into careers and in-valids into menial jobs. Vincent Freeman, played by Ethan Hawke, is born with a predicted lifespan of 30.2 years and borrows the identity of Jerome Morrow, a paralysed former swimmer played by Jude Law, to fly to Titan.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Gattaca
K. Davies, 'Discrimination down to a science', Nature 390 (1997), 33
sources.author: Kevin Davies
sources.confirms: Nature's review of Gattaca (Columbia, 1997) discusses its society of embryo selection and discrimination against naturally conceived 'in-valids'.

sources.title: Kirby, David A., 'The New Eugenics in Cinema: Genetic Determinism and Gene Therapy in GATTACA', Science Fiction Studies 27, no. 2 (2000): 193-215
sources.author: Kirby, David A.
sources.confirms: Peer-reviewed study of the 1997 film's portrayal of genetic selection, discrimination by genotype and the debate over genetic determinism.

gattaca-1997.detail: Its title spells out DNA’s four bases, G, A, T and C. Uma Thurman co-stars, with Loren Dean, Ernest Borgnine, Gore Vidal and Alan Arkin in supporting roles. To keep his cover Vincent scrubs away his own genetic traces daily and passes DNA and urine tests with Jerome’s samples. Columbia Pictures released it in the United States on October 24, 1997; it opened fifth at the box office and ended with $12.5 million domestically against a reported $36 million budget. Reviews were positive, with 82% approval on Rotten Tomatoes from 66 reviews, and it was nominated for an Academy Award for Best Art Direction. Gattaca is cited in debates about genetic testing, which point to privacy laws such as America’s 2008 Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act.

grameenphone-village-phone-1997.summary: In March 1997 Grameenphone launched in Bangladesh and lent village women phones to rent out by the call. Iqbal Quadir, inspired by Grameen Bank’s micro-credit model, had spent three years winning support from Grameen Bank and Norway’s Telenor. Village Phones are owner-operated GSM payphones: borrowers, mostly women in remote villages, take 12,000 taka loans, about US$200, from Grameen Bank to subscribe, are trained to run them and charge neighbours for calls at a profit. By September 2006 more than 255,000 Village Phones operated in 55,000 villages.

sources.title: Grameenphone - Wikipedia
Discover inspiring stories from Grameen Telecom.
Bayes, Abdul. 'Infrastructure and Rural Development: Insights from a Grameen Bank Village Phone Initiative in Bangladesh.' Agricultural Economics 25, no. 2-3 (2001): 261-272.
sources.author: Abdul Bayes
sources.confirms: Independent peer-reviewed evaluation of the Grameen village phone programme launched in 1997; Crossref metadata confirmed, Wiley page did not open.

grameenphone-village-phone-1997.detail: Muhammad Yunus, Grameen Bank’s founder, created Grameen Telecom to hold its stake in Grameenphone. Grameen Telecom states two aims for the program. One was to “bring telecommunication and information technology to the rural people and help them alleviate their poverty,” the other to “get a mobile phone into the hands of poor women and accelerate women’s empowerment.” It also reports that by 31 July 2022 more than 83,000 villages in all 64 districts were covered, with 1.03 million active Rural Phones, and that it has earned international honours for women’s empowerment. Its model was replicated in Uganda and Rwanda, and Grameenphone, 55.8% owned by Telenor, is now Bangladesh’s largest mobile network.

great-pacific-garbage-patch-1997.summary: In 1997 a sailor crossing the North Pacific found plastic in open water for a week and alerted oceanographer Curtis Ebbesmeyer, who named it the “Eastern Garbage Patch.” NOAA scientists had predicted such accumulation in 1988: Alaska-based researchers found marine debris concentrating where currents form relatively stable waters, and pointed to this gyre. It forms no visible island but a dispersed zone of suspended particles, mostly microplastics of fingernail size or smaller.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Great Pacific Garbage Patch
Moore, C. J., Moore, S. L., Leecaster, M. K. and Weisberg, S. B., 'A Comparison of Plastic and Plankton in the North Pacific Central Gyre', Marine Pollution Bulletin 42 (2001) 1297-1300
sources.author: Moore, C. J.; Moore, S. L.; Leecaster, M. K.; Weisberg, S. B.
sources.confirms: Moore's follow-up survey of the gyre he crossed in 1997, finding plastic outweighed plankton six to one.

sources.title: Lebreton, Laurent; Slat, Boyan; Ferrari, Francesco; et al., 'Evidence that the Great Pacific Garbage Patch is rapidly accumulating plastic', Scientific Reports 8 (2018): 4666
sources.author: Lebreton, Laurent; Slat, Boyan; Ferrari, Francesco
sources.confirms: Peer-reviewed survey estimating at least 79 thousand tonnes of plastic across 1.6 million square kilometres of the North Pacific accumulation zone first described by Moore after his 1997 crossing.

great-pacific-garbage-patch-1997.detail:
It lies roughly between 135°W and 155°W and 35°N and 42°N. Ocean Cleanup researchers estimated in 2018 that it covered 1.6 million square kilometres and held 45,000 to 129,000 tonnes of plastic, later growing to twice Texas’s size; by late 2024 their project had removed more than one million pounds, about 0.5% of accumulated trash. Although microplastics dominate by count, 92% of its mass is larger objects, some over 50 years old.

Moore’s Algalita Marine Research Foundation organised a 2008 JUNK Raft voyage to highlight its plastic; Project Kaisei and Scripps’s SEAPLEX expedition studied it in 2009. Similar debris collects in the Atlantic as the North Atlantic garbage patch.

hulhumale-reclamation-maldives-1997.summary: With Male's 2 square kilometres packed beyond capacity, Maldives government begins pumping sand from its lagoon onto a reef flat north of airport island on 16 October 1997. Phase one, 188 hectares, is complete by June 2002, built about two metres above mean sea level, roughly twice Male's height, as a hedge against sea level rise. First residents move in on 12 May 2004 and population passes 50,000 by 2018. A nine week dredging campaign in 2015 adds 244 hectares for phase two. Hulhumale becomes a model, and a warning about reef damage, for atoll states facing rising seas.

hulhumale-reclamation-maldives-1997.detail: Housing Development Corporation gives 16 October 1997 start, 188 ha, June 2002 completion, 12 May 2004 settlement, 50,000 by 2018 and 244 ha for phase two in 2015. Height of about 2 m comes from HDC and UN-Habitat accounts. A 2019 study analyses how Maldives finances land reclamation as adaptation.

picture.credit: NASA/USGS (Landsat)

intel-costa-rica-assembly-plant-1997.summary: On 13 November 1996 Intel announced it would build a 300 million dollar assembly and test plant for Pentium processors in Costa Rica, a country of 3.5 million people chosen over Mexico, Brazil and Chile after a campaign by investment agency CINDE and President José María Figueres, offering a free-zone tax regime, a dedicated electricity feed and new technical training programmes. Construction began in April 1997 and first processors shipped in 1998. By 1999 Intel's exports were about a fifth of Costa Rica's total and swung national GDP growth; Rodríguez-Clare's 2001 study examined how that plant anchored a strategy based on education and technology. Intel closed assembly in 2014, moving it to Asia, but kept engineering and services centres, then reopened assembly and test in 2021.

sources.title: Rodríguez-Clare, Andrés, 'Costa Rica's Development Strategy based on Human Capital and Technology: How it got there, the impact of Intel, and lessons for other countries', Journal of Human Development 2 (2001)
sources.author: Rodríguez-Clare, Andrés
sources.confirms: Site selection, policy package and Intel's weight in exports and GDP.

sources.title: 'Intel to Build Plants in Texas and Costa Rica', New York Times, 14 November 1996
sources.confirms: Announcement date and investment figures.

intel-costa-rica-assembly-plant-1997.detail: Its site decision was studied as a case of a small economy winning a large multinational through institutional coordination without subsidies. Suppliers of packaging, logistics and metrology followed, and Costa Rica's share of high-technology exports grew with medical devices from the 2000s. Debbie Spar's 1998 World Bank case study documented that site selection.

picture.credit: Mariordo Mario Roberto Duran Ortiz, via Wikimedia Commons

kerala-fishermen-mobile-phones-1997.summary: Mobile service reaches Kerala's coast in stages between 1997 and 2001. Fishermen returning with sardines begin calling buyers at several beach markets before choosing where to land, instead of selling at one market and dumping catch when it is glutted. Robert Jensen's survey of markets in three districts, published in Quarterly Journal of Economics in 2007, records price dispersion collapsing, waste dropping to near zero, fishermen's profits up around 8 percent and consumer prices down about 4 percent as each region's towers switch on. His study becomes a standard case for information economics in development and is widely cited in arguments for mobile networks in poor regions; Abraham's fieldwork adds detail on how fishermen and traders adopted phones.

sources.title: Robert Jensen, 'The Digital Provide: Information (Technology), Market Performance, and Welfare in the South Indian Fisheries Sector', Quarterly Journal of Economics 122 (2007) 879-924
sources.author: Robert Jensen
sources.confirms: 1997-2001 mobile introduction, dramatic reduction in price dispersion, elimination of waste, welfare gains

sources.author: Reuben Abraham
sources.confirms: adoption patterns among fishermen and traders

kerala-fishermen-mobile-phones-1997.detail: Jensen (QJE 2007) abstract confirms 1997-2001 rollout, price dispersion fall, elimination of waste. Profit and price figures are from the paper's body. Abraham (Information Technologies and International Development 2007) gives qualitative adoption account.

picture.alt: Fishermen hauling a boat on a beach near Varkala, Kerala, 1997
picture.credit: Philippe Raffard

kismet-robot-1990s.summary: In 1997 Cynthia Breazeal built Kismet at MIT, a robot head whose ears, brows and lips showed moods that people answered as an infant's. Adapted from an active vision platform in MIT’s Cog Shop, its original head dates to about May 1997, its later form to about March 1998. Kismet follows an infant-caretaker model: humans act as caretakers, and its drives and simulated emotions produce expressions through ears, eyebrows, eyelids, lips, jaw and head, which caretakers read as cues and adjust their behaviour so Kismet is neither overwhelmed nor understimulated.

sources.title: Kismet: A Robot for Social Interactions with Humans
Kismet (robot)
Cynthia Breazeal, Designing Sociable Robots (MIT Press, 2002)
sources.author: Cynthia Breazeal
sources.pages: whole book; Kismet is the case study throughout
sources.confirms: Breazeal's monograph presenting Kismet, the expressive robot head she built at MIT, as the model of a sociable robot.
sources.qualifies: The publisher page does not give the 1997 build date.

kismet-robot-1990s.detail: Each eyeball holds a colour CCD camera of 5.6 mm focal length; eyebrows and ears each have two degrees of freedom, eyelids and mouth one. Physical materials cost about US$25,000, and computation ran on four Motorola 68332s, nine 400 MHz PCs and one 500 MHz PC. Its hearing is tuned to infant-directed speech and classifies approval, prohibition, attention, comfort and neutral tones using Gaussian mixture models. Breazeal describes her relationship with it as “something like an infant-caretaker interaction, where I’m the caretaker essentially, and the robot is like an infant.” Its name comes from Turkish, meaning fate or luck, and the MIT page places it within the larger Cog Project.

kyoto-protocol-1997.summary: In December 1997 the Kyoto Protocol bound industrialised countries to cut greenhouse gases; America signed in 1998 but never ratified, its Senate having passed the Byrd-Hagel Resolution 95 to 0. Its parent convention aims to keep greenhouse gases below “dangerous anthropogenic interference with the climate system,” so Kyoto bound developed countries, held historically responsible for existing emissions, to targets while developing countries took none, under common but differentiated responsibilities. Annex I parties committed to cut emissions at least 5 percent below 1990 levels over 2008 to 2012, using three flexibility mechanisms.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Country types and their...
UNFCCC, 'The Kyoto Protocol', UNFCCC (1997)
sources.author: UNFCCC
sources.confirms: The page says the Kyoto Protocol was adopted on 11 December 1997, binds developed countries, and sets targets for industrialized countries and economies in transition while recognizing their responsibility for current high greenhouse gas levels.
sources.qualifies: The source describes targets for industrialized countries and economies in transition, rather than all rich countries.

sources.title: Boisson de Chazournes, Laurence, 'Kyoto Protocol to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change', UN Audiovisual Library of International Law (2008)
sources.author: Boisson de Chazournes, Laurence
sources.venue: UN Audiovisual Library of International Law
sources.confirms: The page says the Kyoto Protocol was adopted on 11 December 1997 and set a goal for Annex I Parties to reduce overall emissions by at least 5 per cent below 1990 levels during 2008 to 2012, while introducing no new commitments for developing countries; it also states that the Convention aims to stabilize greenhouse gas concentrations at a level that would prevent dangerous anthropogenic interference with the climate system.
sources.qualifies: The source specifies a target for Annex I Parties of at least 5 per cent below 1990 emissions during 2008 to 2012, rather than describing the targets broadly for all rich countries.

sources.title: 'The Kyoto Protocol - Status of Ratification', UNFCCC (1997)
sources.confirms: The page says the Kyoto Protocol was adopted on 11 December 1997 and is subject to ratification, acceptance, approval or accession by Parties to the UNFCCC.

kyoto-protocol-1997.verification_note: Sources apply Kyoto's commitments to industrialised or Annex I parties; Boisson de Chazournes (2008) specifies at least 5 per cent below 1990 emissions during 2008 to 2012.
kyoto-protocol-1997.detail:
Its flexibility mechanisms, International Emissions Trading, the Clean Development Mechanism and Joint Implementation, let parties earn credits by funding reductions elsewhere. It covered carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, hydrofluorocarbons, perfluorocarbons and sulfur hexafluoride, with nitrogen trifluoride added for its second period. Russia’s ratification on 18 November 2004 met its threshold of Annex I parties holding 55% of 1990 carbon dioxide emissions, and entry into force followed on 16 February 2005; it had 192 parties in 2020.

All 36 countries that fully took part in the first period complied, nine by funding reductions abroad, yet global emissions rose 32% from 1990 to 2010. Canada withdrew with effect from December 2012, citing $14 billion in liabilities. Doha’s 2012 amendment set a second period to 2020 with 37 countries holding targets, and 2015’s Paris Agreement followed as a separate instrument under the convention.

picture.credit: Jason Riedy, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

long-boom-1997.summary: In July 1997 Wired's cover promised 25 years of prosperity, The Long Boom; a crash came within three. It argued that five waves of technology, in computing, telecommunications, biotechnology, nanotechnology and alternative energy, together with more open economies and political cooperation, could double world output every 12 years, cut poverty and ease international tensions. Its cover line asked: “You got a problem with that?” Schwartz and Leyden also listed ten “scenario spoilers” able to derail it, from renewed Cold War with China to “an uncontrollable plague.”

sources.title: The Long Boom: A History of the Future, 1980-2020
Did Wired Mag Publish 'Scary Accurate' Predictions About 21st Century in 1997?

long-boom-1997.detail:
Its full title was “The Long Boom: A History of the Future, 1980-2020,” and it ran from page 121. Other spoilers included technologies that prove “a bust,” Russia sliding into kleptocracy or nationalism, European integration stalling, ecological crisis disrupting food supply, rising crime and terrorism, pollution-driven cancer overwhelming health systems, energy prices going “through the roof” after Middle East convulsions, and “a social and cultural backlash.” Wired framed its boom as conditional on political leadership and openness.

In November 2021 screenshots of its spoiler list circulated on Twitter as “scary accurate”; Snopes rated their attribution correct and quoted its promise of “a new civilization of civilizations that will blossom through the coming century.”

lstm-1997.summary: In 1997 the LSTM let neural networks remember across long sequences; it later ran speech recognition and translation. Ordinary recurrent networks suffer from vanishing gradients: their training signal fades over many steps, so they forget what happened far back in a sequence. LSTM adds Constant Error Carousel units, memory cells whose values persist over arbitrary intervals, with gates regulating what flows in and out; its 1997 block had cells, input gates and output gates, and such memory can last thousands of timesteps.

sources.title: Long short-term memory
Hochreiter, Sepp, and Schmidhuber, Jurgen, 'Long Short-Term Memory', Neural Computation 9, no. 8 (1997): 1735-1780
sources.author: Hochreiter, Sepp; Schmidhuber, Jurgen
sources.confirms: The 1997 paper introduces LSTM, which overcomes decaying error backflow in recurrent networks and bridges time lags of more than 1000 steps through constant error carousels and gate units.

sources.title: Greff, Klaus, Rupesh K. Srivastava, Jan Koutnik, Bas R. Steunebrink, and Jurgen Schmidhuber. 'LSTM: A Search Space Odyssey.' IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems 28, no. 10 (2017): 2222-2232.
sources.author: Klaus Greff; Rupesh K. Srivastava; Jan Koutnik; Bas R. Steunebrink; Jurgen Schmidhuber
sources.venue: IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems
sources.confirms: Peer-reviewed study of the LSTM architecture introduced in 1997 and its later use in speech recognition and translation; Crossref metadata confirmed, IEEE page did not open.

lstm-1997.detail:
Hochreiter’s 1991 diploma thesis had analysed vanishing gradients, and early LSTM versions appeared in a 1995 technical report and at NIPS 1996. Felix Gers, Schmidhuber and Fred Cummins added forget gates in 1999, letting networks reset their own state; this remains the most used version. Graves and Schmidhuber published bidirectional LSTM in 2005, and connectionist temporal classification followed in 2006.

In 2015 Google adopted an LSTM for speech recognition on Google Voice, cutting transcription errors by 49% according to its blog; in 2016 its neural machine translation system used LSTMs to cut translation errors by 60%, Apple announced LSTM for QuickType and Siri, and Amazon’s Polly used a bidirectional LSTM for Alexa’s voices. Facebook ran some 4.5 billion automatic translations daily with LSTMs in 2017.

picture.alt: Jurgen Schmidhuber, co-author of 1997 LSTM paper, speaking at AI for Good summit in Geneva in 2017
picture.credit: ITU/R. Farrell, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

octopus-card-1997.summary: On 1 September 1997 five Hong Kong transport operators led by MTR Corporation, through joint venture Creative Star, launched Octopus, a card using Sony's FeliCa radio-frequency chip that passengers tap on readers to pay fares on trains, buses and ferries without removing it from a wallet. Three million cards were issued within three months. From 2000 a deposit-taking licence let Octopus handle payments at convenience stores, car parks and vending machines, and by 2001 about 70 percent of residents used one. It was first large-scale contactless payment card in daily use and a model for Singapore's EZ-Link, London's Oyster and Japan's Suica.

sources.author: Chau, Patrick Y. K.; Poon, Simpson

octopus-card-1997.detail: Chau and Poon's article in Communications of the ACM analyses adoption factors and merchant expansion; a TRID transport record gives launch date. Octopus later added personalised cards, mobile wallets and access control, and faced privacy criticism in 2010 over sale of customer data.

picture.credit: Fahad Faisal

robocup-1997.summary: In 1997 RoboCup’s first robot football tournament drew 38 teams to Nagoya; its goal is to beat World Cup winners by 2050. University professors including Hiroaki Kitano, Manuela M. Veloso, Itsuki Noda and Minoru Asada had founded RoboCup in 1996 to drive robotics and artificial intelligence research through public competition; match robots are fully autonomous, with referees providing all human input. Its official goal: by mid-century a team of fully autonomous humanoid robot soccer players “shall win a soccer game, complying with the official rules of FIFA, against the winner of the most recent World Cup.”

shantha-hepatitis-b-vaccine-1997.summary: Varaprasad Reddy founded Shantha Biotechnics in Hyderabad in 1993 after multinational firms declined to transfer hepatitis B vaccine technology at affordable prices. Working with Osmania University and Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology, its scientists expressed hepatitis B surface antigen in Pichia pastoris yeast and launched Shanvac-B in 1997, India's first indigenously developed recombinant vaccine. Price fell from about fifteen dollars to under one dollar a dose. WHO prequalification in 2002 opened UNICEF tenders; by 2009 Shantha had supplied some 120 million doses. Sanofi bought Shantha in 2009 for about 784 million dollars, and Hyderabad became a global vaccine manufacturing hub.

sixdegrees-1997.summary: In 1997 SixDegrees.com, one of the first social networks, let users list their friends and see their connection to any other member. Users listed friends, family and acquaintances whether registered or not; outsiders were invited to join, and those who confirmed a relationship without registering kept receiving occasional email updates. Members could message and post bulletin board items to people within three degrees. Friendster, MySpace, LinkedIn and Facebook followed with social-circles network models.

sources.author: boyd, danah m.; Ellison, Nicole B.
sources.confirms: boyd and Ellison record that SixDegrees.com launched in 1997, let users create profiles and list friends, added browsing of friends lists in 1998, and was the first site to combine these features before closing in 2000.

sixdegrees-1997.detail: MacroView, later renamed SixDegrees Inc., was founded by chief executive Andrew Weinreich in May 1996 in New York City. At its height the company had around 100 employees and the site around 3.5 million fully registered members. YouthStream Media Networks bought it in December 1999 for $125 million; the site shut down on December 30, 2000 and was revived some years later. Weinreich went on to found Joltage, a Wi-Fi hotspot business, in 2001.

toshka-new-valley-project-1997.summary: In January 1997 President Mubarak inaugurates Toshka, or New Valley, project: Mubarak Pumping Station lifts up to 25 million cubic metres a day from Lake Nasser into Sheikh Zayed Canal, 50 kilometres of lined channel with four branches meant to irrigate 540,000 feddans (about 227,000 hectares) and settle millions in a 'second Nile valley'. Station, with 24 pumps in a shaft cut into rock, is finished in 2005 by a Hitachi-led consortium. Investors from Saudi Arabia and UAE take large plots, yet by 2012 satellite surveys show about a tenth of target area under crops, with salinity, remote markets and water allocation disputes slowing settlement. Project becomes a case study in desert reclamation ambition outrunning soils and finance, revived again after 2015.

toyota-prius-1997.summary: In December 1997 Toyota’s Prius went on sale in Japan as history's first mass-produced petrol-electric hybrid. Toyota had shown its hybrid concept at Tokyo’s 1995 motor show and tested it in 1996, calling its goal a “car for the 21st century”; its drivetrain, later named Hybrid Synergy Drive, couples petrol and electric power. It won Car of the Year Japan on introduction, and NHW10 production at Toyota’s Takaoka plant reached 37,425 vehicles by February 2000.

toyota-prius-1997.detail: Prius is Latin for “first,” “original” or “to go before.” Its styling came from California designers chosen over competing Toyota studios. Model NHW11 followed in 2000, when sales went worldwide; since 2003 it has been built only as a compact five-door liftback. In 1998 it also won Japan’s Automotive Researchers’ and Journalists’ Conference Car of the Year award. Prius-family sales had reached 6.1 million units by January 2017, 61% of Toyota’s 10 million hybrids since 1997, across more than 90 markets.

vietnam-internet-connection-1997.summary: On 19 November 1997 Mai Liem Truc, head of Vietnam's General Department of Posts and Telecommunications, announces at a press conference that Vietnam is connected to global Internet. Decree 21/CP of March 1997 had set rules: Vietnam Data Communication Company, a VNPT subsidiary, runs sole international gateway at 64 kilobits per second, while VDC, FPT, NetNam and Saigon Postel sell access to about 300 initial users. Björn Surborg's study shows how this architecture gave state control over content and pricing while use spread through cafés. Users passed 100,000 by 2000 and, with mobile data and Viettel's entry, about 70 percent of population by 2020.

aitape-tsunami-papua-new-guinea-1998.summary: A magnitude 7.0 earthquake off Papua New Guinea's north coast on evening of 17 July 1998 was followed about 20 minutes later by waves up to 15 metres that swept Sissano, Warapu, Arop and Malol. Over 2,100 people died, mostly children. Marine surveys in 2001 and a 2002 analysis showed a submarine sediment slump, rather than fault rupture alone, generated waves, which transformed hazard assessment for modest earthquakes. New Zealand reconnaissance engineers documented run-up heights. Survivors were resettled inland; disaster fed Pacific tsunami warning efforts and research on landslide tsunamis.

celtel-1998.summary: In 1998 Mo Ibrahim founded Celtel to build mobile networks across Africa without paying bribes; it sold for $3.4 billion seven years later. Banks would not lend to it: Ibrahim recalled that investors saw African countries as corrupt, and that lenders demanded every asset as security, so “we in Africa had to build the company with equity, with our money.” Renamed Celtel International in January 2004, it had about 24 million subscribers in 14 African countries when Mobile Telecommunications Company, later Zain, bought it in April 2005 for $3.4 billion.

celtel-1998.detail: Celtel also had to build its own infrastructure, including microwave links and fibre, because little existed. Ibrahim told CNBC: “Whenever there’s a big gap between perception and reality, there’s a wonderful business opportunity.” In September 2006 Celtel launched One Network, billed as the world’s first borderless network, letting subscribers in Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania roam without charges, call at local rates and recharge with local top-up cards; it extended to Gabon and the two Congos in June 2007. Bharti Airtel bought the business from Zain on 8 June 2010 and rebranded it Airtel that November. Ibrahim later founded a foundation and prize for African leadership and governance.

chagai-nuclear-tests-1998.summary: In May 1998 Pakistan tested what it said were five nuclear devices at Chagai, answering India's tests two weeks earlier. Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif cut short a Kazakhstan visit and chose to test after meeting military chiefs, Abdul Qadeer Khan, Ishfaq Ahmad and Munir Ahmad Khan, rejecting aid that U.S. President Bill Clinton offered to stop him. A second test, Chagai-II, followed on 30 May. Both countries’ tests brought United Nations Security Council Resolution 1172 and economic sanctions, particularly from America and Japan.

chagai-nuclear-tests-1998.detail:
Pakistan’s weapons programme began in 1972, with test planning from 1974; Chagai-I made it the seventh country to test nuclear weapons publicly, and 28 May is now celebrated as Youm-e-Takbir. Clinton sent delegations led by Strobe Talbott and General Anthony Zinni to lobby against testing; Pakistani economists concluded that G8 sanctions had little effect on India and doubted U.S. commitments. Ishfaq Ahmad told Sharif: “Mr. Prime Minister, take a decision and, Insha’Allah, I give you the guarantee of success.”

Yield estimates vary: the Theoretical Physics Group claimed about 40 kilotons in total with the largest boosted device at 30 to 36 kilotons, while seismologists put Chagai-I at roughly 9 to 12 kilotons and other scientists at 6 to 13 or 12 to 20.

dmca-1998.summary: In 1998 the Digital Millennium Copyright Act made it a crime to break digital locks and shielded sites that take down content on notice. It implemented two December 1996 World Intellectual Property Organization treaties on copyright online. It criminalises making or distributing technology meant to circumvent access controls on copyrighted works, now called digital rights management, and criminalises circumvention even without infringement, while raising penalties for online infringement. Its Title II created a safe harbor: online service providers escape liability for users’ infringement if they remove material promptly on notice from rights holders.

dmca-1998.detail: That notice-and-takedown process includes counter-notification protecting providers when users dispute claims, and lets rights holders subpoena providers for users’ identities. The European Union adopted this intermediary exemption in its Electronic Commerce Directive of 2000. Section 1201 contains no fair-use exemption and no knowledge requirement, so criminal liability can attach to unintended circumvention for legitimate purposes; the Librarian of Congress issues exemptions every three years for uses where access controls hinder non-infringing use.

furby-1998.summary: In October 1998 Furby went on sale, a toy that seemed to learn English; 1.8 million sold that year and 14 million the next. Dave Hampton and Caleb Chung created it over 18 months; inventor Richard C. Levy brought it to Tiger, whose owner Roger Shiffman bought the rights. New Furbies speak only “Furbish,” short words and simple syllables, and are programmed to replace it with English over time, so they appear to learn; they also talk among themselves through infrared ports between their eyes. Holiday demand drove resale prices past $100.

furby-1998.detail: Furbies retailed for about US$35. More than 40 million were sold in three years of original production, and its speech was translated into 17 languages. On January 13, 1999 it was reported that the National Security Agency had banned Furbies from its property for fear they might record and repeat classified information; Shiffman replied that “Furby has absolutely no ability to do any recording whatsoever,” and Hampton showed its microphone could not record sound. Inside, cams and gears driven by a single electric motor close its eyes and mouth, raise its ears and lift its body. Hasbro revived Furby as the Emoto-Tronic Furby in 2005 and again in 2012.

google-founded-1998.summary: In September 1998 Page and Brin incorporated Google, and finding anything on the web became a matter of seconds. It grew from a Stanford research project begun in January 1996 around PageRank, which Page and Brin published with Rajeev Motwani and Terry Winograd; it ranks pages by what links to them, and Stanford held its patent. Sun Microsystems co-founder Andy Bechtolsheim’s August 1998 cheque for $100,000 prompted incorporation, since funds could not be used without a company. Google misspells googol, 10 to the 100th power, signalling intent to index vast numbers of pages.

google-founded-1998.detail: Google’s first base was Menlo Park, California, and Scott Hassan had written much early code. David Cheriton, who had just sold Granite Systems to Cisco for $220 million, hosted Page, Brin and Bechtolsheim at his Palo Alto home, where the two investors agreed to put in about $200,000 each. With Jeff Bezos, Ram Shriram, friends and family, the founders raised about $1 million. Craig Silverstein, a fellow Stanford PhD student, was hired first. Kleiner Perkins and Sequoia Capital led a $25 million round on June 7, 1999, and Eric Schmidt became chairman and chief executive in 2001. Google went public in 2004 and became Alphabet’s subsidiary in 2015.

iridium-launch-bankruptcy-1998.summary: In November 1998 Iridium switched on 66 satellites for phones that worked anywhere; nine months later it went bankrupt owing $4 billion. It uses 66 satellites in six near-polar orbital planes about 781 kilometres up, linked by Ka-band crosslinks, so handsets connect from any point on Earth without nearby ground stations. The first fleet cost about US$5 billion, yet handsets weighed a pound and cost $3,000, reception failed indoors and cellular phones were spreading; revenue never covered construction debt and Iridium went bankrupt, then among America’s largest bankruptcies.

iridium-launch-bankruptcy-1998.detail: Bary Bertiger, Raymond J. Leopold and Ken Peterson conceived Iridium in late 1987, and Motorola filed patents in 1988. Its name honours element 77, iridium, matching the 77 satellites first calculated; 66 proved enough. Of 99 satellites built, 95 were launched between 1997 and 2002 on Delta II, Proton, Rokot and Long March rockets. Under new ownership, the service turned to customers beyond geosynchronous coverage, including journalists, explorers and military units. In 1999 an analyst told The New York Times that one number carried anywhere was “expensive... There never was a viable market.” Second-generation Iridium NEXT satellites began replacing it in January 2017.

iss-first-module-1998.summary: In November 1998 Zarya launched, the first piece of the International Space Station; it has been continuously inhabited since Expedition 1’s crew arrived on 2 November 2000. On 4 December Space Shuttle Endeavour carried up Unity, America’s first node, on STS-88 and joined it to Zarya; Unity links Russian and U.S. segments and offers ports for later modules and visiting spacecraft. Its design merged two earlier plans, America’s Space Station Freedom and Soviet Mir-2.

sources.confirms: Zarya, the Functional Cargo Block, was the first ISS component launched, on 20 November 1998 on a Proton-K, and orbited alone for 16 days until Endeavour brought Unity.

sources.confirms: Endeavour launched on 4 December 1998 carrying Unity and mated it to Zarya.

iss-first-module-1998.detail: Russian-segment modules, including Zarya and Zvezda, were built at Khrunichev in Moscow; Zvezda dated from 1985, made for Mir-2, which never flew. Much of America’s segment, including Destiny, Unity, truss and solar arrays, came from NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center and Michoud Assembly Facility. Five space programmes and fifteen countries take part under the 1998 Space Station Intergovernmental Agreement; as of August 2025, 290 people from 26 countries had visited. It is the largest human spacecraft ever built and, with China’s Tiangong, one of two operational space stations.

picture.credit: NASA Johnson Space Center, public domain, via NASA Image and Video Library

iss-zarya-1998.summary: In November 1998 a Proton rocket lifted Zarya from Baikonur, the first module of the space station fifteen nations built together. Nine minutes later it reached a 400-kilometre orbit and began unfurling antennas and solar panels; its name means “sunrise.” Khrunichev in Moscow built it between December 1994 and January 1998 under NASA’s US$220 million contract, adapting Soviet TKS spacecraft’s Functional Cargo Block, and it supplied most early power, propulsion and guidance. On 6 December the STS-88 crew used Endeavour’s robotic arm to capture it and mate it to Unity.

iss-zarya-1998.detail: Zarya has a mass of 19,323 kilograms and is 12.56 metres long. Two solar arrays and six nickel-cadmium batteries gave 3 kilowatts on average, and 16 external tanks hold up to 6.1 tonnes of propellant, as NASA required in 1997. Astronauts Jerry Ross and James Newman made two spacewalks to connect cables, and on 10 December 1998 Robert Cabana and Sergei Krikalev ceremonially entered the outpost. As the station grew, Zarya’s role shifted to storage, and its tanks now hold fuel for Zvezda. NASA’s contract cost far less than Lockheed’s rival Bus-1 design, and Khrunichev also built a spare, FGB-2, later completed as Nauka and launched in 2021.

jabiluka-uranium-blockade-1998.summary: Energy Resources of Australia began building a decline at Jabiluka, a uranium deposit surrounded by Kakadu National Park, in June 1998 despite opposition from Mirarr senior traditional owner Yvonne Margarula. A blockade camp from March to November drew about 5,000 people and more than 500 arrests. A UNESCO World Heritage mission in late 1998 recommended halting works; Australia resisted an 'in danger' listing. With uranium prices low and Rio Tinto taking over ERA in 2000, mine was never developed; in 2005 ERA agreed Mirarr consent would be required, and site was rehabilitated. Graetz's two-part study traces relations between Mirarr and Ranger mine from 1970 to 2014.

korea-pc-bang-starcraft-1998.summary: Blizzard's StarCraft reaches Korea in April 1998 as laid-off workers after Asian financial crisis open PC bangs, rooms of networked computers rented by hour. Jun-Sok Huhh shows how these rooms, numbering more than 15,000 by 1999, turned a single-player market into a social one: players met opponents in person, operators paid per-seat licences for online titles such as Lineage, and StarCraft sold several million copies in Korea alone. Televised leagues on Ongamenet and MBCGame from 2000 made professional gamers celebrities and gave e-sports its early institutional form. PC bangs also seeded broadband demand that carriers met with ADSL from 1999.

krugman-fax-machine-1998.summary: In June 1998 Paul Krugman wrote that the internet’s economic impact would be no greater than a fax machine’s; he later called it a joke. In it he wrote that “by 2005 or so, it will become clear that the Internet’s impact on the economy has been no greater than the fax machine’s.” He expected Internet growth to “slow drastically” as a flaw in Metcalfe’s law, which holds that potential connections in a network grow with participants squared, became apparent: “most people have nothing to say to each other!” Snopes rates this attribution correct.

sources.title: Did Paul Krugman Say the Internet's Effect on the World ...

krugman-fax-machine-1998.detail: Snopes says his quote circulated for years as proof of expert fallibility, often with Krugman’s later concession attached. In December 2013 he wrote that he had written it for Times magazine’s 100th anniversary issue, that “the whole point was to be fun and provocative, not to engage in careful forecasting,” and that he was “clearly wrong” about it; Snopes notes it in fact ran in Red Herring. On Business Insider he added, “I don’t claim any special expertise in technology.”

lesotho-highlands-katse-1998.summary: Lesotho Highlands Water Project Phase 1A, inaugurated by King Letsie III and Nelson Mandela on 22 January 1998, sends water from Katse Dam, a 185 m concrete arch in Lesotho's Maloti mountains, through 82 km of tunnels to South Africa's Vaal system at 18 cubic metres a second. Muela hydropower station (72 MW) made Lesotho self-sufficient in electricity, and royalties under a 1986 treaty became a main source of state revenue. Phase 1 cost about US$2.4 billion. Displaced highland communities and downstream villages lost fields and grazing, and later surveys found many said living standards fell despite compensation.

lesotho-highlands-katse-1998.detail: In a Highland Church Action Group survey, three quarters of affected households reported worse living standards. A 1986 treaty between Lesotho and apartheid South Africa set royalties and governance, and a Phase 1 cost of US$2.4 billion was financed through World Bank, European and commercial loans. Phase 2, centred on Polihali Dam, was under construction through 2020s with first water planned for 2028.

mnist-lenet5-1998.summary: In 1998 LeCun's LeNet-5 read handwritten digits with a convolutional network; banks ran it on cheques and MNIST became the first benchmark. It presented LeNet-5, a convolutional neural network, and MNIST, 60,000 training and 10,000 test images of handwritten digits. Using character recognition as their case study, they showed that “hand-crafted feature extraction can be advantageously replaced by carefully designed learning machines that operate directly on pixel images.” LeNet-5 reached 0.95% test error, 0.8% with distorted training data; boosted LeNet-4 reached 0.7%.

sources.title: [PDF] Gradient-based Learning Applied To Document Recognition
Yann LeCun, Leon Bottou, Yoshua Bengio and Patrick Haffner, 'Gradient-based learning applied to document recognition', Proceedings of the IEEE 86 (1998)
sources.author: LeCun, Yann; Bottou, Leon; Bengio, Yoshua; Haffner, Patrick

mnist-lenet5-1998.detail:
LeNet-5 has seven trainable layers on a 32 by 32 pixel input. Convolution layers C1, C3 and C5 detect local patterns through 5 by 5 windows, subsampling layers S2 and S4 halve each map’s resolution, and F6 plus an output layer classify. Since every weight is learned with back-propagation, “convolutional networks can be seen as synthesizing their own feature extractor.” For comparison, a linear classifier scored 12% error, k-nearest neighbour 5.0% and support vector machines 1.4% down to 0.8%.

The paper also introduced graph transformer networks for training whole document-reading systems end to end. Its check reader “has been fielded in several banks across the United States since June 1996,” and “it is deployed commercially and reads several million checks per day.”

nilesat-101-launch-1998.summary: An Ariane 4 lifts Nilesat 101 from Kourou on 28 April 1998 for Egyptian Satellite Company, a firm owned by Egyptian Radio and Television Union and Egyptian banks. Built by Matra Marconi Space for about 158 million dollars, satellite carries 12 Ku-band transponders at 7 degrees West and begins broadcasting that May with capacity for over 80 digital channels. Unlike Arabsat, a 22-state consortium, Nilesat belongs to a single government and sells transponders to private channels, which turns it into principal platform of Arab satellite television boom: by 2010 it carries hundreds of free-to-air channels from Dream TV to religious broadcasters. Its orbital neighbourhood with Eutelsat at 7/8 degrees West makes one dish serve most Arab homes.

open-source-term-1998.summary: In 1998 Christine Peterson coined open source as a term to sell free software to business; Linux and Apache came to run most of the internet. OSI’s history places her proposal at a Palo Alto strategy session on February 3; Peterson herself dates her idea to February 2 and its adoption to February 5 at VA Research, with Eric Raymond, Todd Anderson, Larry Augustin, Sam Ockman and, by phone, Jon “maddog” Hall. “Free software” confused business listeners, who heard “no cost.” Raymond and Bruce Perens founded OSI late that month to promote this new label.

open-source-term-1998.detail:
Peterson writes that Anderson introduced it indirectly. “He simply used the term in a sentence on another topic, just dropped it into the conversation to see what happened.” Minutes later another attendee used it too, which she calls “memetic evolution.” When terminology came up, Raymond listed “free software,” “open source” and “sourceware”; Anderson argued for open source, Raymond endorsed it, and Peterson let them form “the (loose, informal) consensus.”

OSI’s history says Perens adapted its Open Source Definition from his Debian Free Software Guidelines, arguing for openness on pragmatic business grounds. Tim O’Reilly’s April 7, 1998 meeting of leaders was announced as the first “Freeware Summit” and within a week was being called the first “Open Source Summit.” Peterson credits Raymond and O’Reilly with persuading the community and calls her coinage “a small contribution.”

sahami-bayesian-spam-1998.summary: In 1998 Mehran Sahami and Microsoft researchers showed a Bayesian filter could learn to tell junk email from legitimate mail by example. Junk mail, they wrote, was “a problem of growing proportions.” Their filter learned from examples of junk and legitimate messages which words and other features predicted each class, then estimated the probability that a new message was junk, and it weighed errors by differential misclassification cost, so that discarding a legitimate message counted for more than letting junk through.

Androutsopoulos, Ion; Koutsias, John; Chandrinos, Konstantinos V.; Paliouras, George; Spyropoulos, Constantine D., 'An evaluation of Naive Bayesian anti-spam filtering', in Proceedings of the Workshop on Machine Learning in the New Information Age, 11th European Conference on Machine Learning, Barcelona (2000), pp. 9-17

sahami-bayesian-spam-1998.detail: Its abstract describes automated construction of filters to remove unwanted messages from a user’s mail stream. By “casting this problem in a decision theoretic framework,” they could “make use of probabilistic learning methods in conjunction with a notion of differential misclassification cost.” They also found that “the incorporation of domain-specific features” beyond words alone improved filtering, drawing on hand-built phrases and on message properties such as sender domain.

trastuzumab-herceptin-1998.summary: In September 1998 the FDA approved Herceptin, an antibody aimed at one protein on breast cancer cells; targeted cancer therapy began. HER2 is amplified in 20 to 30% of early-stage breast cancers; its receptor normally tells cells to grow and divide, and when overexpressed “cell growth accelerates beyond its normal limits.” Trastuzumab, a monoclonal antibody, binds HER2 and slows cell replication. In metastatic disease it raised median survival from 20.3 to 25.1 months, and given after surgery it cuts recurrence risk.

trastuzumab-herceptin-1998.detail:
Axel Ullrich and H. Michael Shepard at Genentech discovered this drug, building on Robert Weinberg’s work on the neu oncogene and Mark Greene’s antibody against its receptor; Dennis Slamon at UCLA worked on development, and 15 women entered the first trial in 1992. By 1996 trials covered over 900 women, and under pressure from advocates Genentech and the FDA set up a lottery giving 100 women each quarter access outside those trials.

In early-stage disease, absolute reduction in recurrence within three years was 9.5% and in death 3%, against a 2.1% absolute rise in serious heart problems, which may resolve when treatment stops. Standard treatment runs one year and is costly, so trial lengths and public funding remain debated. Its approval date of September 25, 1998 is not independently confirmed.

us-v-microsoft-1998.summary: In May 1998 the United States sued Microsoft for using Windows to crush Netscape; courts found it a monopoly and opened room for Google. They accused it of illegally monopolizing the web browser market by bundling Internet Explorer with Windows and restricting PC makers and users from removing it, so every Windows user had Microsoft’s browser and rivals such as Netscape Navigator and Opera took extra effort to install. Judge Thomas Penfield Jackson found in 1999 and 2000 that Microsoft held and defended a monopoly, and ordered it split in two.

sources.title: United States v. Microsoft Corp.
United States v. Microsoft Corp., Court's Findings of Fact, Civil Action No. 98-1232 (D.D.C. 5 November 1999)
sources.author: Thomas Penfield Jackson, US District Judge
sources.venue: United States District Court for the District of Columbia; US Department of Justice archive
sources.confirms: The court found Microsoft held monopoly power in Intel-compatible PC operating systems, with share above 90 percent, and had bound Internet Explorer to Windows to hinder Netscape; page fetched.

sources.title: Gilbert, Richard J. and Michael L. Katz, "An Economist's Guide to U.S. v. Microsoft"
sources.author: Richard J. Gilbert, Michael L. Katz
sources.confirms: Peer-reviewed analysis of the case filed in May 1998 and the 1999-2000 findings.

us-v-microsoft-1998.detail:
Jackson’s findings of fact on November 5, 1999 held that Microsoft’s dominance of x86 personal computer operating systems was a monopoly. He found it had been used to crush threats from Apple, Java, Netscape, Lotus, RealNetworks, Linux and others. His April 3, 2000 conclusions of law found monopolization, attempted monopolization and tying under the Sherman Antitrust Act, and on June 7, 2000 he ordered Microsoft split into an operating-system company and a software company.

On June 28, 2001 the D.C. Circuit overturned his rulings, partly because he had discussed it with news media mid-trial, while upholding the monopoly finding and sending remedies to Judge Colleen Kollar-Kotelly. Under John Ashcroft the Justice Department dropped its breakup demand on September 6, 2001 and settled on November 1: Microsoft would share its application programming interfaces with third parties and accept three investigators with full access to its systems, records and source code for five years, but need not change code and could still tie software to Windows. Those obligations expired on November 12, 2007, with parts extended two years.

vmware-1998.summary: In 1998 VMware was founded to run several operating systems on one PC; virtual machines became the unit of the data centre. It was the first commercially successful company to virtualize the x86 architecture, meaning one physical computer runs several operating systems at once as separate “virtual machines.” Unlike IBM mainframes, x86 had seventeen instructions that behaved differently in privileged mode without trapping, so VMware ran user-mode code directly and translated kernel-mode code, rewriting problem instructions as they ran.

sources.confirms: VMware was founded in 1998 by Diane Greene, Mendel Rosenblum, Edward Wang, Edouard Bugnion and Scott Devine to bring virtual machines to x86 processors; a beta drew about 75,000 downloads in 1999 and VMware Workstation shipped commercially that year.

sources.title: Vance, Ashlee, 'The End of an Era at VMware', New York Times Bits blog, 10 September 2008
sources.author: Ashlee Vance
sources.confirms: Rosenblum and Greene founded VMware to bring virtualization, long confined to mainframe-class systems, down to basic servers on Intel and AMD chips, after a Stanford presentation to Microsoft prompted them to start a company.

vmware-1998.detail: Its approach grew from Rosenblum’s Disco project at Stanford, which virtualized MIPS in the mid-1990s. Greene found fundraising hard because investors wanted consumer internet startups. VMware worked in stealth with about 20 employees at the end of 1998, launched at DEMO in February 1999 and released VMware Workstation in May 1999 for developers and testers running several operating systems on one desktop. In 2001 it entered servers with GSX Server and bare-metal ESX Server, which consolidated workloads where servers ran at low utilization. EMC bought VMware for $625 million in cash on January 9, 2004 and floated 15% in 2007; Broadcom acquired it on November 22, 2023 for $69 billion in cash and stock, selling its end-user computing division to KKR as Omnissa.

age-of-spiritual-machines-1999.summary: In 1999 Ray Kurzweil predicted a computer would pass the Turing test by 2029; that date is now argued with a straight face. Kurzweil, inventor and futurist, argues from his law of accelerating returns that “key events” arrive ever more often and computing capacity grows exponentially. He expects Moore’s law to end “by the year 2020” but some replacement technology to keep that curve going, so that “by around the year 2020” a $1,000 personal computer will match a human brain.

sources.title: Analysis
Kurzweil, Ray, The Age of Spiritual Machines: When Computers Exceed Human Intelligence
sources.author: Ray Kurzweil
sources.confirms: Digitised edition of the 1999 book containing the forecast that a computer passes the Turing test by 2029; archive.org record fetched.

sources.title: Hafner, Katie, 'The Soul of the Next New Machine: Humans', New York Times, 6 November 1999
sources.author: Katie Hafner
sources.confirms: Kurzweil's The Age of Spiritual Machines (Viking, 1999) argues from the exponential growth of computing that within decades machines will exceed human intelligence and claim consciousness, a thesis John Searle attacked in the New York Review of Books.

sources.title: 'Ray Kurzweil', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: The Age of Spiritual Machines (1999) presents the 21st century as a time when computers reach a level equivalent to the human brain and the line between human and machine blurs.
sources.qualifies: Kurzweil himself says the book put a Turing test pass at 2029, while the 1990 Age of Intelligent Machines had given a wider range.

age-of-spiritual-machines-1999.detail:
Each of 2009, 2019, 2029 and 2099 gets its own chapter of predictions. By 2019 images are mostly projected onto the retina and there are “prevalent reports” of computers passing Turing’s test; by 2029 machines “routinely” pass it and communicate through direct neural pathways. Kurzweil writes that machines “will appear to have their own free will” and even “spiritual experiences,” and that humans will in effect live forever as humanity and its machinery merge.

Reviewers praised his record with predictions and clear explanations, but philosophers John Searle and Colin McGinn insisted computation alone cannot make a conscious machine; Searle answered Deep Blue with a “Chess Room” variant of his Chinese room argument. Kurzweil expanded these ideas in The Singularity Is Near.

aibo-1999.summary: In May 1999 Sony introduced AIBO, a robot dog for $2,500; its first 5,000 sold out online in 20 minutes, and owners later held funerals for them. The ERS-110 went on sale on 1 June at 250,000 yen, 3,000 units for Japan and 2,000 for the United States. AIBO stands for Artificial Intelligence Robot and sounds like aibō, Japanese for “pal.” Toshitada Doi had begun robot work at Sony’s Computer Science Laboratory in 1994 with Masahiro Fujita, who argued that robot behavior should “be sufficiently complex or unexpected so that people keep an interest in watching or taking care of it.”

sources.title: AIBO
'A Smart Dog with Megabytes', New York Times, 13 May 1999
sources.author: New York Times
sources.confirms: The Times reports Sony's introduction of Aibo, meaning companion, on 11 May 1999 at $2,500.

sources.title: 'News Watch: Robotic Dogs Take Center Stage', New York Times, 3 June 1999
sources.author: New York Times
sources.confirms: The Times reports that Sony's Japanese allocation of Aibo sold out within 20 minutes of online sales opening on 1 June 1999, with about 1,000 of 2,000 US units sold by day's end.

aibo-1999.detail:
ERS-110 hardware included a 64-bit RISC processor, 16 megabytes of RAM, touch, camera, range-finder, microphone, acceleration and angular-velocity sensors, speaker, and motorised legs, neck, mouth and tail. Its OPEN-R architecture used swappable hardware and software modules; Doi called it the project’s “masterpiece” because outside programmers could add capability. Since it packaged computer, vision and limbs far more cheaply than research robots, AIBO became standard in AI teaching and in RoboCup’s Four-Legged League.

Sony announced AIBO’s end on 26 January 2006 to improve profitability; Doi staged a mock funeral with more than 100 colleagues, calling AIBO a symbol of a risk-taking spirit now dead. Repairs stopped in July 2014. Its fourth-generation ERS-1000, which learns through a cloud connection, launched in Japan on 11 January 2018. AIBO entered Carnegie Mellon’s Robot Hall of Fame in 2006.

bhutan-television-internet-1999.summary: On 2 June 1999, marking 25 years of King Jigme Singye Wangchuck's reign, Bhutan Broadcasting Service begins television transmission in Thimphu and state carrier Druknet opens internet access. Bhutan had kept television out while neighbours filled with satellite dishes, citing cultural protection. Within months cable operators offer dozens of Indian and international channels, and early BBS bulletins reach eastern towns days late on VHS tapes sent by bus. Wangchuk's 2008 study in Media Asia and foreign reporting trace debates about wrestling shows and advertising that follow, and a 2006 ban on some channels. Bhutan's gross national happiness framework shapes how officials talk about this opening.
