bhutan-television-internet-1999.detail: BBS history pages give 2 June 1999 launch, silver jubilee timing, VHS distribution. Wangchuk (Media Asia 2008) analyses impact and policy debates. PBS Frontline World report describes early reception.

blackberry-1999.summary: In 1999 Research In Motion sold the BlackBerry, a pager with a keyboard that pushed email; executives did not put it down for a decade. Named for its keyboard's likeness to blackberry druplets, it received mail from Microsoft Exchange through RIM's companion server software: new mail reached the device as it arrived rather than when fetched. RIM, founded in 1984, had worked on Mobitex packet-switched wireless data since 1988, and its 1998 Inter@ctive Pager, sized like a bar of soap, competed with Motorola’s Skytel paging.

sources.title: BlackBerry Limited
Encyclopaedia Britannica, "BlackBerry"
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Reference entry stating the BlackBerry line of wireless handhelds was made by Research in Motion of Waterloo, Ontario, from 1999, beginning with a two-way pager offering push email.

sources.title: Reuters, 'Timeline: From RIM to BlackBerry, a company in transition', 30 January 2013
sources.author: Reuters
sources.confirms: In January 1999 RIM launched the BlackBerry email service across North America, the first wireless device to sync with corporate email, and later that year introduced the BlackBerry 850 handheld with a QWERTY keyboard.

blackberry-1999.detail: This BlackBerry 850 led to RIM’s business products, starting with its BlackBerry 957 of April 2000, RIM’s first smartphone. Encryption and S/MIME support won BlackBerry devices use in governments and businesses. BlackBerry led smartphone markets in many countries, including the United States, until the iPhone 4’s 2010 announcement, then lost ground to Apple and Android. Under John S. Chen, BlackBerry moved into cybersecurity software, released its last phone, Key2 LE, in 2018, and ended BlackBerry 10 support in 2022.

emoji-1999.summary: In 1999 Shigetaka Kurita drew 176 emoji on a 12 by 12 grid for Japanese phones; they now sit in every keyboard and in MoMA. Unicode made emoji universal in 2010, Apple put its emoji keyboard on iPhones outside Japan in 2011, and in October 2016 New York’s Museum of Modern Art took Kurita’s original set into its collection.

sources.title: MoMA, Inbox: The Original Emoji, by Shigetaka Kurita
The New York Times, Look Who's Smiley Now: MoMA Acquires Original Emoji

gallup-y2k-poll-1999.summary: In November 1999 Gallup found only 12 percent of Americans expected major problems from the Y2K bug, and a December poll found 7 percent; worry had faded through the year. In a telephone survey of 1,010 U.S. adults taken November 18 to 21 for USA Today and the National Science Foundation, 12% believed Y2K computer mistakes would cause major problems for society, down from 34% in December 1998; 3% expected major problems personally, down from 14%. Most expected minor trouble: 71% foresaw minor problems for society and 14% none.

sources.title: Public Considers Major Y2K Computer Failures Unlikely
National Science Foundation press release, 'Poll Shows Continuing Decline in Y2K Concern', 22 December 1999 (reproduced by ScienceDaily)
sources.author: National Science Foundation
sources.confirms: The fifth NSF-sponsored Gallup poll in December 1999 found only seven percent of Americans, down from 12 percent in November, expected major problems from Year 2000 computer mistakes.

sources.title: Los Angeles Times, 'Turnover Turning Into a Nonevent', 30 December 1999
sources.author: Los Angeles Times
sources.confirms: Public concern over Y2K peaked a year earlier and declined steadily; only 5 percent in an AP poll earlier in December 1999 expected major problems in the United States.

gallup-y2k-poll-1999.verification_note: The 12 percent figure comes from Gallup's 18 to 21 November 1999 poll; a fifth NSF and USA Today Gallup poll in December 1999 found 7 percent expecting major problems, and an AP poll that month found 5 percent.
gallup-y2k-poll-1999.detail: Gallup’s trend for major societal problems ran 34% in December 1998, 21% in March 1999, 11% in August and 12% in November. Personal worry fell from 14% to 9%, 7% and 3%. Asked how long problems would last, 41% said a few days and 32% several weeks, so 73% expected a short disruption against 45% in December 1998, while 24% expected several months to a year. Sampling error was plus or minus 3 percentage points. Lydia Saad wrote the release.

geforce-256-1999.summary: In 1999 Nvidia sold GeForce 256 as the first GPU; a chip built for games became deep learning’s engine. It marketed the chip as “the world’s first ‘GPU’, or Graphics Processing Unit,” defined as “a single-chip processor with integrated transform, lighting, triangle setup/clipping, and rendering engines that is capable of processing a minimum of 10 million polygons per second.” Older 3D accelerators left transform and lighting, geometry work that places and shades a scene, to a PC’s CPU; moving it onto one chip cut hardware costs and brought such power to cheap consumer cards.

Lindholm, Erik, John Nickolls, Stuart Oberman and John Montrym, 'NVIDIA Tesla: A Unified Graphics and Computing Architecture', IEEE Micro 28 (2008), pp. 39-55
sources.author: Lindholm, Erik; Nickolls, John; Oberman, Stuart; Montrym, John
sources.confirms: States that the first GPU was the GeForce 256, introduced in 1999, with fixed-function vertex transform and lighting and pixel pipelines, before programmable shaders in 2001.
sources.qualifies: Authors are Nvidia engineers writing in a peer-reviewed IEEE magazine.

sources.author: John Nickolls; William J. Dally
sources.confirms: Peer-reviewed account tracing GPU computing from the 1999 GeForce 256, the first chip marketed as a GPU, to general-purpose use; Crossref metadata confirmed, IEEE page did not open.

sources.title: Dally, William J., Stephen W. Keckler, and David B. Kirk. 'Evolution of the Graphics Processing Unit (GPU).' IEEE Micro 41, no. 6 (2021): 42-51.
sources.author: William J. Dally; Stephen W. Keckler; David B. Kirk
sources.confirms: Retrospective on the GPU's path from graphics hardware to the engine of deep learning; Crossref metadata confirmed.

geforce-256-1999.detail: Its chip, NV10, improved on RIVA TNT2 with more pixel pipelines, hardware transform and lighting, and motion compensation for MPEG-2 video, and was the first fully Direct3D 7-compliant accelerator. Its “256” refers to its 256-bit QuadPipe rendering engine of four 64-bit pipelines. Against 3dfx’s Voodoo3 3500 and TNT2 Ultra it gave 50% or more higher frame rates in games written for hardware T&L when paired with low-budget CPUs. An SDR memory version shipped in October 1999 and a DDR version in mid-December; its T&L engine also let Nvidia enter CAD with its first Quadro cards. TSMC made NV10 on a 220 nm process.

picture.credit: Hyins, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

hole-in-the-wall-kalkaji-1999.summary: On 26 January 1999 Sugata Mitra's team at NIIT cuts an opening in a wall between their Kalkaji office and an adjoining settlement in south Delhi and fixes a computer with internet behind it, facing out. Children with no prior exposure learn to browse and draw within days, teaching each other. Repeats at Shivpuri and Madantusi show similar patterns, published by Mitra in British Journal of Educational Technology in 2001 and 2003 as minimally invasive education. Hole-in-the-Wall Education Limited, formed with International Finance Corporation, places over 30 learning stations across India and abroad. Claims of learning without teachers draw sustained criticism from educationists, yet this experiment shapes debates on self-organised learning for two decades.

hole-in-the-wall-kalkaji-1999.detail: Hole-in-the-Wall project page confirms date, Kalkaji, NIIT, later sites and IFC partnership, 30 plus learning stations. Mitra and Rana (BJET 2001) and Mitra (BJET 2003) report findings. Critiques appear in Arora (BJET 2010) and press.

i-mode-1999.summary: In February 1999 NTT DoCoMo launched i-mode, the web on an ordinary phone; 30 million Japanese used it before the iPhone. Unlike WAP, used elsewhere, which ran its own markup language on a separate protocol stack, i-mode carried web access and email over a packet-switched network using C-HTML, cut-down HTML that DoCoMo designed for phones with little memory, small monochrome screens and limited input. Mari Matsunaga shaped the service, Takeshi Natsuno led business development and Keiichi Enoki oversaw it. Within months KDDI launched EZweb and J-Phone launched J-Sky in imitation.

i-mode-1999.detail:
Users paid for data sent and received plus about ¥200 to 300 a month, and reached DoCoMo-supervised official sites from a dedicated i-mode button. There were more than 12,000 official sites and around 100,000 unofficial ones. Bandai’s Dokodemo Aso Vegas service, launched in May 1999, passed one million paid subscribers by March 2000. By June 2006 i-mode, EZweb and J-Sky together had over 80 million subscribers in Japan, and usage peaked around 2008.

Operators in Europe, Asia and Australia licensed i-mode, reaching 17 markets under Natsuno. On 29 October 2019 DoCoMo announced that i-mode would end on 31 March 2026.

ilo-convention-182-1999.summary: In June 1999 the ILO adopted a convention against child labour’s worst forms; it became ILO’s first convention ratified by every member state. A ratifying country commits to immediate action to prohibit and eliminate slavery, forced labour and trafficking of children, their use in armed conflict, prostitution, pornography and illegal activities such as drug trafficking, and dangerous work. On 4 August 2020 Tonga deposited its ratification, making it the first international labour convention ratified by all 187 ILO members.

International Labour Organization, "ILO Child Labour Convention achieves universal ratification" (news release, 4 August 2020)

sources.title: International Labour Organization, "Universal protection against the worst forms of child labour"

ilo-convention-182-1999.detail: ILO’s International Programme on the Elimination of Child Labour helps countries comply and monitors them, and Recommendation No. 190, adopted that same year, lists hazards each country should weigh when defining dangerous work in its own law. Convention 182 had the fastest ratification pace in ILO history; 152 million children were in child labour, almost half in dangerous work, most of it agricultural and driven by poverty. According to ILO, the proportion of children in child labour fell by almost 40 percent between 2000 and 2016 as ratifications rose and countries passed laws, including minimum employment ages.

infosys-nasdaq-1999.summary: In March 1999 Infosys listed on Nasdaq, the first Indian company to do so; India's outsourcing industry had a flagship. It was then among the top 20 companies on Nasdaq by market capitalization. N. R. Narayana Murthy and six fellow engineers had founded it in Pune on 2 July 1981 with $250, moving to Bangalore in 1983; its offshore custom software business grew after India’s 1991 liberalisation, and it listed in India in February 1993. In 1996 it released In2000, a toolset for the Y2K date problem, alongside its banking products.

infosys-nasdaq-1999.detail: Nasdaq chief executive Robert Greifeld gave Infosys’s 25th anniversary gathering a share-price comparison. “On March 11, 1999, when Infosys came to NASDAQ, you could buy 100 shares for $3,400; today that would cost you about $50,000, which is a 1387% return,” he said. Its ADR listing later moved to NYSE Euronext to give European investors better access, and in 1999 Infosys also rolled out its Finacle core banking suite and founded its research arm SETLabs.

intel-kiryat-gat-fab-18-1999.summary: Intel brings Fab 18 into production at Kiryat Gat in southern Israel in 1999, a 1.6 billion dollar plant making Pentium III processors on 0.18 micron process with 200 millimetre wafers. Israeli government grants about 600 million dollars, some 38 percent of cost, under its capital investment law, largest subsidy it had given a single firm. Plant employs about 3,500 and turns a development town into a semiconductor hub; Fab 28 follows in 2008 on 45 nanometre process and later nodes. Together with Haifa design centre that produced 8088 and Centrino, Kiryat Gat makes Israel one of few places outside United States and East Asia running leading-edge fabs, and Intel becomes Israel's largest private employer and exporter.

internet-of-things-1999.summary: In 1999 Kevin Ashton coined, or at least popularised, “Internet of Things” as a name for everyday objects online, pitching radio tags to Procter and Gamble. He has said he would prefer “Internet for things.” Ashton saw radio-frequency identification tags as essential: if objects carried tags that networks could read, computers could manage every individual object without anyone typing in where it was. His phrase came to describe physical objects fitted with sensors, processing and software that exchange data over networks.

sources.qualifies: Notes a claim that Peter Lewis used the exact term in 1985.

internet-of-things-1999.verification_note: Britannica, Wired and MIT confirm Ashton's 1999 coinage in a Procter and Gamble presentation while at MIT's Auto-ID Center; an MIT working paper notes a claim that Peter T. Lewis used that exact phrase in 1985, so first use is contested.
internet-of-things-1999.detail: This idea has earlier roots. In 1982 Carnegie Mellon graduate students connected their department’s Coca-Cola vending machine to the Internet so it could report stock and temperature; Mark Weiser’s 1991 paper “The Computer of the 21st Century” set out ubiquitous computing; Reza Raji described moving small data packets to large sets of nodes in IEEE Spectrum in 1994; and Peter T. Lewis used the exact phrase in a 1985 speech to the Congressional Black Caucus Foundation. Bill Joy presented device-to-device communication as one of his “Six Webs” at Davos in 1999. IoT Analytics counted 16.6 billion connected IoT devices in 2023 and about 17 billion as of October 2024.

iridium-bankruptcy-1999.summary: In August 1999 Iridium filed for bankruptcy eight months after launch, owing $4 billion; the satellites kept flying under new owners. Hours earlier a group of bondholders holding about 25 percent of its $1.45 billion in senior notes had filed an involuntary petition in New York to force the issue. Iridium had spent more than $5 billion on 66 low-orbiting satellites to reach “anyone, anytime, virtually anywhere in the world.”

sources.title: For Iridium, A Quick Trip Back to Earth
Iridium Declares Bankruptcy

iridium-bankruptcy-1999.detail: Motorola, largest shareholder with 18 percent, said it believed restructuring could be done within 30 days and would keep supporting operations and subscribers. The New York Times attributed Iridium’s collapse to slower-than-expected subscriber growth, marketing and distribution missteps and earlier handset problems, and described its service as “outdated, outmoded and unpopular with consumers” by the filing. Nippon Iridium, second-largest investor, said it still believed in long-term viability. Neither source gives subscriber numbers or handset prices, so none are stated.

jesse-gelsinger-1999.summary: In September 1999 Jesse Gelsinger, 18, died in a gene therapy trial in Philadelphia; the field stalled a decade and consent rules tightened. He had partial ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, liver disease that blocks clearance of ammonia from blood, which he managed with restricted diet and drugs. On September 13 researchers at the University of Pennsylvania injected him with adenovirus carrying a corrected gene to test its safety; his immune system reacted massively to this viral vector, causing multiple organ failure and brain death.

B. Sibbald, 'Death but one unintended consequence of gene-therapy trial', CMAJ 164 (2001), 1612
sources.author: Barbara Sibbald
sources.confirms: Jesse Gelsinger, 18, received an experimental gene-therapy infusion at the University of Pennsylvania on 13 September 1999 and died four days later of a severe immune reaction.

sources.title: Sheryl Gay Stolberg, 'The Biotech Death of Jesse Gelsinger', New York Times Magazine, 28 November 1999
sources.author: Sheryl Gay Stolberg
sources.confirms: Jesse Gelsinger died on 17 September 1999 after taking part in a University of Pennsylvania gene therapy trial for ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency.

jesse-gelsinger-1999.detail: Researchers hoped to treat infants born with severe OTC deficiency, usually fatal at birth. FDA investigators found that scientists including co-investigator James Wilson, director of Penn’s Institute for Human Gene Therapy, had broken several rules: Gelsinger replaced a volunteer who dropped out although his ammonia levels should have excluded him, Penn failed to report two earlier patients’ serious side effects, and consent documents omitted deaths of monkeys given similar treatment. Penn and Children’s National Medical Center each paid more than $500,000 to the government; Wilson and Penn are reported to have held financial stakes in the research. All U.S. gene therapy trials halted for a time, a severe setback for the field.

mcnealy-zero-privacy-1999.summary: In January 1999 Sun's chief executive McNealy told reporters, “You have zero privacy anyway. Get over it.” He was launching Jini, meant to let consumer devices find one another, communicate and share processing power, which raised questions about what such networks would reveal about their owners; he called privacy a “red herring.” Privacy advocates and the FTC’s consumer protection chief condemned him, and his line has been quoted ever since.

sources.title: Sun on Privacy: 'Get Over It'
Scott McNealy's view on privacy: You still don't have any

mcnealy-zero-privacy-1999.detail: Jodie Bernstein, director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, objected. “Millions of American consumers inform us that privacy is a serious concern when they consider shopping online,” she said, noting that Sun belonged to the Online Privacy Alliance, which argued for industry self-regulation; Lori Fena of the Electronic Frontier Foundation called McNealy’s statements “completely irresponsible.” In June 2015 Computerworld reported that he stood by his line but now saw big government, not business, as privacy’s main threat. Google and AT&T holding information about him did not bother him, he said, “because I can always switch to another provider,” whereas “there’s only one DMV.”

mercado-libre-founded-1999.summary: In August 1999 Marcos Galperin, fresh from Stanford, founded MercadoLibre in a Buenos Aires garage; it became Latin America's largest online market and most valuable firm. It runs online marketplaces for e-commerce and auctions, where sellers list goods and the company earns from the platform, payments and advertising around them. Galperin raised money from John Muse of HM Capital Partners, then from JPMorgan Partners, Flatiron Partners, Goldman Sachs, GE Capital and Banco Santander Central Hispano. In August 2007 it became the first Latin American technology company listed on Nasdaq, and by 2016 it had 174.2 million users, the region’s most visited e-commerce site.

sources.title: Wikipedia: MercadoLibre
'Argentine Entrepreneur Makes Campus Gift', Stanford Graduate School of Business (2012)
sources.confirms: The page says Galperin and several Stanford GSB classmates founded MercadoLibre, and that a small team launched it from a garage in Buenos Aires in August 1999; it describes the company as Latin America’s largest e-commerce platform.
sources.qualifies: The page says the team launched from a Buenos Aires garage in August 1999, not from Stanford.

sources.title: Caselli, Irene, 'The man behind the eBay of Latin America', BBC News (2014)
sources.author: Caselli, Irene
sources.confirms: The article says MercadoLibre was founded in Argentina in 1999 by Marcos Galperin as an online marketplace and auction house, and that investor John Muse agreed to back his idea after Galperin pitched it during a car journey.
sources.qualifies: The article says Galperin launched the business after returning to Argentina, not from Stanford.

mercado-libre-founded-1999.verification_note: Stanford's page says Galperin's team launched from a Buenos Aires garage in August 1999, and BBC says he launched after returning to Argentina, rather than from Stanford.
mercado-libre-founded-1999.detail: eBay bought 19.5% of MercadoLibre in September 2001 and sold it in 2016, though both companies still cooperate to bring eBay sellers into Latin America. MercadoLibre bought Brazil’s iBazar.com, its competitor DeRemate in 2008 and Classified Media Group that year; it now operates in 17 other countries from Bolivia to Venezuela from headquarters in Montevideo. Business units include MarketPlace, MercadoPago payments, Mercado Publicado advertising, MercadoShops and Mercado Crédito. Time named it to its TIME100 Companies list for 2023.

mobileye-founded-1999.summary: Hebrew University computer-vision professor Amnon Shashua and Ziv Aviram start Mobileye in 1999 on a bet that a single forward camera and purpose-built processor can detect vehicles, pedestrians and lane markings well enough for safety systems, against industry belief in radar and stereo rigs. Their 2005 papers show monocular range estimation and collision warning on a custom chip, EyeQ1, built with STMicroelectronics. BMW, GM and Volvo ship EyeQ systems from 2007, Tesla's first Autopilot in 2015 runs on EyeQ3, and by 2017 Mobileye chips sit in millions of cars when Intel buys it for 15.3 billion dollars, its largest acquisition in Israel. Shashua's group also publishes Responsibility-Sensitive Safety, a formal model for driving policy adopted into standards work.

napster-1999.summary: In June 1999 Napster let anyone copy any song from anyone's hard drive; the record industry sued, and its revenues halved in a decade. Its central database, hosted by Napster, indexed every song that connected users were sharing; a search found who held a file, and downloading then ran between those two users’ computers. It offered songs hard to find elsewhere, from older recordings to concert bootlegs. College networks clogged, with MP3 transfers up to 61% of external traffic, and in December 1999 A&M Records and other labels sued through RIAA for contributory and vicarious copyright infringement.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Napster
A&M Records, Inc. v. Napster, Inc., 239 F.3d 1004 (9th Cir. 2001)
sources.author: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
sources.confirms: The Ninth Circuit upheld a preliminary injunction against Napster for contributory and vicarious copyright infringement.

sources.title: Rob, Rafael and Waldfogel, Joel, 'Piracy on the High C's: Music Downloading, Sales Displacement, and Social Welfare in a Sample of College Students', Journal of Law and Economics 49 (2006) 29-62
sources.author: Rob, Rafael; Waldfogel, Joel
sources.confirms: Economic study of music downloading in the Napster era and its displacement of sales.

napster-1999.detail: Metallica sued in April 2000 after its demo “I Disappear” circulated, saying it had identified 335,000 users sharing its songs; Dr. Dre followed within a month. Judge Marilyn Hall Patel issued her preliminary injunction in July 2000, stayed two days later by the Ninth Circuit, which in February 2001 ordered Napster to track its network and block infringing material. Verified use peaked at 26.4 million users in February 2001, with unofficial estimates of 80 million registered. Napster shut its network in early July 2001, settled with Metallica and Dr. Dre, agreed in September to pay $26 million plus $10 million in advances, and filed for bankruptcy in June 2002; Roxio bought its name for $5.3 million and relaunched it as subscription music. Decentralized networks such as Gnutella, FastTrack and BitTorrent emerged after Napster’s shutdown.

nipah-virus-malaysia-1999.summary: From September 1998 pig farmers in Perak, then Negeri Sembilan, fall ill with fever and encephalitis; authorities blame Japanese encephalitis and spray for mosquitoes, but adults without pig contact stay healthy. In March 1999 Chua Kaw Bing at University of Malaya isolates an unknown paramyxovirus from cerebrospinal fluid of a patient from Sungai Nipah village; CDC Fort Collins confirms a new agent related to Hendra virus. Chua's team reports 265 cases and 105 deaths in Malaysia plus 11 cases in Singapore abattoir workers. Culling of about one million pigs ends transmission. Fruit bats of genus Pteropus are later identified as reservoir.

sources.author: Chua, K. B. et al.

sources.author: CDC
sources.confirms: Contemporary public health report of the 1998-99 outbreak, the initial attribution to Japanese encephalitis, and the identification of the new virus in March 1999.

nipah-virus-malaysia-1999.verification_note: Case counts vary by cut-off date: Science (June 1999) gives 265 cases; later Malaysian tallies give 283 cases and 109 deaths.

remote-agent-1999.summary: In May 1999 NASA's Remote Agent ran the Deep Space 1 probe for 29 hours by pursuing goals rather than executing commands sent from Earth. Instead of executing command sequences sent from Earth, it pursued high-level goals by planning and issuing its own commands, and it detected, diagnosed and recovered from simulated failures. JPL said on June 7 that every objective was met, showing AI could run spacecraft millions of miles from Earth.

sources.title: Remote Agent Experiment Meets All Objectives
Rayman, Marc D., Varghese, Philip, Lehman, David H. and Livesay, Leslie L., 'Results from the Deep Space 1 technology validation mission', Acta Astronautica 47, no. 2-9 (2000), 475-487
sources.author: Marc D. Rayman, Philip Varghese, David H. Lehman and Leslie L. Livesay
sources.confirms: Deep Space 1 tested an onboard artificial intelligence remote agent whose planner turned high-level goals into activities, whose executive issued spacecraft commands, and which diagnosed and worked around four simulated faults without help from the ground.

sources.title: Bernard, Douglas E. et al., 'Spacecraft Autonomy Flight Experience: The DS1 Remote Agent Experiment', AIAA Space Technology Conference, Albuquerque, September 1999 (NASA Technical Reports Server)
sources.author: Douglas E. Bernard, Edward B. Gamble, Nicola Muscettola, P. Pandurang Nayak and others
sources.confirms: In May 1999 the Remote Agent autonomy software took command and control of the Deep Space 1 spacecraft during the Remote Agent Experiment.

remote-agent-1999.detail:
Less than 24 hours in, Remote Agent turned on Deep Space 1’s ion engine but failed to turn it off. The cause was a timing error while two parts of its program exchanged information, never seen in about 3,000 ground runs; with 70 percent of objectives met, controllers paused on May 18. “Remote Agent showed us how powerful it is by providing a list of possible reasons for the bug,” said Ames computer scientist Nicola Muscettola, and engineers then asked it to make a new plan and fly solo for six hours on May 21.

Among simulated faults, it replanned around a camera stuck on, reactivated a “failed” electronics unit, which JPL’s Marc Rayman likened to rebooting a frozen PC, recognised that a failed sensor rather than its device was at fault, and switched thruster sets when one stuck off. Pandu Nayak of Ames said onboard planning saved days of ground work; JPL’s Doug Bernard said it would allow missions once judged “too elaborate, too costly or too dependent on teams of Earth-bound controllers.”

salesforce-1999.summary: In March 1999 Marc Benioff founded Salesforce to sell software by subscription in a browser. It delivered customer relationship management software over the internet rather than as programs for customers to install; its first prototype launched in November 1999. Larry Ellison of Oracle and CNET founder Halsey Minor invested early. Its “end of software” campaign, including actors holding signs outside Siebel Systems’ conference, made that model’s name.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Salesforce
'Salesforce's Benioff Aims to Reshape Business Software', New York Times, 13 November 2007
sources.author: New York Times
sources.confirms: Benioff founded Salesforce.com in 1999 to turn software into a service delivered over the internet, starting with customer management.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Salesforce, Inc.'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Salesforce, founded 1999, develops cloud-based customer relationship management software sold by subscription.

salesforce-1999.verification_note: An earlier title called this a “no software” model, which its sources do not support; its title now uses Salesforce’s own tagline.
salesforce-1999.detail: The dot-com crash hit hard and Salesforce laid off 20% of its staff, yet revenue rose from $5.4 million in 2000 to $22.4 million in 2001. Its first Dreamforce conference drew about 1,300 people in 2003; Salesforce listed on the New York Stock Exchange in June 2004 as CRM, raising $110 million, and passed $1 billion in annual revenue in 2009. Fiscal 2026 revenue was $41.5 billion; acquisitions include Tableau and Slack.

saudi-public-internet-filtered-1999.summary: After a 1997 cabinet decision and two years of building, Saudi Arabia lets licensed private ISPs sell public access in early 1999, with all traffic routed through King Abdulaziz City for Science and Technology's Internet Services Unit in Riyadh. A proxy farm running commercial filtering software blocks pornography and sites deemed political or religious threats, and a web form invites citizens to request blocks or unblocks. About forty ISPs are licensed, and subscriptions pass a million within three years. Model of a national chokepoint with published rules, rather than outright refusal, influences Gulf neighbours and anticipates later national-network architectures in Iran. Human Rights Watch reads it as censorship; Saudi officials present it as cultural protection.

sources.author: Al-Tawil, Khalid M.
sources.confirms: KACST gateway architecture, filtering, licensed ISPs, 1999 launch

sources.title: Teitelbaum, J. (2002). Dueling for Da'wa: state vs. society on the Saudi internet. Middle East Journal 56(2), 222-239.
sources.author: Teitelbaum, Joshua
sources.confirms: Politics of filtering and user response

sources.title: Jehl, D. 'The Internet's open sesame is answered warily.' New York Times, 18 March 1999.
sources.author: Jehl, Douglas
sources.confirms: Opening of public access and early user reaction

saudi-public-internet-filtered-1999.verification_note: Launch month differs across sources: Human Rights Watch gives December 1998, Al-Tawil and press give January to February 1999. Record uses January 1999.
saudi-public-internet-filtered-1999.detail: Al-Tawil (Telecommunications Policy 2001), then at KACST, describes architecture and policy from inside; Human Rights Watch's 1999 report covers region-wide controls; New York Times reports on opening in March 1999. Date of public launch is given as December 1998, January or February 1999.

seti-at-home-1999.summary: In May 1999 SETI@home let home computers sift radio telescope data as a screensaver; 5.2 million volunteers logged over two million years of computing time, though no extraterrestrial signal has been shown. Radio telescope data recorded “piggyback” at Arecibo while its dish served other programs were cut into work units of 107 seconds, about 350 kilobytes each, and sent to volunteers’ computers, where free software running as a screensaver or in the background searched for spikes, Gaussian rises and falls, triplets and pulses that could mark artificial signals.

sources.title: SETI@home (Wikipedia)
SETI@home: an experiment in public-resource computing
sources.author: Anderson, David P.; Cobb, Jeff; Korpela, Eric; Lebofsky, Matt; Werthimer, Dan
sources.confirms: Millions of volunteers' computers processed Arecibo radio data for SETI@home, the largest computation then performed.
sources.qualifies: Does not give the May 1999 launch date or the 5.2 million figure.

sources.title: Reichhardt, Tony, 'A million volunteers join the online search for extraterrestrial life', Nature 400 (1999): 804
sources.author: Reichhardt, Tony
sources.confirms: Nature news report of 26 August 1999 that SETI@home, a downloadable screensaver using idle time on home and office computers to look for patterns in radio telescope data, had drawn a million volunteers.

sources.title: Marriott, Michel, 'News Watch; Got a Computer? Help Find E.T.'s Home by Calling From Yours', New York Times, 20 May 1999
sources.author: Marriott, Michel
sources.confirms: Contemporary report that the Berkeley project began offering its software that week in May 1999, that 200,000 copies had been downloaded, and that the program analysed Arecibo data as a screensaver while the computer was idle.

seti-at-home-1999.detail: It was the third large-scale volunteer computing project, after GIMPS in 1996 and distributed.net in 1997, and the one with most participants. Its team had planned on 50,000 to 100,000 home computers. By September 26, 2001 it had performed 10 to the 21st floating-point operations, and Guinness World Records 2008 listed it as the largest computation in history. Since Arecibo lacked broadband, tapes went to Berkeley by post. Users formed teams and competed, and to defeat cheats each work unit went to at least two computers, with credit granted only when results agreed. Original software ran until December 15, 2005, when SETI@home moved to BOINC; in March 2020 it stopped sending new work and entered hibernation to analyze 20 years of data, planning follow-up observations with China’s Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Telescope.

sift-1999.summary: In 1999 David Lowe's SIFT found the same points in an image at any scale or angle; computer vision could match pictures until deep learning. It is a computer vision algorithm that detects, describes and matches local features in images. It picks out points at maxima and minima of a difference-of-Gaussians function applied across image scales, then discards low-contrast and edge points. Each remaining point gets a dominant orientation and a 128-element descriptor vector. Each vector stays stable under translation, scaling and rotation and partly under lighting changes, so objects learned from reference images can be found in new ones.

sources.title: Scale-invariant feature transform
D. G. Lowe, 'Object Recognition from Local Scale-Invariant Features', Proceedings of the International Conference on Computer Vision, Corfu (1999), 1150-1157
sources.author: David G. Lowe
sources.venue: IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision
sources.confirms: Lowe's 1999 ICCV paper introduces the Scale Invariant Feature Transform for matching image features invariant to scale, rotation and viewpoint.

sources.title: Lowe, David G., 'Distinctive Image Features from Scale-Invariant Keypoints', International Journal of Computer Vision 60, no. 2 (2004): 91-110
sources.author: Lowe, David G.
sources.confirms: Lowe's full journal account of the SIFT method first presented at ICCV in 1999, giving the detector, descriptor and matching procedure.

sift-1999.detail: To recognise objects, features from new images are compared with a keypoint database by Euclidean distance. Clusters of three or more matches that agree on location, scale and orientation are found with a hash-table version of the generalised Hough transform, then verified, and the probability of a true match computed; this runs at close to live speed for small databases. Lowe’s mechanism draws on neurons in primate inferior temporal cortex. Applications include robotic mapping and navigation, image stitching, 3D modeling, gesture recognition, video tracking, identifying individual wild animals and match moving. SIFT was patented, and its patent expired in 2020.

thawte-verisign-1999.summary: In December 1999 VeriSign bought Thawte, started in a Cape Town garage four years earlier, for $575 million. Shuttleworth, 26 and sole owner, had started it to build a secure web server free of U.S. limits on exporting cryptography. Both firms had certificates built into early Netscape browsers, so later browsers trusted them too, and each held about half the market for certificates that let browsers verify a site’s identity and encrypt traffic.

VeriSign, Inc., Form 8-K, filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission 6 January 2000
sources.confirms: VeriSign's filing stating that on 19 December 1999 it agreed to acquire Thawte Consulting, all share capital of Thawte Holdings (Pty) Ltd and Thawte USA, in exchange for VeriSign stock with an aggregate market value of $575 million.
sources.qualifies: The filing gives the agreement date; closing followed in February 2000 after South African regulatory approval.

sources.title: Reuters, 'Company News; VeriSign Buying Two in Deals Worth $1.2 Billion', New York Times, 21 December 1999
sources.confirms: Contemporary wire report that VeriSign planned to buy Thawte Consulting, a privately owned South African digital certificate firm, for $575 million in VeriSign shares.

thawte-verisign-1999.detail: Thawte’s server, Sioux, forked Apache and was later folded into Stronghold as Thawte concentrated on certificates. VeriSign’s root certificate was due to roll over on 1 January 2000, an awkward date beside Y2K; owning Thawte, which had rolled over in July 1998, insured against lost business. Business Report described Thawte as the world’s second-largest provider of digital certification and quoted Shuttleworth saying he wanted to turn his focus elsewhere. The proceeds let him become the second space tourist and found Canonical and Ubuntu. Symantec took over VeriSign’s security business, including Thawte, in August 2010, and Thawte passed to DigiCert in 2017.

the-matrix-1999.summary: In 1999 The Matrix imagined humanity farmed inside a machine-run simulation, a lasting image of reality that might be fake. Written and directed by the Wachowskis after their 1996 film Bound, it stars Keanu Reeves as Neo, a hacker who learns that his life is a simulation projected into the minds of humans held in pods by machines, and who joins Laurence Fishburne’s Morpheus and Carrie-Anne Moss’s Trinity in rebellion. Made for about $63 million, it grossed over $460 million, fourth-highest of 1999, and won all four of its Academy Award nominations: visual effects, film editing, sound and sound effects editing.

sources.title: The Matrix
The Matrix | 1999 Film, Cast, Plot, & Facts | Britannica
Constable, Catherine, "Baudrillard reloaded: interrelating philosophy and film via The Matrix Trilogy"
sources.author: Catherine Constable
sources.confirms: Peer-reviewed film-studies analysis of the 1999 film's simulated-reality premise and its use of Baudrillard.

the-matrix-1999.detail: Its fights drew on anime and Hong Kong wire work. Its ideas drew on Plato’s cave, 1990s Telnet hacker communities and William Gibson’s Neuromancer, and Reeves and Moss read Jean Baudrillard’s Simulacra and Simulation before filming. It popularized “the red pill” and “bullet time,” in which action within one shot runs in slow motion while its camera seems to move through it at normal speed; Britannica says Reeves performed his rooftop dodge on a green-screen set ringed by more than 120 still cameras. America’s Library of Congress added it to its National Film Registry in 2012. Two sequels followed in 2003 and a fourth film, Resurrections, in 2021.

tuvalu-tv-domain-1999.summary: Tuvalu, nine atolls with about 10,000 people, was assigned country-code top-level domain .tv in 1996. After a failed 1998 deal with a Canadian firm, government signed in 1999 with Idealab-backed dotTV of Pasadena, receiving 50 million US dollars over ten years plus equity; VeriSign bought dotTV in 2002 and paid Tuvalu roughly 2 to 5 million dollars a year. Conway's Island Studies Journal paper and Baldacchino's volume analyse .tv as entrepreneurship by a microstate with few other exports beyond fishing licences and stamps. Revenue funded Tuvalu's United Nations membership in 2000, roads and electrification. Streaming platform Twitch.tv made its domain far more valuable; a 2021 deal with GoDaddy Registry raised payments.

tuvalu-tv-domain-1999.detail: Stratford, Farbotko and Lazrus examine Tuvalu's sovereignty and climate vulnerability, including dependence on external rents. Critics question association of a devout nation with adult content on .tv sites. Trust fund income, .tv fees and fishing licences together exceed domestic tax revenue. Tuvalu's later Falepili Union with Australia and plan for a digital nation preserving statehood online extend this strategy of turning sovereignty into income.

wifi-1999.summary: In 1999 802.11b, formally published in January 2000, and the Wi-Fi name arrived. That year six companies sponsored WECA, later renamed Wi-Fi Alliance, which holds Wi-Fi’s trademark, under which most 802.11 products sell. Wi-Fi lets nearby devices exchange data by radio in 2.4 and 5 gigahertz bands, so homes and offices link computers to routers without cables. Apple’s adoption of Wi-Fi for its 1999 iBook laptops, branded AirPort, made it a mass consumer product.

sources.title: Wi-Fi

'802.11b-1999 - IEEE Standard for Information Technology - Telecommunications and information exchange between systems - Local and Metropolitan networks - Specific requirements - Part 11: Wireless LAN Medium Access Control (MAC) and Physical Layer (PHY) specifications: Higher Speed Physical Layer (PHY) Extension in the 2.4 GHz band', IEEE Xplore (2000)
sources.confirms: The page identifies 802.11b-1999 as a higher-speed physical-layer extension for wireless LANs operating in the 2.4 GHz band, and says the project aimed to increase data rates for 802.11-compatible networks.

sources.confirms: University-press history of the 802.11 standard and the 1999 formation of WECA, later the Wi-Fi Alliance.

wifi-1999.verification_note: IEEE's 802.11b standard carries a 20 January 2000 publication date; Wi-Fi Alliance says six companies initially sponsored WECA, which later rebranded.
wifi-1999.detail: Interbrand was hired to find a name catchier than its technical label, IEEE 802.11b Direct Sequence. Founding member Phil Belanger says Wi-Fi was picked from ten candidates, partly because it sounds like Hi-Fi, and Interbrand also drew a yin-yang logo marking products certified for interoperability. Whether Wi-Fi stands for “Wireless Fidelity” is disputed, though Wi-Fi Alliance briefly used the slogan “The Standard for Wireless Fidelity.” Apple worked with Vic Hayes, Bruce Tuch, Cees Links and others from Lucent who had helped create 802.11. Wi-Fi Alliance had more than 800 member companies as of 2017, and over 3.05 billion Wi-Fi devices shipped each year as of 2019.

y2k-1999.summary: Through 1999 the world feared programs that stored years as two digits would fail at 2000; fixes cost hundreds of billions and worked. Writing 1985 as 85 meant 2000 could not be told from 1900, a habit from decades when memory cost from $10 to over $100 per kilobyte in 1975 that now threatened computer-reliant industries. Companies estimated repairs at $400 to $600 billion. Survivalist interest hit its second peak that decade, and writers including Gary North, Ed Yourdon, James Howard Kunstler and Ed Yardeni anticipated widespread power outages, food and gasoline shortages, and other emergencies, North because he thought fixes were too slow.

sources.title: Year 2000 problem - Wikipedia
US Senate Special Committee on the Year 2000 Technology Problem, Y2K Aftermath: Crisis Averted, Final Committee Report, S. Prt. 106-42 (29 February 2000)
sources.author: US Senate Special Committee on the Year 2000 Technology Problem (Bennett, Dodd)
sources.confirms: The Senate committee's final report on the two-digit year problem, the remediation effort and the uneventful rollover.

sources.title: 'Y2K bug', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Programs that stored years as two digits were feared to misread 2000 as 1900 and disrupt banking, utilities and government systems; the article covers the remediation effort and its cost.

y2k-1999.detail: Religious figures joined in. Jerry Falwell suggested Y2K would confirm Christian prophecy and, like many survivalists, advised stocking up on food and guns, while some people bought generators and withdrew large sums of cash. In the United States, John Koskinen’s President’s Council on Year 2000 Conversion coordinated remediation with FEMA. Contrary to expectations, few major errors occurred in 2000: Telecom Italia sent bills dated January 1900 and 902 heating systems failed near Seoul, but little worse. IDC estimated U.S. spending at $134 billion before the date and $13 billion fixing problems afterward, and worldwide remediation at $308 billion. President Bill Clinton called Y2K “the first challenge of the 21st century successfully met.” Retrospectives credit programmers, while critics note that countries and sectors that did little also saw minimal problems.

asimo-2000.summary: In October 2000 Honda unveiled ASIMO, a humanoid robot that walked on two legs like a child; it shook hands with presidents for 18 years. Development began in 1999 at Honda's Wako Fundamental Technical Research Center in Japan. Three updated models followed from 2004 to 2011, and Honda retired the line in 2022 to concentrate on remote-controlled robots.

bill-joy-why-future-doesnt-need-us-2000.summary: In 2000 Bill Joy, Sun's chief scientist, warned in Wired that robotics, genetics and nanotech could make humans an endangered species. He warned robotics, genetic engineering, and nanotechnology could threaten humanity, noting robots, engineered organisms, and nanobots can self-replicate. John Seely Brown and Paul Duguid answered that his forecast ignored social factors.

bogota-transmilenio-2000.summary: On 18 December 2000 Bogotá began TransMilenio service under mayor Enrique Peñalosa: articulated buses on segregated median busways along Avenida Caracas and Calle 80, enclosed stations with level boarding and smart-card fares, passing lanes for express services, and private operators paid per kilometre under contract to a public agency. Within sixteen months it carried about 650,000 passengers a day at speeds around 26 kilometres an hour, with capacity later measured above 40,000 passengers per hour per direction, a level previously thought to need rail. Built at a fraction of metro cost, it drew on Curitiba's design and exceeded it in scale. Planners from Mexico City, Guangzhou, Johannesburg and dozens of other cities adopted its model for BRT.

bogota-transmilenio-2000.detail: Sandoval and Hidalgo's ASCE paper documents design and early ridership; Gilbert's Bulletin of Latin American Research article assesses benefits and limits, including crowding and fare levels. Network expansion stalled after 2006 amid political disputes. Peñalosa's administration chose BRT after rejecting a proposed metro as too costly for a city of six million; Phase 1 cost about 240 million dollars for 42 kilometres. Stations in road medians are reached by footbridges, and feeder buses serve peripheral neighbourhoods at no extra fare. Critics note crowding of six to eight passengers per square metre and lack of later network expansion.

brazil-xylella-genome-2000.summary: On 13 July 2000 Nature published a 2,679,305 base-pair genome of Xylella fastidiosa, bacterium behind citrus variegated chlorosis that was damaging São Paulo's orange groves. Its paper, with 116 authors, came from Organization for Nucleotide Sequencing and Analysis, a 'virtual institute' of 34 laboratories that research foundation FAPESP had funded from 1997 to build sequencing capacity rather than concentrate it in one centre. Teams coordinated by Andrew Simpson and João Setubal identified genes for adhesion, toxins and xylem colonisation. No plant pathogen had been fully sequenced before, nor any bacterial genome in Latin America; ONSA went on to sequence sugarcane ESTs, Xanthomonas and Leifsonia, and seeded Brazil's genomics and bioinformatics community.

brazil-xylella-genome-2000.detail: Nature ran an editorial welcoming Brazil's entry into genomics. FAPESP spent about 15 million dollars on the project and trained students in each lab, so sequencing capacity spread across São Paulo state rather than concentrating in one institute. Fundecitrus, a growers' body, co-funded work because chlorosis affected a third of orange trees. Findings on adhesion and bacteriophage-derived genes informed later work on Pierce's disease of grapevines in California.

carnivore-fbi-2000.summary: In 2000 the FBI revealed Carnivore, a system that intercepted suspects' email under court order. It let FBI agents intercept criminal suspects’ email without their knowledge or consent.

concorde-crash-2000.summary: In July 2000 a Concorde crashed on takeoff near Paris after a tyre burst and 113 died. Metal debris from a DC-10 that took off minutes earlier burst one tyre; tyre fragments ruptured a fuel tank and leaking fuel ignited. Every Concorde was grounded; service resumed on 7 November 2001 with Kevlar-lined fuel tanks and burst-resistant tyres, and Air France retired Concorde in May 2003, British Airways in October 2003.

dot-com-crash-2000.summary: On 10 March 2000 the Nasdaq peaked and began a 78 percent fall, wiping out internet firms valued on hopes alone. Late-1990s investors had bid up internet shares at almost any valuation. Technology stocks then fell sharply; by October 2002 Nasdaq had lost 78% from its peak, giving up every bubble-era gain, and online retailers such as Pets.com and Webvan shut down.

folding-at-home-2000.summary: In October 2000 Folding@home began using volunteers' idle PCs to simulate protein folding. Each computer simulates one piece of how proteins fold; misfolded proteins are linked to diseases such as Alzheimer's and cancer. During 2020's COVID-19 pandemic it reached 2.43 exaflops, 2.43 billion billion calculations per second, by April 12, 2020, becoming the world's first exaflop computing system.

gavi-vaccine-alliance-2000.summary: In 2000 Gavi, formed at end of 1999, was launched to buy vaccines for children in poor countries; it reports helping to immunize more than 760 million children and prevent over 13 million deaths. Launched at Davos in January 2000, it succeeded the Children's Vaccine Initiative, with Gates Foundation's initial $750 million commitment helping establish it and drawing other donors.

germany-renewable-energy-act-2000.summary: In 2000 Germany fixed a 20-year price for anyone feeding solar or wind into the grid. It guaranteed renewable generators grid connection, priority dispatch and a government-set payment for each kilowatt hour fed in, varying by technology. Photovoltaic remuneration rose to as much as 51 cents per kilowatt hour, with tariffs designed to fall 5 percent a year. This law drove rapid uptake of solar and wind.

golden-rice-science-2000.summary: On 14 January 2000 Science publishes work by Xudong Ye, Ingo Potrykus at ETH Zurich and Peter Beyer at Freiburg University inserting carotenoid pathway genes into japonica rice so that endosperm, normally white, accumulates provitamin A and turns yellow. Its authors note vitamin A deficiency is a serious public health problem in at least 26 countries. The Rockefeller Foundation funded it; Syngenta's Golden Rice 2 of 2005 raised carotenoid 23-fold. Regulatory approval takes two decades: the Philippines approves commercial propagation in July 2021 and registers it as Malusog 1 in April 2022, but on 17 April 2024 the Court of Appeals grants a Writ of Kalikasan halting propagation; PhilRice petitioned the Supreme Court on 24 October 2024 and Golden Rice remains on hold in late 2026.

Critics questioned beta-carotene levels in its first version and distraction from supplementation and diet diversity. Patents on components were licensed free for farmers earning under 10,000 dollars a year. USDA FAS Manila's November 2026 biotechnology report counts five GE products in four crops approved for propagation in the Philippines.

iloveyou-2000.summary: In May 2000 the ILOVEYOU worm arrived as a love letter and mailed copies to every contact; it infected 45 million PCs in a day. Opening it overwrote files with worm code and mailed copies to every address-book contact. Spread began on 4 May 2000, moving westward through corporate email systems from Hong Kong to Europe and then the United States. Within ten days, tens of millions of infections had been reported; an estimated 10% of internet-connected computers worldwide were eventually affected.

itc-e-choupal-2000.summary: In June 2000 ITC's agribusiness division installs computers with VSAT links in Madhya Pradesh villages, each run by a trained local farmer called a sanchalak who shows soybean growers daily mandi prices, ITC's own buying price and weather, and sells inputs. Farmers can then sell at an ITC hub with transparent weighing rather than through commission agents at distant markets. Kumar's 2004 study in Information Technologies and International Development documents lower transaction costs for both sides. By 2020 government evaluators count about 6,100 kiosks serving over 35,000 villages and four million farmers across seven states and crops from wheat to shrimp. e-Choupal becomes a textbook case of a company building rural internet for procurement.

m-systems-diskonkey-2000.summary: Dov Moran's M-Systems, founded in 1989 to sell flash-based disk emulators for embedded systems, files in 1999 for a patent on an architecture joining NAND flash, a controller and a Universal Serial Bus connector in a keyring-sized package needing no driver on Windows 2000 or Mac OS 9. Granted in November 2000 as US 6,148,354, it underlies DiskOnKey, launched late that year with 8 megabytes at about 50 dollars and sold through IBM. Trek 2000 in Singapore shows a ThumbDrive in early 2000 and later litigates priority; Netac in China holds a parallel Chinese patent. Capacities double yearly, Sony's floppy sales end in 2011 and SanDisk buys M-Systems in 2006 for 1.55 billion dollars.

millennium-development-goals-2000.summary: In 2000 the UN's Millennium Declaration set targets for 2015, including halving extreme poverty, codified in 2001 as eight measurable goals; that poverty target was met early. plos-2000.summary: In 2000 three scientists founded the Public Library of Science to publish research free for anyone to read. It grew from a petition by Harold Varmus, Patrick Brown and Michael Eisen asking scientists to stop submitting to journals that did not make full text freely available; tens of thousands signed but few acted, so Brown and Eisen started their own publisher. Its first journal, PLOS Biology, launched on October 13, 2003.
